- Russo-Ukrainian war, day 1680: Ukraine brings 14 more children home from occupied Kherson
- Russo-Ukrainian war, day 1679: Russia raises its war budget by 27% to a record as it looks to grow its war in 2027

articles.title: Ukraine war briefing: Zelenskyy says new ballistic missile used in combat
articles.body:
- Ukraine used its FP-7 tactical ballistic missile in combat for the first time, Volodymyr Zelenskyy said. Writing on Telegram on Thursday, the Ukrainian president said: “First combat use. Thank you for the result. Next – production.” He did not say where or how the FP-7 had been used. The missile’s manufacturer, Fire Point, says it is being developed as a ballistic interceptor within the European missile defence programme, called Freyja, launched this year. Ukrainian military analysts describe the FP-7 as a short-range missile with a range of about 200km (125 miles), likening it to the US army Tactical Missile System but much cheaper. Ukraine – whose missile production is well behind Russia’s – has viewed development of its own tactical ballistic missiles as an important element of its response to Russia’s frequent use of them in its attacks.
- Russian drones smashed into a school in Kyiv and an important bridge over the Dnipro River on Thursday, triggering fires in the capital, officials said. The school was struck early in the morning, but all the students were in a shelter and no injuries were reported, city authorities said. As Russian forces engaged in almost non-stop attacks on the city, Mayor Vitali Klitschko said two drones hit the Southern Bridge around noon. A new strike late in the evening damaged a support, part of the road surface and protective structures around the metro crossing the bridge. On Wednesday, Russian forces unleashed what Ukrainian officials described as the start of a cold-weather strike campaign against Ukraine’s power grid.
- Meanwhile, Ukraine is pressing on with strikes on Russian oil refineries, defying Donald Trump, who blames the attacks for exacerbating a global diesel shortage and pushing up fuel prices. Kyiv struck an oil facility in Russia’s southern Samara region overnight, Zelenskyy said on Thursday in a statement on social media. He added that a Russian vessel in the Black Sea was hit, as well as a launch and storage site for attack drones in the Oryol region. Ukraine also attacked the Russian city of Volgograd, home to a large oil refinery, with drones targeting industrial facilities, Governor Andrei Bocharov said on Telegram on Friday. Ukraine’s campaign in recent months has knocked out more than 45% of Russia’s refining capacity, according to Ukrainian estimates, prompting fuel rationing in some regions and long queues at petrol stations.
- Europe has become increasingly dependent on US fuel after banning Russian imports because of the war and after the US-Israeli war against Iran disrupted supplies from the Middle East. The Trump administration has told Germany and France to draw down emergency diesel inventories to help ease soaring global fuel prices or face a potential US diesel export ban, according to three people close to the discussions.
- At a Group of 20 meeting this week, trade ministers agreed it was “not acceptable” for countries to target food supplies in conflicts, France’s minister delegate for international trade, Nicolas Forissier said on Thursday, adding that European leaders took aim at Russia on the issue. Forissier’s comments come as trade ministers from the G20 met for a second day in the midwestern US city of Milwaukee, where European officials criticised Russia’s attacks on Ukraine’s grain sector. Forissier said European leaders’ comments against “the aggression of Russia in Ukraine” on food exports merely constituted “the truth”.
- Moscow warned Nato that it would not hesitate to use nuclear weapons to defend Kaliningrad, a Russian exclave and seaport located on the Baltic Sea, should any members of the military alliance try to cut it off. Several Russian embassies in Europe this week issued statements that said Moscow has “information that Nato is preparing [an] air and naval blockade of Kaliningrad and [the] Kaliningrad region”. Asked on Thursday whether Russia was on the cusp of a war with Nato or whether both were trying to intimidate each other, Putin said: “It’s not intimidation, it’s a response to an attempt to intimidate us.”
- Putin said also on Thursday Russian assets of western companies that Moscow had seized could be returned in a “favourable scenario”. Last month, the Russian president ordered the seizure of businesses and assets of Swiss food giant Nestlé, French retailer Auchan, the former Leroy Merlin DIY chain and German wholesaler and food retailer Metro. He also said Russia would prefer to end the conflict in Ukraine through talks and wanted Ukraine to be a neutral country after the end of hostilities.

articles.title: Ukraine war latest: Russia takes aim at key Kyiv bridge for second day
articles.body:
Key developments on Oct. 2:
- Key Kyiv bridge hit by Russian drones fourth time in 2 days
- Ukraine aims to produce up to 400 interceptor drones as Russian jet-powered drone use grows, Zelensky says
- UK sanctions 7 Russians over deportation, indoctrination of Ukrainian children
- Russian Mi-8 helicopter reportedly shot down in friendly-fire incident over Voronezh Oblast
- Russian glide bombs strike Kharkiv, kill women, injure children
- Russia planning to increase "hybrid warfare" activity in Europe, Ukrainian intelligence warns
A Russian drone struck the Southern Bridge over the Dnipro River in Kyiv around 5:40 p.m. local time, as Russia takes aim at the bridge for two days straight.
At the time of the fourth drone strike, the bridge was still closed for traffic from an earlier attack in the morning, said Kyiv Mayor Vitali Klitschko. Black smoke could be seen rising over the bridge, while the damage to the structure is not yet determined.
The Russian attack coincided with Kyiv's evening rush hour, adding further stress to the already congested city. Kyiv's other main bridges across the Dnipro River, the Darnytskyi Bridge, Metro Bridge, and Podilskyi Bridge, have been changed to single direction traffic, according to the Kyiv City Military Administration (KMDA).
Kostiantyn Kryvolap, an aviation expert and former Antonov test engineer, told the Kyiv Independent that destruction of the bridge is most likely not the intent behind Russia's strikes.
"Destroying a bridge with a 50-kilogram explosive charge, even with a highly effective warhead designed to destroy steel bridge structures, is a major exaggeration. It is practically impossible. For a bridge like this, these strikes are more like mosquito bites," he said.
Instead, the idea behind the Russian strikes may rather be to halt traffic, interrupt logistics, and exert psychological pressure on Kyiv's population, according to him.
The Southern Bridge is one of the capital's main traffic arteries and connects important transport routes like the the M-05 Kyiv-Odesa, M-06 Kyiv-Chop, and M-03 Kyiv-Kharkiv-Izyum-Sloviansk highways. Every day, between 100,000 and 110,000 cars use the bridge, according to information from the Darnytskyi District administration from 2019.
Head of the Desnyanskyi district of Kyiv, Maksym Bakhmatov, told The Village in a 2020 interview that about 90% of transit traffic between the two banks passes through the Southern Bridge.
Hlib Vyshlinsky, executive director of the Center for Economic Strategy told the Kyiv Independent that the Southern Bridge is also crucial for the daily commute of the Pozniaky-Osokorky-Kharkivsky districts conglomeration that houses up to 500,000 people.
read also
Ukraine aims to produce up to 400 interceptor drones as Russian jet-powered drone use grows, Zelensky says
Ukraine will be able to produce up to 400 interceptor drones by the end of October to counter Russia's growing use of jet-powered attack drones, President Volodymyr Zelensky said in an interview with the Financial Times published on Oct. 2.
As Russia scales up production of its jet-powered drones — the Geran-4 and Geran-5 — Ukraine is struggling to shoot them down amid the hours-long attacks.
Russia launched around 500 drones against Ukraine over the past day, about half of which were jet-powered and significantly harder to intercept, Zelensky said.
Only 57% of jet-powered versions of Shahed-type drones are currently shot down by Ukraine, Zelensky said in his evening address on Sept. 28, a figure he described as "much less than necessary."
According to Zelensky, Ukraine is testing five types of high-speed interceptor drones designed to counter Russian weapons. One of the models is expected to reach production of around 400 units by the end of October, while the other four remain in the testing stage.
The development of the interceptors is being slowed by a shortage of engines. Ukraine imports most of the engines used for the drones, while domestic production remains insufficient, Zelensky said.
Russia's jet-powered drones target civilian infrastructure such as supermarkets, schools, shopping malls, telecommunications infrastructure, data centers, gas stations, and medical facilities.
Russia has increased its use of jet-powered drones while launching attacks on Kyiv in recent months. The onslaught began last month but has intensified over the past week.
read also
UK sanctions 7 Russians over deportation, indoctrination of Ukrainian children
The U.K. sanctioned seven Russian individuals involved in the forced deportation and re-education of Ukrainian children from occupied territories on Oct. 1, the Ukrainian President's initiative, Bring Kids Back, said on Oct. 2.
Russia is militarizing Ukrainian children and youth in the occupied territories, removing their Ukrainian identity to "raise future soldiers" and involve them in the fight against their own people.
Russia has abducted tens of thousands of Ukrainian children since the start of the full-scale invasion. As of September 2026, Ukraine's Justice Ministry has officially confirmed 20,610 cases of deportation, though Ukrainian officials estimate the real total could number in the hundreds of thousands.
According to Bring Kids Back's press release, the sanctions target Artur Orlov, head of Russia's Movement of the First, a state-backed organization for children and young people, as well as five heads of its regional branches in occupied parts of Donetsk, Luhansk, Kherson, and Zaporizhzhia oblasts and Crimea.
The Movement of the First was established in 2022 at the initiative of Russian President Vladimir Putin and has more than 344,600 members in occupied Ukrainian territories, according to a report from an Organization for Security and Co-operation in Europe (OSCE) expert mission.
The sanctioned officials are Denis Chernobay, Ruyal Aliyev, Aleksey Lavrentyev, Viktoriya Kostromina, and Ekaterina Kozyr.
The list also includes Elena Milskaya, chair of the board of trustees of Russia's National Center for Assistance to Missing and Injured Children. Ukraine's military intelligence agency said Milskaya used the organization's volunteers in October 2022 to facilitate the mass abduction and unlawful deportation of Ukrainian children, including orphans, from occupied territories to Russia's Krasnodar Krai via occupied Crimea.
The sanctioned individuals face asset freezes and travel bans, as well as restrictions on trust services and director disqualification. At least three of the seven — Orlov, Chernobay, and Milskaya — have previously been sanctioned by Canada, while Milskaya has also been sanctioned by the European Union.
The U.K. announced the sanctions on Oct. 1 as part of a wider package targeting 31 individuals over Russia's war against Ukraine. The package also includes eight people accused of involvement in arbitrary detention, torture, and ill-treatment of civilians in Russian-occupied Ukrainian territories, including Kherson and Zaporizhzhia oblasts.
read also
Russian Mi-8 helicopter reportedly shot down in friendly-fire incident over Voronezh Oblast
A Russian Su-35 fighter jet reportedly shot down a Russian Mi-8 military helicopter in a friendly-fire incident in Russia's Voronezh Oblast on Oct. 1, killing all three crew members, according to several Russian and Ukrainian Telegram channels.
The helicopter crashed in the Anninsky district of Voronezh Oblast, around 80 kilometers from the regional capital, while Russian forces were responding to a supposed Ukrainian drone attack, according to reports.
The Ukrainian Telegram channel Exilenova Plus said the Su-35 crew mistakenly identified the Mi-8 as a Ukrainian drone and opened fire. The helicopter's pilot, navigator, and onboard gunner were killed, according to the channel.
Another Ukrainian Telegram channel, Dossier of a Spy, also said that the Mi-8 was mistakenly shot down by a Su-35 during a drone attack.
Russian military blogger Ilya Tumanov, who runs the Fighterbomber Telegram channel, reported the loss of the helicopter without directly identifying the cause.
The reports have not been independently verified, and Russian authorities have not publicly confirmed that the Mi-8 was shot down by the fighter jet.
read also
Russian glide bombs strike Kharkiv, kill women, injure children
At least two people were killed and 36 injured after Russian glide bombs struck two areas of the city of Kharkiv on the afternoon of Oct. 2.
"Three glide bombs were recorded hitting the Slobidskyi and Nemyshlyansky districts of the city," Oleh Syniehubov, head of the Kharkiv Regional State Administration, said in a statement on Telegram.
"Two women aged 66 and 80 died as a result of the strike by the Russian army. 32 people were injured," Syniehubov said.
The State Emergency Service (DSNS) in Kharkiv later raised the number of injured to 36. Three of the injured were children, according to DSNS.
One of the Russian glide bombs "completely destroyed" a residential building, Kharkiv Mayor Ihor Terekhov said in a statement.
read also
Russia planning to increase "hybrid warfare" activity in Europe, Ukrainian intelligence warns
Russia's secret services have been tasked with increasing the number of attacks in Europe, Ukrainian military intelligence (HUR) warned in a statement on Oct. 2.
"The special services of the aggressor state of Russia have been tasked with increasing activity on the territory of the European Union and NATO states — this involves preparing for hybrid operations aimed at undermining aid to Ukraine and weakening the Alliance's capabilities," the statement says.
Acts of Russian "hybrid warfare" have included arson, assassinations, and a recent attempt to blow up Ukrainian Antonov cargo aircraft with modified FPV drones in Leipzig in August. On Sept. 1, Germany formally accused Russia of carrying out the attack.
"To carry out operations, including sabotage operations, the Kremlin plans to involve agents recruited by the General Staff of the Russian Armed Forces (GRU) and the FSB of the Russian Federation in Europe. The Russian special services are targeting military facilities, critical infrastructure, and communication systems," the statement says.
"Among the aggressor's likely targets are Starlink satellite internet receiving stations located in European countries," HUR said.
Starlink, manufactured and operated by Elon Musk's SpaceX, is widely used for communications by the Ukrainian military.
European governments are stepping up preparations for possible Russian hybrid attacks as officials across the continent warn that Moscow could increasingly use drones, missiles, sabotage, and cyberattacks to test NATO countries and pressure them over their support for Ukraine.
"The Ukrainian Defense Ministry's Directorate of Defense warned its partners about the criminal plans of the aggressor state of Russia," the statement says.

articles.title: UK plays the blame game, terror in the skies, Russia’s red lines: RT stories that shaped the week
articles.body:
UK plays the blame game, terror in the skies, Russia’s red lines: RT stories that shaped the week
The terror plot that wasn’t
The arrest of five men at RAF Fairford in the UK on Sunday sparked a terror panic whose consequences are still playing out almost a week later. Shortly after the arrests, British Foreign Secretary Ed Milliband described the incident as an example of “the threats our country faces,” while the British media’s ‘security experts’ pinned the blame on Iran – or in some cases Russia.
The men – all British nationals aged between 21 and 25 – were released on bail on Monday, and no explosives were found in their vehicles. Nevertheless, Prime Minister Andy Burnham announced on Thursday that “we can confirm our belief that we believe Iran to have played a part.”
“Our belief that we believe” is not the most confident assertion, and this was immediately picked up in Tehran. “I can confirm Iran’s belief that releasing supposed terrorists working for foreign states really says it all. You’re barking up the wrong tree,” Iranian Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi wrote on X.
Counterterror police arrested a British-Iranian dual national in connection with the supposed plot on Thursday, but it’s still unclear whether he’ll be charged.
Russia reveals its red lines
It is unsurprising that the British media immediately used the incident to escalate tensions with Iran and Russia. After days of intensifying war rhetoric from Ukraine’s British and European backers – which RT is tracking in our ‘Escalation Watch’ special – Russia definitively restated its red lines this week.
In a statement released by three of its embassies on Wednesday, the Russian Foreign Ministry said that Moscow “would be ready to use all its arsenal, including nuclear weapons, to defend its territory if NATO countries try to isolate Kaliningrad region from the rest of the country.”
⚡️ Statement by the Embassy of Russia in Ireland (September 29, 2026)
There has been an abundance of talk, recently, from the European political circles that Russia somehow is planning to launch a military invasion of Europe, escalate its alleged hybrid campaign against… pic.twitter.com/eQsrIUFwmL
— Russia in Ireland (@Rus_Emb_Ireland) September 30, 2026
NATO has carried out several military exercises near Kaliningrad this year, and Polish Foreign Minister Radoslaw Sikorski recently called on the bloc’s military chiefs to surge troops to the Kaliningrad border so that Moscow would be “uncertain of what we will do.”
However, Moscow’s statement – the second of its kind this week – was intended to “remind those hotheads in Europe” of Russia’s long-established conditions for the use of nuclear weapons, Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov explained on Wednesday. In his speech at the Valdai Discussion Club’s annual forum on Thursday, Russian President Vladimir Putin reiterated that any military action against Kaliningrad would “inevitably” trigger nuclear retaliation.
Western “hotheads,” however, would do well to consider that NATO’s Article 5 – the bloc’s mutual-defense clause – isn’t as clear-cut as it’s sometimes portrayed. As Russian International Affairs Council President Dmitry Trenin wrote for RT this week, it’s “deliberately ambiguous,” heavily mythologized, and doesn’t guarantee US intervention.
Meanwhile, Russia has continued to intensify its strikes on Ukrainian military and dual-use targets, hitting data centers and logistics hubs in Kiev, and ports and warehouses on Ukraine’s Black Sea coast.
Speaking at Valdai, Putin ruled out any kind of ‘energy ceasefire’. With Ukraine striking Russian refineries and sanctions impairing Russia’s ability to export oil, the idea that Moscow “is supposed to stop hitting things that are important to their economy” is “absurd,” the Russian president stated.
The FlyDubai emergency
Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu’s warnings of an imminent attack against the Jewish state were almost realized on Wednesday, when the first officer of a FlyDubai Boeing 737 en route to Tel Aviv allegedly stabbed his captain and attempted to crash the airliner.
Little is known about the incident beyond what the Israeli government and media has shared, but it appears that a group of passengers overpowered the first officer and pulled the jet out of its dive, before two pilots on board took control and landed in Tabuk, in northern Saudi Arabia.
The pilot, Captain Smit Machchhar, has become a national hero in his native India, while the passengers who reportedly stormed the cockpit were lauded by Netanyahu upon arrival in Tel Aviv. Netanyahu has claimed that the first officer had acted based on “Islamist radical indoctrination,” while his government considers the incident an attempted “terrorist attack.”
Although Netanyahu’s ministers have already used the incident to justify – in the words of National Security Minister Itamar Ben Gvir – taking their war against “Iran, Lebanon, Gaza and Judea and Samaria [the West Bank]... to the next level”, the unanswered questions are piling up, as Middle East analyst Farhad Ibragimov wrote for RT.
Lavrov shuts down the propaganda
Another unanswered question: what exactly do Western leaders mean when they accuse Russia of waging “hybrid war?” The accusation, typically leveled at Russia after drone sightings, fires and accidents at weapons factories, and even natural disasters, is almost never substantiated, yet serves to justify the West’s rearmament and escalating war rhetoric against Moscow.
Russian Foreign Minister Sergey Lavrov refused to play into the narrative when he was questioned by the BBC’s Steve Rosenberg on Tuesday. The British state journalist asked Lavrov if he would admit “that Russia is waging a covert hybrid war against European countries,” but Lavrov flipped the questioning.
“Are you referring to when we destroy the drones and missiles that Britain and continental Europe supply to Ukraine, which are then fired at us?” the Russian foreign minister retorted. “Is that what you mean by hybrid war?”
Rosenberg wasn’t the only Western antagonist humiliated this week. On Tuesday, German Chancellor Friedrich Merz suffered the indignity of having to stand beside Kazakh President Kassym-Jomart Tokayev in Berlin, as Tokayev described Putin as “an outstanding statesman” possessing “the qualities that are most essential for the leader of a great country.”
Merz, fresh from his party’s back-to-back election losses last month, then traveled to Munster on Thursday, where NATO had inexplicably been awarded the ‘Westphalian Peace Prize’. After NATO Secretary-General Mark Rutte accepted the award, he and Merz were met with boos, whistles, and chants of “murderers” and “blood on your hands” when they stepped outside to greet the public.
Russia expands its Arctic footprint
Finally, while it’s easy to assume that the world’s great powers have traversed, mapped, and tamed every inch of the Earth’s surface, that’s not the case, and new milestones are still being reached. On Tuesday, the Russian Navy’s Northern Fleet announced that it had traversed the iceberg-filled Shokalsky Strait for the first time in history.
The strait runs between October Revolution Island and Bolshevik Island in the Severnaya Zemlya archipelago, deep inside the Arctic Circle along the strategically important Northern Sea Route.
The Russian Navy group, consisting of the ice-class patrol ship Ivan Papanin, the large landing ship Kondopoga, the salvage tug Pamir, and the naval tanker Sergey Osipov, successfully passed from the Laptev Sea into the Kara Sea, after repeatedly changing course and speed at short notice to avoid icebergs in the treacherous strait.
Russia is invested in the development of the Northern Sea Route, which is the shortest maritime passage between the Asia-Pacific region and northern Europe. Moscow has also renovated some of its Soviet-era military bases along its northern coast, and stepped up military exercises in the Arctic. As the Northern Fleet passed through the Shokalsky Strait this week, its reconnaissance teams practiced amphibious assault maneuvers on the western side of October Revolution Island.

articles.title: US to send third aircraft carrier towards Iran: US official to Al Jazeera
articles.body:
US to send third aircraft carrier towards Iran: US official to Al Jazeera
Massive US military deployment in the Middle East includes 50,000 troops, F-35s and Marines to pressure Tehran.
The United States is deploying a third US aircraft carrier to the waters around Iran, a US official told Al Jazeera, as the war enters its eighth month and both sides weigh escalation and diplomatic engagement.
The official told Al Jazeera that the USS Theodore Roosevelt carrier strike group left its San Diego base on Sunday, bound for the region, followed a day later by the Makin Island Marine Expeditionary Force, carrying more than 2,000 Marines.
By the end of November, the official said, three aircraft carriers and two amphibious landing groups will be positioned around Iran.
The official said the concentration of force would hand President Donald Trump a wider menu of options if he decides to act.
Al Jazeera’s Tanya Noury, reporting from Washington, said the new deployment includes thousands of troops and extra air power, including F-35 fighter jets, layered on top of the roughly 50,000 US service members already stationed in the region.
The goal, Noury said, citing sources inside the Pentagon and White House, is to keep military options “on the table” for Trump regardless of how diplomacy unfolds, with the Pentagon not planning to withdraw any assets even if an agreement with Iran is reached. Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth has said forces are “ready to go” should Trump order new strikes.
Trump himself has kept the threat alive in public. He told Fox News he believes the US is “going to win the war” with Iran “very soon”, while suggesting in other remarks that a return to military action “is possible” but something he would rather not spell out before November’s midterm elections.
Washington has paired the show of force with new economic pressure, sanctioning Iran’s rail and automotive conglomerates this week, as the Treasury Department called the new measures an effort to drain what remains of Tehran’s revenue.
Diplomatic track
Parallel to the military build-up, Iran has pushed a seven-day roadmap, conveyed through Qatar, that would see it reopen the Strait of Hormuz and resume nuclear talks in exchange for an end to the US naval blockade, sanctions relief and a regional ceasefire covering Lebanon and Yemen.
The plan was then rejected by Trump.
US Ambassador to the UN Mike Waltz told NBC the plan’s demand for frozen funds and sanctions relief was non-negotiable, noting “these aren’t just the United States’ sanctions … these are global sanctions”, and pointing to seven UN Security Council resolutions against an Iranian nuclear weapons programme.
Iran’s response, in the meantime, has been similarly two-pronged.
Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi told NBC that Tehran was “fully prepared” to resume the war, before writing on X that “we did not come to New York to sell a war. We came to forge peace.”
Analysts say the mixed signals are deliberate.
Abas Aslani of the Center for Middle East Strategic Studies said the dispute has shifted from whether to negotiate to “who is going to abandon the primary leverage first”, while former US ambassador Richard Schmierer said Trump is caught between delaying past the midterms and the political cost of offering concessions that mirror a June deal he was already criticised for.
Nearly 70 percent of Americans now say the war has not been worth fighting, according to a new AP-NORC poll, with Trump brushing off the slide in his approval ratings by insisting “the pollsters are corrupt”.

articles.title: IN BRIEF: Putin speaks on Russia’s economic sustainability, Europe’s aggression
articles.body:
MOSCOW, October 2. /TASS/. Despite the existing problems, Russia continues to develop, and its economy remains healthy and sustainable, Russian President Vladimir Putin told the plenary session of the 23rd Valdai International Discussion Club.
He also said that Russia’s offensive in the special military operation zone is gaining momentum, and that Europe’s aggressive attitude towards Russia is aimed at diverting attention from domestic economic failures.
Below are the Russian leader’s key remarks.
Russia’s sustainability and way to future
Russia is ready to forge its path to the future with realistic assessment of risks, opportunities and necessary goals, "and, of course, it is ready to engage in such efforts jointly with other countries and peoples."
"We do have some difficulties, but we are resolving them. Macroeconomic indices show that our economy is healthy, and that our financial system and economic institutions are working in a sustainable manner."
Russia’s economy has certain problems and issues that need to be solved, but "who does not?" "Look at any other region of the world. Everyone has its own problems."
Russia had inflation problems: "We jump-started the economy, we overheated it. And we made a deliberate choice to cool it down. We did it deliberately, being perfectly aware that if the Central Bank raises the key rate, investment will decline. It was obvious to everyone, and it did lead to such consequences. What matters now is to make sure that we don’t overcool the economy."
This year, inflation nearly halved compared to 2025. "This year’s budget deficit is around three percent. I’m sure that next year it will be two."
Situation in special operation zone
The situation in the special operation zone is gaining momentum, with over 1,300 square kilometers of territory taken under Russia’s control in September alone. "This is 2.5 times higher than in the previous months."
The government of Ukraine and the European Union claim they will be able to hold the remaining 11% of Donbass’s territory over the next year and a half or two. "We believe that it will happen way sooner, given the pace of our advance, which, as I have just mentioned, is accelerating."
For Russia, the situation around Ukraine is not a question of land, it’s a question of people. "It’s not about a piece of territory, it’s about people. The point is that we need to create conditions not for a temporary truce, but for a lasting peace. And we need security guarantees for that."
It is necessary to strive for peace agreements on Ukraine: "If they [Western countries and Ukraine] agree to terms that Russia also finds acceptable, it will be better to put an end to these sad events and avoid additional casualties on both sides."
Russia is ready to launch and complete negotiations on Ukraine as promptly as possible, but, "naturally, on conditions that the Russian Federation and its people find acceptable."
"However, it appears that the other side simply does not want to end the hostilities."
Russia’s response
Kiev troops started to strike Russian cargo ships in the Black Sea, and Russia had to respond: "Well, we gave our answer. And now they are asking us to stop via all channels. But they [the Kiev government] were the ones to start this."
"They started attacking our refineries, openly declaring that their objective is to harm our economy. They attained their goal to a certain extent because, according to our estimates, we lost about 1% of our GDP. They deliberately started striking civilian targets. Well, they got a tit-for-tat response."
The Russian armed forces started delivering strikes on sites that are crucial for the Ukrainian economy: "Now, by their own admission, they effectively have no metallurgical industry left."
Europe’s aggression
At this point Europe’s leading countries "are much more hostile towards Russia than the United States."
While the United States "is seeking to end the conflict," many European countries, "have now perhaps become the ‘instigators’ of aggressive attitude toward Russia, creating additional crises between Russia and Europe." They are "driven by the unfavorable situation in their own economies, and, consequently, by the unfavorable situation for the ruling elites, combined with shifting political moods."
European politicians want "to justify the need of preparations for war, and to mobilize as many supporters around themselves as possible in order to remain in power." "The logic is very simple, and I’m sure that this constitutes a significant portion of the reasoning behind Europe’s behavior towards the Russian Federation."
"We are not threatening anyone, and we have no intention of attacking anyone, neither in 2029, nor in 2030, nor in 2050. However, if we face aggression, we will be forced to respond. European citizens should clearly understand this and distinguish between our position and the stance taken by certain political leaders in their countries."
The continuous stoking of rhetoric by many European countries is driven by the serious worsening of their domestic economic and political situation. "Look at what is happening in the economy, look what is happening in the social sphere and the quality of life in major European countries. In this situation, they have to shift the focus of their citizens’ attention from domestic issues to outside problems."
"We have no preconditions for resuming and restoring relations with Europe in general or with particular countries."
EU countries "will collapse on their own" because they continue to make mistakes that negatively impact their own economies. "But this is none of our business. We are not interfering."
Weapons as competitive advantage
Russia understands that in case of a direct attack by NATO, it will have to face "an adversary more than twice our size in terms of numbers." "They have huge economic potential, huge military potential. Indeed, our forces and assets would not be that extensive to counter such a threat. And we will have to use our competitive advantages in this struggle."
One of Russia’s main competitive advantages are its strike capabilities. "Yes, of course, France and the United Kingdom are nuclear powers. We understand that, and we are fully aware of that. However, no one else possesses the strike capabilities that Russia has today. And this is our competitive advantage."
"We are not threatening anyone. We simply make it clear that our tools to defend ourselves are not that numerous."
Russia has advanced new weapons systems: "We have new, modern capabilities, including entirely new missile defense penetration systems, advanced medium-range weapons, and state-of-the-art systems that other nations do not possess yet."
"All nuclear powers are highly technologically advanced countries. They will have it at some point in the future. But now they don’t, only we do."
While building new facilities, Russia is taking modern methods of warfare into account: "I assure you, we are currently considering this, and, when we build new enterprises in this sector, we are taking modern methods of warfare into account and do everything possible to ensure they are located in the safest areas possible." "Construction is under way."
Relations with US
Factors marring and damaging Russia-US relations have developed over decades: "We would very much like to see these divisive factors to become a thing of the past, allowing new prospects for mutually beneficial cooperation to emerge."
Russia has proposed and continues to propose to the United States to resume dialogue on strategic arms limitations: "We don not mind resuming this dialogue; we have never been against it. We have offered it, and we are offering it now. There is no answer. Well, if there is no answer, then so be it."
It was Washington that withdrew from agreements curbing the arms race and the proliferation of nuclear weapons: "We were not the ones to walk out of these treaties. The United States did it, under this or that pretext."
"I have quite good, long-standing relations with President (of the US Donald - TASS) Trump. I’m thankful for his efforts to resolve the Ukrainian crisis, and, as I’ve said many times, he is doing it in good faith. And I’m thankful for that, too."
Partnership with China
Putin and Chinese President Xi Jinping understand each other without words or interpreters: "You know, what is interesting. It only took one word from him or me, and without interpreters - and without knowing each other's languages - we understood each other instantly."
China never seeks to resolve emerging problems and issues through pressure or military force. This is alien to its philosophy, which is fundamentally rooted in pursuing solutions through peaceful means. For its part, Russia recognizes Beijing's approach, shares this perspective, and notes the strong outcomes generated by the joint efforts of Moscow and Beijing.
"Can China play any role [in promoting peace] at this point? Of course it can. And, first of all, this stems from its growing economic and military potential, from its readiness to expand the zone of free cooperation, and this is what Chinese President Xi Jinping’s initiative ‘One belt, One Road’ is aimed at."
"Together with China, we are developing this initiative, aligning it with Russia's respective projects, including the Greater Eurasian Partnership. We are working jointly, and this is yielding strong, positive results."
Moscow and Beijing will undoubtedly establish a joint framework to actively utilize the Northern Sea Route (NSR) to serve the interests of Russia and China.
Indian premier and peace initiatives
The diversity and unity of Indian culture are highly admirable: "There is something about Indian culture that possesses such uniqueness - a distinctiveness and unity at the same time - that it undoubtedly serves as an exemplary model. This, of course, deserves to be an example."
At every meeting, Indian Prime Minister Narendra Modi raises the question of resolving the conflict in Ukraine: "He comes up with very good ideas, aimed at searching for mutually acceptable - specifically mutually acceptable - solutions."
The head of the Indian government has a neutral stance, which is nevertheless aimed at bringing the conflict to an end: "By the way, we are grateful to the Indian premier for his desire to resolve this conflict peacefully, and as quickly as possible."
Multipolarity and BRICS
The world should be multipolar; it cannot be bipolar: "It should take into account the interests of all participants of international relations. And, as we have said many times, there is the cornerstone, basic principle: the security of one nation cannot be achieved at the expense of the security of others. This is one of the cornerstones that we believe should form the foundation of the future world order."
"We cannot say exactly how this world will look like. <...> But we need to strive to jointly determine <…> the pillars of the future world order. And this needs to be done without any preconditions."
"An organization such as BRICS may certainly become the prototype for building the future world order."
At this point, BRICS represents nearly half of the planet’s entire population, and its share in the global economy is constantly growing. "This is happening every year, and we can see it in the statistics. And, most importantly, the principles of BRICS' formation and functioning stipulate that everyone is equal. There is no domination of any kind there, and this is what makes it so attractive."
So far, it is hard to say what role BRICS will play in the new architecture of international relations, but it can already be said with certainty that it is "a useful mechanism."

articles.title: How Iran surprised the world?
articles.body:
How Iran surprised the world?
Putin says the whole world is amazed by Iran's courage and resilience
TEHRAN - Russian President Vladimir Putin is not alone in saying that Iran’s resilience in the war with the United States and Israel has surprised the world. From a former head of Britain’s MI6 to senior American analysts, politicians and major international think tanks, a recurring assessment has emerged during the conflict: Iran proved considerably more resilient than many in Washington and Tel Aviv had anticipated.
“The whole world is closely following what is happening and is amazed at the courage and heroism of the Iranian nation and its resilience,” Putin said Thursday at the plenary session of the 23rd annual meeting of the Valdai Discussion Club in Moscow.
The Russian president also pointed to what he described as a deep pool of experienced personnel within Iran’s administration, armed forces and Islamic Revolution Guards Corps, including people prepared to sacrifice themselves for their country. He said Moscow hoped the Strait of Hormuz would reopen and that what he called illegal sanctions against Iran would be lifted.
Putin’s assessment echoes observations made by a number of Western and international figures since the war began.
‘More resilient than anyone would have expected’
Perhaps the most striking assessment came from Sir Alex Younger, the former head of Britain’s Secret Intelligence Service, or MI6.
Speaking to The Economist in March, Younger said: “The reality is the US underestimated the task.” He added: “In practice, the Iranian regime has been more resilient than I think anyone would have expected.”
Younger attributed part of Iran’s resilience to decisions made before the war to disperse military capabilities and delegate authority for the use of weapons, making it harder for an intensive air campaign to paralyze the country.
He also said Iran had understood the importance of the energy dimension of the conflict and had used the threat to the Strait of Hormuz to “globalize” the war. His conclusion was striking: Iran had “played a weak hand pretty well.”
That assessment was subsequently highlighted by The Guardian, which reported that Younger believed the United States had lost the strategic initiative to Iran. 
 
‘The Iranians have consistently surprised us’
The surprise was not confined to Britain.
Dennis Ross, a veteran US diplomat and former Middle East peace negotiator, made an unusually direct assessment in a Reuters report in September.
“The Iranians have consistently surprised us in terms of their resiliency,” Ross said, arguing that economic and military pressure alone might not force Tehran to retreat.
Ross’s observation came as Washington was attempting to use economic pressure and a naval blockade to force Tehran to alter its position over the Strait of Hormuz. Reuters reported that Iranian leaders appeared prepared to absorb considerable economic pain rather than simply concede under pressure.
The significance of the comment lies in its source: Ross was not describing Iran from Tehran, but from the perspective of a former senior American negotiator who has spent decades dealing with Middle Eastern security and diplomacy.
An Israeli and American miscalculation
The argument that Iran’s resilience was underestimated has also appeared in major international think tanks.
Mohsen Milani, professor of politics at the University of South Florida, wrote for Chatham House that Washington and Tel Aviv correctly assessed some of Iran’s vulnerabilities but “underestimated the resilience of the Iranian state, the cohesion of its elites and institutions and the nationalist surge a foreign attack would unleash.”
According to Milani, the United States and Israel mistook Iran’s regional setbacks and domestic discontent for signs that the state itself was approaching strategic collapse.
Instead, he wrote, Iran “fought with resilience, regionalized the war, [and] weaponized the Strait of Hormuz,” demonstrating that geography could compensate, at least in part, for military weakness.
This distinction is important. The argument is not that Iran avoided severe losses. It is that the damage inflicted by the United States and Israel did not produce the political and strategic effects that some planners had anticipated.
Even Israel’s assessments pointed to unexpected endurance
A March report by The Washington Post, based on a US State Department cable, offered another revealing indication.
According to the cable, Israeli officials privately assessed that Iran was “not cracking” and was willing to “fight to the end” despite the killing of its supreme leader and the continuing US-Israeli bombing campaign.
The report also quoted Suzanne Maloney, an Iran expert at the Brookings Institution, as saying she was surprised that Israeli officials had underestimated the regime’s resilience.
“That really badly informed assumption is interesting given how impressive Israeli intelligence penetration of Iran has been,” Maloney said, arguing that the miscalculation lay at the root of the strategic problems Washington and Tel Aviv encountered.
What surprised the outside world?
The sources point to several distinct dimensions of Iran’s resilience.
1. The political system did not collapse
One of the central assumptions surrounding the opening phase of the war was that the elimination of senior political and military figures could trigger a rapid breakdown of the Iranian state.
That did not happen. Even the Washington Post report based on the US diplomatic cable described the Iran’s state as still holding power and willing to continue fighting.
Putin’s reference to a “deep bench” of experienced officials and commanders points to the same phenomenon from another perspective: the survival of institutional capacity despite the loss of senior figures.
2. Iran retained the ability to respond
The second surprise was military endurance.
The United States and Israel possessed overwhelming advantages in airpower and precision strike capabilities. Yet Iran retained the ability to launch missiles and drones and to continue imposing costs on its adversaries.
Former MI6 chief Younger specifically linked this resilience to the dispersal of military capabilities and the delegation of launch authority before the war.
Senator Dave McCormick, a member of the US Senate Foreign Relations Committee, also acknowledged that Iran had shown “resilience” and said he was surprised by the scale of its missile inventory and accumulated military capabilities.
3. Hormuz became a strategic lever
Perhaps no aspect of the conflict attracted more international attention than the Strait of Hormuz.
Iran could not match the United States ship-for-ship or aircraft-for-aircraft. Instead, it used geography to create a strategic problem that military superiority alone could not easily solve.
The International Institute for Strategic Studies noted that Iran’s ability to disrupt maritime traffic in the strait “defied expectations.”
Milani similarly described Hormuz as the central strategic lever through which Iran regionalized and globalized the conflict.
The consequence was that a war against Iran rapidly became an international energy and shipping crisis.
4. Iran imposed costs beyond the battlefield
Iran’s strategy did not depend solely on surviving air strikes.
The conflict increasingly involved energy infrastructure, shipping routes and the economies of Gulf states. This created a second front in which Iran could exploit geography and asymmetric capabilities.
Younger said Iran had understood the significance of the “energy war” and used the threat to the strait to globalize the conflict.
5. The expected short war became a prolonged confrontation
The ability of Iran to continue resisting also changed the time horizon of the conflict.
Instead of a rapid campaign producing political capitulation, the war evolved into a prolonged confrontation involving military strikes, economic pressure, maritime restrictions and repeated diplomatic efforts.
By September, Reuters was reporting that US economic pressure was imposing severe costs on Iran, but also quoting analysts who believed Tehran might continue enduring those costs rather than concede.
6. National cohesion proved stronger than expected
Another important factor was the reaction of Iranian society to the foreign attack.
Milani argues that the assault generated a nationalist response that strengthened the state’s ability to endure the war. Chatham House likewise identifies the “nationalist surge” unleashed by the attack as one of the factors Washington and Tel Aviv underestimated.
This does not mean that Iranian society was politically uniform. Rather, the evidence suggests that opposition to the government did not automatically translate into support for externally imposed regime change.
7. The conflict exposed the limits of military superiority
The broader lesson identified by several analysts is that overwhelming military superiority does not automatically translate into political success.
The IISS analysis emphasized that Iran had taken severe losses but had deliberately chosen to impose costs on its opponents and on the wider regional economy.
Milani went further, arguing that the war could mark a challenge to the foundations of the US-led security order in the Persian Gulf.
The result is a paradox: Iran suffered military and economic damage, yet the campaign did not produce the rapid strategic collapse that aggressors had anticipated.
A war that changed the calculation
Taken together, these assessments suggest that the most significant surprise has been the gap between the scale of the damage inflicted and the political and strategic outcome that some expected it to produce.
From the former head of MI6 saying Iran was “more resilient than I think anyone would have expected,” to former US negotiator Dennis Ross saying the Iranians have “consistently surprised us,” the recurring theme is clear: Iran proved capable of absorbing an extraordinary level of military pressure, preserving its governing structures, maintaining the capacity to retaliate and using the geography of the Persian Gulf to turn a military confrontation into a much wider strategic and economic crisis.
All of this demonstrates that Trump’s notion and expectation of the Islamic Republic of Iran’s capitulation are nothing more than a fantasy; even if the conflict escalates in the future, this American dream will not come to pass. As Iranian Foreign Minister Seyed Abbas Araghchi recently stated in an interview, Iran is "fully prepared" for war—even if it proves to be an "apocalyptic war."
It is now up to US: withdraw from the quagmire of war or brace for even greater costs and losses.

articles.title: Russian Strike on European Arms Factory Would Trigger Article 5, EU Defense Chief Tells TVP World
articles.body:
A Russian strike on a weapons factory in a European NATO country would trigger the alliance’s mutual defense clause, EU Defence Commissioner Andrius Kubilius told TVP World on Thursday.
His comments came a day after Russian Foreign Ministry spokeswoman Maria Zakharova warned that European factories producing weapons for Ukraine were “potential military targets for Russia.” Her words raised concerns about the prospect of a direct confrontation between Moscow and NATO.
JOIN US ON TELEGRAM
Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official.
Speaking to TVP World on the sidelines of a meeting of the European Parliament’s Security and Defence Committee in Brussels, Kubilius said: “I would say if Russia will hit our factories in European territory, that would be Article 5.”
Article 5 treats an armed attack against one NATO member as an attack against all, requiring allies to come to the assistance of the country targeted.
“If Russia were to hit our factories, I would say that would be Article 5,” said EU Defense Commissioner Andrius Kubilius [@KubiliusA], speaking exclusively to TVP World. 
His comment was in response to Russian claims that European factories could be considered legitimate… pic.twitter.com/rqxBp6L48Y
— TVP World (@TVPWorld_com) October 1, 2026
Putin issues nuclear warning over Kaliningrad
Tensions along NATO’s eastern flank have risen amid suspected Russian-linked sabotage and cyberattacks across Europe, as well as a series of Russian missile and drone strikes close to the alliance’s borders.
The incidents have fueled fears that the war in Ukraine could spill over into NATO territory.
Russian President Vladimir Putin added to those concerns on Thursday by warning that Moscow could resort to its entire arsenal, including nuclear weapons, if Kaliningrad, Russia’s heavily militarized exclave bordering NATO members Poland and Lithuania, came under direct attack.
Russia Turns Its Drone War on Kyiv’s Dnipro Bridges – Why Now?
“This is inevitable,” Putin said.
No Western official has indicated there are any plans to attack Kaliningrad.
                                                                                                                                                                         Poland shares 210-kilometer land border with Russia's Kaliningrad region. Paulius Peleckis/Getty Images.                              
‘Familiar intimidation tactic’
Philippe Dickinson, deputy director of the Transatlantic Security Initiative at the US-based Atlantic Council think tank, told TVP World that Putin’s remarks were consistent with Moscow’s previous use of nuclear threats.
“It’s a very familiar intimidation tactic. It is not at all outside of the usual Vladimir Putin playbook,” Dickinson said.
He said NATO should remain “calm,” “united” and “focused” rather than allow Moscow’s nuclear rhetoric to alter the alliance’s course.
Dickinson also backed drawing clear red lines over any attacks on NATO territory.
He said, however, that any decision to invoke Article 5 rested with NATO members, rather than the European Union.
“I’m glad that Commissioner Kubilius has done so, but... we need to note that he’s an EU commissioner. This is a NATO decision,” Dickinson said. “These are different bodies, and it’s for NATO member states to make that determination.”
He added that despite Russia’s escalating rhetoric and actions, he did not believe Moscow wanted a direct Article 5 confrontation with NATO.
Russia ‘not capable’ of NATO invasion
Lieutenant General Piotr Błazeusz, Poland’s military representative to the NATO and EU military committees, said on Thursday that Russia currently lacked the military capacity to invade a NATO country.
“Russia, for the moment thanks to the Ukrainian side, is not able to start any invasion on [a] NATO country. They are just not capable,” Błazeusz said.
He warned, however, that Moscow could continue to challenge NATO through hybrid operations designed to remain “below the threshold of war.”

articles.title: ‘No Rules Now’: Putin Orders Civilian Attacks, Zelensky Says
articles.body:
Russian President Vladimir Putin ordered his military commanders to abandon previous constraints on aerial attacks and intensify strikes on civilian sites, President Volodymyr Zelensky told the Financial Times in an interview published Friday, Oct. 2.
Zelensky cited intelligence obtained by Ukrainian agencies, including what the FT described as intercepted communications between Kremlin officials. Kyiv has not publicly released the intercepts, and their contents could not be independently verified.
JOIN US ON TELEGRAM
Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official.
“He said there are no rules now,” Zelensky said, referring to the alleged order from Putin.
According to Zelensky, the instruction was issued in September, as Russia intensified attacks on Kyiv and increasingly struck schools, hospitals, telecommunications facilities and data centers.
Zelensky speaks from school bomb shelter
Zelensky spoke to the FT inside the bomb shelter of a Kyiv school struck by a Russian jet-powered drone on Thursday.
The school’s director said 104 students and 60 teachers survived because they reached the underground shelter before the drone hit shortly after 9 a.m.
The drone’s 50-kilogram (110-pound) warhead pierced the floor but failed to detonate, Ukrainian authorities said. The impact nevertheless damaged the building and started a fire.
Zelensky later called attacks on educational institutions “a deliberate tactic”, saying Russia was attempting to terrorize civilians and disrupt ordinary life.
Kyiv Grinds to a Halt as Russian Strikes Shut Bridges, Force People to Walk
The FT said debris recovered at the school bore markings from Russian manufacturers and handwritten Russian text. Some components were reportedly manufactured in Russia on July 28, while others appeared to be Western-made.
Russia has denied deliberately attacking civilian sites. Kremlin spokesperson Dmitry Peskov told the FT that Russian forces do not strike schools or hospitals.
However, Ukraine’s Education Ministry has recorded more than 4,700 attacks on educational institutions since the beginning of Russia’s full-scale invasion. The World Health Organization has verified more than 3,000 attacks affecting healthcare facilities.
Deliberately attacking civilians or civilian objects constitutes a war crime under international humanitarian law.
Russia seeks to pressure civilians
Zelensky said Russia had previously concentrated much of its long-range campaign on military and energy infrastructure, although civilian sites have been repeatedly struck throughout the full-scale invasion.
He alleged that Moscow had now deliberately expanded its target list because Russian forces had failed to achieve their objectives on the battlefield, particularly in the Donbas.
The new campaign seeks “to pressure people,” Zelensky said, describing the strikes as an attempt to frighten civilians, force residents to leave Ukrainian cities and weaken the country’s ability to continue resisting Russia.
On Monday, a Russian drone struck Ukraine’s National Academy of Sciences in central Kyiv. Russia also repeatedly attacked the Pivdennyi Bridge in Kyiv on Thursday, damaging a support column, the road surface and a barrier and disrupting transport across the Dnipro.
Recent Russian strikes have also damaged Ukrainian schools, healthcare facilities, warehouses, businesses and communications infrastructure. A Sept. 23 attack damaged Kyiv data centers, disrupting internet service for some residents.
Jet-powered drones strain Ukrainian defenses
Zelensky said Russia had launched around 500 drones over the previous day, approximately half of them jet-powered models that fly considerably faster than conventional Shahed-type drones.
Ukraine intercepted around 57% of the jet-powered drones, compared with between 85% and 90% of conventional models, he said.
Russia’s use of jet-powered drones increased eightfold between June and August, according to figures previously released by Ukraine’s Air Force. Their higher speed gives defenders less time to detect and intercept them and can force Ukraine to use comparatively expensive aircraft and missiles.
Zelensky said F-16 fighter jets had proven effective against the new drones. However, around half of Ukraine’s F-16 fleet was spending extended periods outside the country for maintenance and repairs, he said.
Kyiv is seeking Western assistance to move more maintenance work into Ukraine so that aircraft can return to service faster.
Ukraine is also testing five high-speed interceptor drone models. Zelensky said one model could enter production at a rate of approximately 400 units by the end of October, while the other four remained in testing.
He identified shortages of suitable engines and insufficient financing as the main obstacles to mass production.
Western pressure ‘not enough’
Zelensky also criticized the US and European governments for failing to apply sufficient economic and diplomatic pressure on Putin to end the war.
Asked whether Ukraine’s partners were doing everything possible to help, he replied: “Not enough, of course not enough.”
Zelensky argued that Russia’s partners had the leverage required to increase the cost of continuing the invasion but lacked the political will to use it fully.

articles.title: Zelensky: Putin’s Goal Is Not Donbas but All of Ukraine
articles.body:
President Volodymyr Zelensky warned that Russian President Vladimir Putin’s latest rhetoric shows the Kremlin’s ambitions extend far beyond Donbas, as Moscow seeks control over all of Ukraine and the restoration of Soviet-era influence across Russia’s neighborhood.
Speaking remotely at the fifth annual Helsinki Security Forum on Friday, Zelensky cited Putin’s own rhetoric to challenge European skeptics and the idea of neutral mediation.
JOIN US ON TELEGRAM
Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official.
“So his goal is not the east of Ukraine. It is not Donbas. His aim is to occupy our entire state,” Zelensky said.
Pointing to remarks Putin made at Russia’s Valdai Forum a day earlier, the president argued that the Kremlin’s objectives extend far beyond eastern Ukraine.
“An independent Ukraine, a strong Ukraine, is a big problem for Putin,” Zelensky said.
He highlighted Putin’s assertion that Ukraine cannot exist independently and that other states are supposedly using Ukrainians to wage war against Russia.
“There were important signals yesterday,” he said. “I don’t think he said it accidentally: ‘Ukraine is not a state, and it is not an independent state.’”
Zelensky linked Putin’s latest rhetoric directly to the Russian leader’s long-running fixation on the collapse of the Soviet Union.
He recalled Putin’s infamous 2005 declaration that the fall of the Soviet Union was the greatest geopolitical catastrophe of the 20th century, contrasting that political grievance with the actual human tragedies of the era.
Poland Drafts ‘Pre-War’ Readiness Law to Speed Up Allied Troop Deployment
“He did not speak about the First World War as a tragedy. He did not recognize the Second World War as [the greatest tragedy]. He did not mention other wars,” Zelensky said.
“He could have mentioned Afghanistan and other things, or the Chornobyl disaster – a horrible disaster. He mentioned none of the things that were connected to human lives.”
Instead, Zelensky argued, Putin focused entirely on the loss of Soviet power.
“Therefore, his goal is obvious: to bring it all back, to bring the USSR back.”
“The fact that he was saying this again yesterday serves as yet another indication of what he wants – of his attitude toward peace, whether he wants the war to end and, even if he does, at what price.”
Zelensky argued that Moscow seeks to recreate not necessarily the Soviet Union in its former institutional form, but the sphere of influence the Kremlin once exercised across neighboring states.
“Undoubtedly, this is about bringing back the influence of the USSR – or Russia’s influence – but making it comparable with the influence the former USSR once had,” he said.
“He has total influence over Belarus. But I am sure that he wants all of that back.”
Warning for the Baltic states and Russia’s neighbors
Zelensky warned that the implications extend beyond Ukraine.
If Putin’s ambition is to restore Moscow’s former regional dominance, he argued, the Baltic states and other countries sharing borders with Russia would also face pressure.
“Therefore, these challenges would also concern the Baltic states and countries with which Russia shares borders,” Zelensky said.
He urged those in Europe who remain skeptical about the scale of Russia’s ambitions to look directly at Putin’s own words.
“And nobody stops him in these messages,” Zelensky said. “And that is weakness of the world.”
Asked about Ukraine’s biggest EU obstacle, Zelensky answers: ‘Putin’
Zelensky was also asked what he considers the greatest obstacle facing Ukraine as it pursues European Union membership while simultaneously fighting Russia’s full-scale war.
His answer was one word:
“Putin.”
“He really doesn’t want that to happen,” Zelensky said.
“And it’s not about his opinion, but what he’s doing for this not to happen – against the development of our state, against the geopolitical choice of the people.”
“When we are talking about what the EU means for Ukraine, it is a victory over Russia – even a victory over Putin,” he said.
“Because the EU is the choice of our people.”
Security guarantees, he added, are critical because they protect Ukraine’s ability to follow the geopolitical course chosen by its citizens.
“And therefore it is important to have security guarantees, because these guarantees protect the path that the people of Ukraine have chosen.”
The Helsinki Security Forum is being held in the Finnish capital from Oct. 2–4 under the theme “Layers of Security.” The fifth annual gathering brings together policymakers and experts to discuss European defense, technological sovereignty, transatlantic relations, energy security, nuclear deterrence and Russia’s role in European security.
‘You cannot build total defense’ by buying weapons
Zelensky also used the forum to lay out lessons Ukraine has learned after years of defending itself against Russia.
A country seeking genuine security must first develop strength from within, he said, beginning with its military.
“The main guarantee for Ukraine is the army of our state.”
But an experienced army alone is not sufficient, Zelensky argued.
He emphasized the importance of a technologically advanced force, a domestic military-technology sector and defense production capable of rapidly adapting to battlefield requirements.
Energy resilience is another critical component, he said, particularly decentralization of infrastructure vulnerable to attack.
Ukraine shifts from weapons recipient to security partner
The second layer of security, Zelensky said, is international cooperation.
He thanked the EU, European countries and the US for financial, technological and military assistance since the outbreak of the war.
Ukraine received weapons it previously lacked, including NATO-standard systems, he noted, but its relationship with partners is increasingly becoming a two-way exchange.
Ukraine is now sharing knowledge gained through years of high-intensity warfare.
Zelensky highlighted a recent drone cooperation agreement with Finland as an example.
“It’s not about just selling or buying drones or missiles,” he said.
“It’s about sharing your security experience throughout the duration of this agreement.”
Ukraine is willing to share that knowledge with countries that supported it, Zelensky said, pointing to the trust built between Kyiv and Helsinki.
The third layer is collective security, particularly NATO.
Zelensky congratulated Finland on securing guarantees through membership in both the European Union and NATO.
“These are allies in economy, allies in technology, and allies in security,” he said.
“This is of utmost importance, and this is what Ukraine is counting on.”
