articles.title: Russia Plans Up to 1,000 Strikes to Cripple Ukraine’s Energy Grid This Winter
articles.body:
- Category
- War in Ukraine
Russia Plans Up to 1,000 Strikes to Cripple Ukraine’s Energy Grid This Winter
Russia is preparing what Ukrainian officials describe as its most ambitious campaign yet to cripple Ukraine’s power, heating, and water systems this winter, The New York Times reported on October 2.
The assessment is based on a document Ukrainian Energy Minister Denys Shmyhal recently presented to European partners in Paris. Two people familiar with the briefing told The New York Times that Shmyhal described it as an intercepted Russian plan for a methodical campaign against Ukraine’s energy system.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
Last winter, Russian missile and drone strikes repeatedly targeted Ukraine’s energy and civilian infrastructure, leaving large parts of Kyiv without electricity, heating, and water in subzero temperatures. UNITED24 Media reported that one January attack alone left more than 1 million people without power and over 4,000 apartment buildings without heat.
According to the document obtained by The New York Times, Russia could use up to 1,000 missiles, drones, and guided bombs against electrical substations, hydroelectric and thermal power plants, boiler houses, and other infrastructure.
The plan also envisages attacks on electrical switchyards connecting Ukraine’s three operating nuclear power plants to the national grid. The facilities are located less than a mile from the reactors, The New York Times noted.
By striking those switchyards, Russia would seek to force the nuclear plants offline without directly attacking the reactors themselves.
The document also describes attacks on Ukraine’s water infrastructure, including pumping stations and wastewater treatment plants, using dozens of ballistic missiles and guided bombs. The New York Times wrote that Russia has not previously targeted such facilities on that scale.
Kyiv, Kharkiv, and Odesa are identified as priority targets. The document outlines plans to reduce electricity and heating supplies in those cities by as much as 90% while severely disrupting sewage systems.
The New York Times could not independently authenticate the document, which is dated August and written in Russian. However, the Russian leader, Vladimir Putin, has publicly threatened an expanded campaign against Ukraine’s energy infrastructure this winter.
“Our partners, like us, were struck by its cynicism, by this cold, terrorist calculation of how to destroy our energy sector,” Shmyhal stated previously when discussing the document publicly.
The apparent plan is divided into three stages, The New York Times reported. The first would target substations near Ukraine’s western border that allow the country to import electricity from Europe.
The second stage would focus on hydroelectric power plants, while the third would attempt to disconnect Ukraine’s three operating nuclear power plants from the grid. The document estimates that the campaign could eliminate nearly 15 gigawatts of generating capacity.
Ukraine has spent recent months strengthening critical infrastructure, repairing power plants and substations, and installing smaller distributed energy facilities that are harder to destroy. Authorities have also reinforced parts of the grid to reroute electricity when transmission infrastructure is damaged.
Those preparations remain vulnerable to renewed attacks. Energy analyst Maria Tsaturian told The New York Times that only a small number of major strikes could eliminate much of the five gigawatts of generating capacity Ukraine restored in recent months.
Russia has already begun renewed attacks on energy infrastructure ahead of winter. Before dawn on September 30, missiles and drones struck a major thermal power plant and other facilities, leaving parts of Kyiv without electricity and water, The New York Times reported.
Ukraine endured prolonged outages during the previous winter as Russian attacks repeatedly damaged power and heating facilities. In Kyiv, residents sometimes went 12 hours or more without electricity, while outages also disrupted water supplies, elevators, and heating systems in apartment buildings.
UNITED24 Media previously reported that Kyiv was stockpiling emergency food and drinking water ahead of the 2026–2027 winter, preparing for possible prolonged blackouts caused by renewed Russian strikes on energy infrastructure. The city also planned to expand emergency food reserves and support Points of Invincibility during extended outages.

articles.title: Russia planning to increase "hybrid warfare" activity in Europe, Ukrainian intelligence warns
articles.body:
Russia planning to increase 'hybrid warfare' activity in Europe, Ukrainian intelligence warns
Russia's secret services have been tasked with increasing the number of attacks in Europe, Ukrainian military intelligence (HUR) warned in a statement on Oct. 2.
"The special services of the aggressor state of Russia have been tasked with increasing activity on the territory of the European Union and NATO states — this involves preparing for hybrid operations aimed at undermining aid to Ukraine and weakening the Alliance's capabilities," the statement says.
Acts of Russian "hybrid warfare" have included arson, assassinations, and a recent attempt to blow up Ukrainian Antonov cargo aircraft with modified FPV drones in Leipzig in August. On Sept. 1, Germany formally accused Russia of carrying out the attack.
"To carry out operations, including sabotage operations, the Kremlin plans to involve agents recruited by the General Staff of the Russian Armed Forces (GRU) and the FSB of the Russian Federation in Europe. The Russian special services are targeting military facilities, critical infrastructure, and communication systems," the statement says.
"Among the aggressor's likely targets are Starlink satellite internet receiving stations located in European countries," HUR said.
Starlink, manufactured and operated by Elon Musk's SpaceX, is widely used for communications by the Ukrainian military.
On Sept. 24, Polish Deputy Prime Minister and Digital Affairs Minister Krzysztof Gawkowski told reporters that a fire at a Starlink ground station in Poland may have been a deliberate attempt to disrupt internet access used by Ukrainian forces at the front.
Gawkowski said there were indications that the fire at the station in Wola Krobowska, in Poland's Masovian Voivodeship, on the evening of Sept. 23, may have been an attempt to disrupt its operations.
The station is operated by the state-owned telecommunications company Exatel and serves as an internet hub that carries traffic through Poland, including to Ukraine, Gawkowski said.
He suggested Russia could be behind the incident, describing it as potentially part of Moscow's hybrid warfare. Polish authorities have not concluded their investigation into the incident.
European governments are stepping up preparations for possible Russian hybrid attacks as officials across the continent warn that Moscow could increasingly use drones, missiles, sabotage, and cyberattacks to test NATO countries and pressure them over their support for Ukraine.
"The Ukrainian Defense Ministry's Directorate of Defense warned its partners about the criminal plans of the aggressor state of Russia," the statement says.

articles.title: South Korea warns of 'further measures' if Ukraine refuses public apology over POW transfer disclosure
articles.body:
The POWs were captured by Ukrainian forces early last year after being deployed alongside thousands of North Korean troops to support Russia's war against Ukraine.
South Korean President Lee Jae-myung said on Friday that Seoul would take "further measures" if Ukraine refuses to publicly apologise over what he called its unilateral disclosure of North Korean prisoners of war being sent to South Korea.
Seoul has taken a hard stance on Ukraine disclosing the transfer of two soldiers captured fighting for Russia, warning that their families could be targeted by Pyongyang.
North Korea is known to retaliate against defectors and their families.
Both POWs are identifiable as they had been photographed by South Korean media before their arrival to the South.
The POWs were captured by Ukrainian forces early last year after being deployed alongside thousands of North Korean troops to support Russia's war against Ukraine, in exchange for economic and military assistance to Pyongyang.
Hours after Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy disclosed last week the transfer in remarks at the United Nations, Lee expressed his dismay, with Seoul claiming confidentiality was key to protecting the POWs' relatives.
Seoul later demanded an official apology from Ukraine, saying that both sides had reached a "clear understanding" during consultations to keep the transfer confidential.
"If Ukraine continues to refuse to acknowledge the facts and publicly apologise, we will take further measures," the South Korean president said on Friday, accusing Kyiv of making him out to be a "liar."
"This is a matter concerning the dignity of the Republic of Korea and its people and cannot be overlooked," Lee posted on X.
Analysts say that from South Korea's perspective, keeping the transfer of the POWs confidential may have partly been for Ukraine's sake, as making it public could have complicated Kyiv's own prisoner exchanges with Russia.
In domestic South Korean politics, however, Seoul's approach "could prove problematic," Shin Yul, a political science professor at Myongji University, said given the current administration's dovish approach to the nuclear-armed North.
"The government has acted swiftly in this case involving Ukraine, while exercising extreme caution over the North Korean landmine incident (that injured South Korean soldiers). That contrast could leave the public deeply dissatisfied."
Diplomatic misunderstanding
Lee referred on Friday to an interview with Ukraine's Foreign Minister Andrii Sybiha published by RBC-Ukraine and other Ukrainian outlets on Thursday.
Sybiha said he would "not like to call it an incident," describing it instead as a "diplomatic misunderstanding."
"South Korea is an important country for us. And I very much hope for momentum, continued cooperation, and concrete results that we are indeed achieving with them," he said.
Seoul's spy agency said that Zelenskyy may have disclosed the transfer of the North Korean soldiers to boost public support in South Korea for Seoul providing arms to Ukraine, a lawmaker said on Wednesday.
South Korea has in recent years emerged as a major arms exporter, particularly since Russia's full-scale invasion of Ukraine in early 2022, including through a multibillion-dollar arms deal with Poland.
But it has refrained from supplying Kyiv with lethal weapons, citing its longstanding policy of not arming countries engaged in active conflicts.

articles.title: Mirage 2000 Makes History—Russian Banderol Cruise Missile Shot Down With Guns
articles.body:

Mirage 2000 Makes History—Russian Banderol Cruise Missile Shot Down With Guns
A Ukrainian Mirage 2000-5F has reportedly scored a first, shooting down a Russian S8000 Banderol cruise missile not with an air-to-air missile, but with bursts from its built-in 30mm cannons.
“Late-night information: the Mirage 2000-5F was the first Western fighter aircraft to destroy a Russian S8000 Banderol cruise missile with the cannon,” according to Militarnyi, citing OSINT analyst French Aid to Europe on October 2.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
The claim has not yet been publicly confirmed by the Ukrainian or French defense ministries.
France transferred Mirage 2000-5F fighters from its own Air and Space Force inventory to Ukraine beginning in 2025, giving Kyiv another Western fighter type for air-defense and strike missions.
The aircraft is particularly well suited to interception work. France describes the 2000-5F as an air-defense-focused variant equipped with an RDY multimode radar, MICA air-to-air missiles and two internal 30mm cannons.
Those guns are DEFA 554 revolver cannons mounted inside the fuselage. Each carries roughly 125 rounds and can fire at rates reaching about 1,800 rounds per minute, giving the pilot an extremely short but intense window of fire during a close-range interception.
If confirmed, the engagement would be particularly notable because the target was not a slow propeller-driven Shahed.
The S8000 Banderol is a small Russian jet-powered cruise missile developed by Kronstadt JSC. Ukraine’s Defense Intelligence lists its top speed at roughly 620–650 kilometers per hour, with a cruising speed of 520–560 km/h and a range of around 500 kilometers.
The weapon is primarily launched from Russia’s Orion UAV and is also being adapted for use from Mi-28N attack helicopters. It combines relatively low production cost with the speed and flight characteristics of a small cruise missile, making it a more difficult interception target than conventional Shahed-type drones.
The Banderol carries a large high-explosive fragmentation warhead and has increasingly appeared in Russian attacks against Ukraine since its first documented combat use in spring 2025. Ukrainian intelligence says the weapon relies on numerous foreign-made components, including its propulsion and electronics.
Earlier, two Mirage 2000 fighter jets crewed by French and Ukrainian pilots participated in France’s Bastille Day military parade on July 14, with one aircraft expected to appear in the colors of the Ukrainian flag.

articles.title: Trump talking his own imagination about Iran
articles.body:
Trump talking his own imagination about Iran
TEHRAN – Trump has claimed that Iran would have “wiped” Israel and Saudi Arabia “off the face of the planet” with nuclear bombs if he had not been president.
Modern history may not have seen a statesman as fabulist as Trump. He seems to be losing his sense of reality more and more as the midterm congressional elections approach.
Trump is living in a world of his own imagination, indulging in his own fantasies. It is in this imaginary world that Iran would have developed nuclear weapons and destroyed Israel, Saudi Arabia and many other countries if he had not been president.
“If I weren't president, Saudi Arabia wouldn't be here right now. Neither would Israel. They'd be wiped off the face of the planet. I do a lot for Saudi Arabia. My relationship with them is very good. I like the crown prince. My relationship is very good. But remember, if I weren't here, there wouldn't be a Saudi Arabia. There wouldn't be an Israel. There wouldn't be various other countries also,” Trump told the Time magazine in an interview published on October 1.
According to such a statement, Iran gained access to nuclear arms in Trump’s world of imagination and dropped atomic weapons on Israel and Saudi Arabia and wiped them out.
It is open to all that Trump is the laughing stock of the world.
Even Israeli hardliners who have been seeking hard to demonize Iran laugh about such remarks from the bottom of their heart.
In August 2016, former French President François Hollande made a statement about Trump that history will not forget. At the time, when Trump was running for the White House, Hollande said that Trump's “excesses end up making you feel like you want to retch.”
The way Trump speaks is degrading for a top official, let alone that the official be the president of the United States. His remarks and approach to domestic and foreign policy is extremely reckless and shameful.
Even the far-right government of Netanyahu, whose barbarity against Gazans has shocked the world, suspended Heritage Minister Amihay Eliyahu in November 2023 who suggested dropping nuclear bomb on Gaza.
Unfortunately, Trump is surrounded by sycophants. There is no unbiased official in his inner circle to advise him against making such ridiculous remarks.
Trump cannot fool anyone with such ridiculous remarks if he is referring to Iran’s strikes on U.S. military bases in the Persian Gulf Arab states that were used as launchpads for the U.S. war against Iran. Iran had repeatedly and unequivocally announced that it would target any location from which an attack was launched against it. Who could expect Iran to come under attack from a military base in a regional country and not strike that base?
Confusing Iran’s retaliatory defensive strikes on military bases from which U.S. fighter jets flew to drop bombs on Iran with the fantasy that Iran would have used nuclear weapons to “wipe off the face of the planet” Saudi Arabia and “various other countries” if Trump had not attacked Iran is not only laughable but also a distortion of the realities on the ground.
Iran also fired missiles at Israel, which, along with the United States, launched joint aggression against Iran in both June 2025 and February 2026. Even before the full-scale wars of 2025 and 2026, it was Israel that launched attacks on Iran’s diplomatic headquarters in Damascus and carried out assassinations inside Iran, forcing Tehran to respond.
Trump is seeking to sell his imagined narrative to the American people and others around the world in a futile attempt to justify his ill-gotten war against Iran and portray the country as a demon. In doing so, however, he risks making himself appear even more ridiculous.

articles.title: Ukraine sends mixed signals on F-16 repair delays
articles.body:
- Zelensky told the Financial Times that about half of Ukraine's F-16s have spent long periods in Europe for repairs and maintenance.
- Ukraine's Foreign Ministry later called reports of catastrophically low F-16 availability false, saying overhauled jets are returning at an increasing pace.
About half of Ukraine’s F-16 fighter jets have spent long stretches in Europe for repairs and maintenance, President Volodymyr Zelensky said, and some have taken so long to come back that Ukraine lost time when it needed them most to defend its skies.
Zelensky made the comments in an interview with the Financial Times published on Oct. 2. He said Kyiv wants Western partners to help move more of the maintenance work inside Ukraine, arguing that keeping the jets closer to the front would get them back into service faster. He did not say how many aircraft are affected, where in Europe the work is done, or how long the jets have been away.
Zelensky said the F-16s have been effective against Russia’s newer jet-powered drones, which fly faster than the propeller-driven Shahed-type drones Russia has used for most of the war. In the same interview, he said Ukrainian forces are shooting down about 57% of jet-powered drones and between 85% and 90% of conventional ones.
Hours later, Ukraine’s Foreign Ministry pushed back on reports describing a readiness crisis in the F-16 fleet. Spokesperson Heorhiy Tykhyi said on X that claims of catastrophically low aircraft availability and excessively long maintenance turnaround times were false. He said Ukraine’s industrial partners are returning overhauled aircraft at an increasing pace and that maintenance times are getting shorter, not longer.
Tykhyi acknowledged that the fleet is hard to keep flying. Ukraine flies the jets intensively under demanding conditions, he said, and some components for its early-model F-16s are no longer produced and are getting harder to find. He warned that such reports should not undermine international funding for F-16 maintenance or cast doubt on the need for more jets from partner nations.
Ukraine’s F-16s are older jets from European air forces, mainly the Netherlands, Denmark, Norway and Belgium. The first ones arrived in the summer of 2024. They have been used to intercept Russian cruise missiles and drones and to strike ground targets, and Ukraine has lost several of them in combat and accidents.
Because the jets are Western-built, much of their deeper maintenance has been done outside Ukraine, where parts, tools and trained technicians are available and the aircraft are out of reach of Russian strikes on airfields. Moving that work into Ukraine would bring the jets closer to the fight but would also put repair sites within range of Russian missiles and drones.

articles.title: Putin Warns West Over Kaliningrad, Admits Ukrainian Strikes Cut Russia's GDP by 1%
articles.body:

Putin Warns West Over Kaliningrad, Admits Ukrainian Strikes Cut Russia's GDP by 1%
Russian leader Vladimir Putin stated that Moscow will consider using all available weapons, including its nuclear arsenal, if Kaliningrad or any other Russian territory faces a direct attack or blockade.
Speaking at the Valdai Foreign Policy Forum, Putin addressed Western claims of potential Russian aggression by 2029 or 2030, claiming that Moscow has no intent to initiate hostilities against European nations, as reported by BBC on October 1.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
He noted that Ukrainian strikes on domestic energy sites reduced Russia's gross domestic product by approximately 1%.
The statements follow claims from Moscow accusing NATO of planning a blockade of Kaliningrad, the Baltic exclave bordering Lithuania and Poland. Putin pointed to NATO naval drills in the Baltic Sea as a threat to the region's security.
NATO General Secretary Mark Rutte rejected these claims, emphasizing that alliance exercises are purely defensive and calling Moscow's nuclear messaging unhelpful.
Addressing the situation in Ukraine, Putin alleged that Russian strikes against Ukrainian energy and economic targets were direct responses to strikes on Russian oil refineries and Black Sea vessels, according to BBC.
Ukraine maintains that targeting oil infrastructure aims to weaken funding for the military operation. Meanwhile, strikes continue across Ukrainian territory, including drone attacks on critical infrastructure and key transit points.
Putin reiterated his position that broader international instability is driven by Western policies, warning of rising global risks associated with advanced weaponry and emerging technologies like artificial intelligence, BBC reported.
He called for updating global international rules, arguing that global tensions will shift as traditional international power dynamics continue to adjust.
Amid growing security concerns over potential aggression around Kaliningrad, Lithuania designed its future Gizai power substation, located 30 kilometers from the Russian exclave, to withstand physical sabotage and drone strikes, including attacks from multiple explosive-laden Shahed drones.
The 35-hectare facility, which formed part of the Harmony Link project connecting the Baltic power grid to Poland, featured reinforced concrete protective walls, vehicle-proof fencing, and underground tunnel sensors.
Litgrid CEO Andrius Semeskevicius emphasized that the grid was planned for hybrid and military threats following Russia’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine and the Baltic states' disconnection from the Russian electricity system in 2025. Regional security concerns had escalated due to recent infrastructure sabotage in Germany and fears of potential false-flag operations near the Suwalki Gap.

Ukraine’s Acoustic SkyFortress Will Track Low-Flying Drones and Missiles Over Lithuania
Lithuania is deploying the Ukrainian-developed SkyFortress system to test acoustic and radio-frequency detection of low-flying drones and cruise missiles, the country’s Defense Ministry announced on October 2.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
The Lithuanian Defense Ministry reported that SkyFortress will operate as an experimental airspace surveillance system capable of identifying objects by their acoustic or electromagnetic signatures. The system uses artificial intelligence to classify and track detected threats in real time.
“Instead of developing everything from scratch, we are adapting systems that are already operating in Ukraine,” Lithuanian Defense Minister Robertas Kaunas stated.
“SkyFortress complements the first stage of this chain—surveillance: with the help of artificial intelligence, the system detects and tracks low-flying drones or cruise missiles.”
Under an agreement signed this summer, the deployment includes processing sensor-collected data, using libraries of acoustic and radio-frequency digital signatures based on unclassified information, and training Lithuanian personnel.
Testing will assess SkyFortress’ ability to detect and identify low-flying unmanned aircraft under Lithuanian conditions.
Earlier in September, Lithuania itself confronted the challenge directly when NATO fighter jets shot down an unidentified drone that had entered Lithuanian airspace from Belarus, highlighting the urgency of enhanced detection capabilities across the Baltic region.

articles.title: Ukraine aims to produce up to 400 interceptor drones as Russian jet-powered drone use grows, Zelensky says
articles.body:
Ukraine aims to produce up to 400 interceptor drones as Russian jet-powered drone use grows, Zelensky says
Ukraine will be able to produce up to 400 interceptor drones by the end of October to counter Russia's growing use of jet-powered attack drones, President Volodymyr Zelensky said in an interview with the Financial Times published on Oct. 2.
As Russia scales up production of its jet-powered drones — the Geran-4 and Geran-5 — Ukraine is struggling to shoot them down amid the hours-long attacks.
Russia launched around 500 drones against Ukraine over the past day, about half of which were jet-powered and significantly harder to intercept, Zelensky said.
Only 57% of jet-powered versions of Shahed-type drones are currently shot down by Ukraine, Zelensky said in his evening address on Sept. 28, a figure he described as "much less than necessary."
According to Zelensky, Ukraine is testing five types of high-speed interceptor drones designed to counter Russian weapons. One of the models is expected to reach production of around 400 units by the end of October, while the other four remain in the testing stage.
The development of the interceptors is being slowed by a shortage of engines. Ukraine imports most of the engines used for the drones, while domestic production remains insufficient, Zelensky said.
Russia's jet-powered drones target civilian infrastructure such as supermarkets, schools, shopping malls, telecommunications infrastructure, data centers, gas stations, and medical facilities.
Russia has increased its use of jet-powered drones while launching attacks on Kyiv in recent months. The onslaught began last month but has intensified over the past week.
Zelensky also said in the interview that Ukraine is unable to use all of its F-16 fighter jets during Russian attacks because around half of the aircraft are undergoing scheduled maintenance and repairs in Europe.
F-16s, which Ukraine first received in the summer of 2024, are used in both offensive and defensive operations. The aircraft have been used to intercept Russian missiles and drones during aerial attacks on Ukraine. They could also be deployed to launch missiles and bombs against Russian positions along the front line.
The lengthy maintenance periods leave some aircraft unavailable when they are particularly needed for air defense. Kyiv wants to move some F-16 maintenance work to Ukraine to allow the jets to return to service faster.
Zelensky also said Ukraine faces a budget shortfall that is limiting the development and mass production of critical defensive weapons.

articles.title: ‘The enemy is tearing our city apart’: terror in Kyiv as Russia ramps up attacks
articles.body:
Valeriya Tkachenko was dropping her son off at school in central Kyiv when the air raid alert sounded. Staff hurried the children and parents into the shelter, where the frightened lawyer spent the next two hours with her son.
“I’m scared to death all day about what could happen to my son,” she said as she emerged from the shelter, already late for work.
A day earlier, a Russian jet-powered drone had struck a school nearby. “And I can’t plan anything any more,” she said. “It’s not sustainable like this.”
Across the city on Friday morning, Artem Marchenko, an IT worker, was forced to abandon his car and walk for 20 minutes across the Pivdennyi Bridge on his way to work after repeated Russian strikes damaged the crossing.
He feared Russia would soon target Kyiv’s other bridges, paralysing movement across a city of about 3 million people, the two halves of which are divided by the Dnipro.
Kyiv is entering its most difficult period since the early days of the invasion, as intensifying Russian attacks reshape everyday life in a capital that Moscow is seeking to plunge into darkness.
For weeks, the main worry in the capital had been the coming winter, when Russia is expected once again to try to plunge Ukraine into darkness and cold. But a sharp escalation in Russian attacks has left many residents feeling that some of the hardship they had been bracing for is already here.
“The capital is in a very dramatic situation. And it’s no longer possible to pretend that we can live now as we do in peacetime,” the Kyiv mayor, Vitali Klitschko, said on Friday. “The enemy is tearing Kyiv apart.”
This week alone, Russian missiles and drones have struck offices, datacentres, a school and hospital and one of Kyiv’s main bridges. Moscow has also started its attacks on Ukraine’s energy, targeting a thermal power plant and other energy facilities, leaving several neighbourhoods without power and water by morning.
Volodymyr Zelenskyy underlined the apparent shift in Russian tactics in an interview with the Financial Times this week, saying Vladimir Putin had recently ordered his commanders to abandon the rules of war.
“They want Ukrainians to leave the capital … and show that if you don’t have the capital you don’t have the country,” Zelenskyy said in separate comments to reporters.
Until recently, Kyiv had retained a deceptively normal rhythm, while cities closer to the front, including Kharkiv and Dnipro, absorbed the brunt of daily missile and drone attacks. Now, residents joke grimly that the balance is beginning to shift, with those cities at times feeling safer than the capital.
The city is confronting a particularly dangerous combination of an acute shortage of Patriot interceptors for ballistic missiles and a new generation of faster, jet-powered Russian drones that are harder to shoot down.
Kyiv is racing to fast-track a new generation of interceptor drones capable of taking down the jet-powered models. Several are already in use, according to three defence industry sources, though they said it could still take weeks or months to deploy them at a scale sufficient to provide meaningful protection for the capital.
At the same time, Russia’s advances on the battlefield remain relatively slow and are coming at enormous cost.
Moscow captured about 361 sq km in September, according to the military analyst Konrad Muzyka, an increase on recent months but still far short of the pace needed to seize the rest of the Donbas before winter, when offensive operations typically become more difficult.
Ukraine, meanwhile, has clawed back about 126 sq km in a series of counteroffensives in the east, being conducted under the codename Vivaldi. That slower-moving battle on the ground is increasingly at odds with what is happening far behind the front. The contrast reflects a broader shift in the war, as Ukraine’s major cities come under growing pressure.
“You can be quite successful in the land domain, but if you are vulnerable in the air, especially in the rear, that is the vulnerability your opponent is going to exploit,” said Mykola Bielieskov, a military analyst at Ukraine’s government-run National Institute for Strategic Studies.
Ukrainian officials have been warning their European counterparts about the scale of the looming threat. According to the New York Times, Ukraine’s energy minister, Denys Shmyhal, recently briefed European counterparts on an intercepted Russian plan to use as many as 1,000 missiles, drones and bombs against the country’s energy system. The targets included electrical substations, hydroelectric and thermal power plants and boiler houses, in what appeared to be an effort to plunge Ukrainian cities into darkness and cold and create a humanitarian crisis.
“Russia plans to freeze Kyiv out, to throw it back into the stone age,” said one senior western diplomat in Kyiv, speaking on condition of anonymity.
Western diplomats say publicly that they intend to remain in Kyiv, mindful that leaving would hand Moscow a propaganda victory and risk creating the impression that Ukraine was being abandoned. However, privately two senior diplomats said contingency plans were being drawn up to relocate embassies to Lviv or eastern Poland if Russia began deliberately targeting foreign missions.
“The situation is obviously deteriorating fast,” the diplomat said.

articles.title: The New York Times obtains a purported Russian plan to cripple Ukraine’s power grid, including by cutting electricity and heat supplies to three major cities by 90%
articles.body:
The New York Times obtains a purported Russian plan to cripple Ukraine’s power grid, including by cutting electricity and heat supplies to three major cities by 90%
Russia plans to disable Ukraine’s entire energy system. Ukrainian authorities have obtained a Russian Defense Ministry document outlining the plan, The New York Times reported. Ukrainian Energy Minister Denys Shmyhal showed it to two European politicians in late September, sources told the newspaper. The Times also obtained a copy of the Russian-language document but said its authenticity could not be verified.
The plan calls for a large-scale campaign using various types of missiles, guided aerial bombs, and drones, including jet-powered models. According to the document, Russia plans to carry out the campaign in three stages:
- First stage: Strikes on substations along Ukraine’s western border to prevent the country from importing electricity from Europe.
- Second stage: Strikes on hydroelectric power plants.
- Third stage: Strikes on substations that supply electricity to the three nuclear power plants still under Ukrainian control. Russian troops occupy Ukraine’s fourth nuclear power plant, the Zaporizhzhia Nuclear Power Plant.
The campaign’s ultimate goal is to cut off electricity, heat, and water to major Ukrainian cities to provoke a humanitarian crisis.
The plan identifies Kyiv, Kharkiv, and Odesa as the main targets. It calls for reducing electricity and heat supplies to these cities by 90% and disabling a substantial portion of their sewage systems.
The document indicates that Russia plans to eliminate nearly 15 gigawatts of generating capacity — almost as much as Ukraine had at the end of summer 2026, the Times reported.
In August, Shmyhal told Ukraine’s parliament, the Verkhovna Rada, that the country would have 21 gigawatts of generating capacity by the end of the year. That would be enough to meet peak demand, which reached 18 gigawatts last winter. But Russia continues to strike Ukraine’s energy facilities, which could undo the country’s efforts to increase capacity ahead of winter, experts told the Times.
The war in photographs
On October 1, Russian forces deliberately struck a bridge across the Dnipro River in Kyiv for the first time since Russia’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine. Russian drones attacked the bridge three times that day. On the morning of October 2, the Southern Bridge was closed to traffic, and traffic was restricted on the Paton Bridge and the Metro Bridge. Kyiv saw massive traffic jams.

articles.title: Pentagon planning for more naval forces in Mideast as Trump weighs renewed strikes on Iran - report
articles.body:
The US military is planning a potential increase of thousands of naval forces in the Middle East in the coming weeks, the Washington Post reported on Friday.
The Pentagon intends to move up three aircraft carriers and escort ships into the region to create flexibility in overseeing the war, according to the report.
Administration deliberates next move on Iran
The planning comes as US President Donald Trump’s administration deliberates on how to approach the Iran war, which has now entered its eighth month, causing dissatisfaction among the American public and roiling the global economy, according to the WP.
Additional forces deployed to the region will include 20,000 troops, up to 150 fighter jets, and numerous destroyers to launch and fend off missile attacks, it added.
The USS George Washington, last deployed to the Arabian Sea, the USS George H.W. Bush, currently in the Indian Ocean, and the USS Theodore Roosevelt are among the carriers involved in the discussions, the WP said, citing an earlier report by the Wall Street Journal.
The USS Theodore Roosevelt was deployed recently to San Diego and must make its way across the Pacific Ocean, it added.
The plans come as Trump considers renewing strikes on Iran following November’s midterm elections, the WP said, citing US officials who spoke on the condition of anonymity. 
In an interview published by Time magazine on Thursday, the US President said that it’s  “possible” he will ramp up bombing after the midterms, according to the WP’s report. 
50,000 troops are currently deployed
Around 50,000 US troops are currently deployed in the Middle East, the WP cited US officials as saying.
The Navy, according to the report, recently deployed the Makin Island Amphibious Ready Group, a three-ship task force of Marines and sailors from California.
The Boxer Amphibious Ready Group, a similar unit, has already been in the Middle East for months and includes more than 4,000 sailors and Marines, the report added, citing officials.
If Trump decides against expanding the conflict with Iran, the recently deployed vessels would likely replace those that have been there for months, the WP cited officials as saying.
The war, according to the report, has challenged the Pentagon as troop morale declines and ships require additional maintenance.
The war with Iran has cost the US billions of dollars, it added, left more than 800 troops wounded, and killed at least 19 others.

articles.title: Lawmakers Push for Bipartisan Solution to Golden Dome’s Funding Crunch
articles.body:
Some lawmakers in the Senate are advocating for a more bipartisan approach to paying for the Pentagon’s $185 billion Golden Dome missile defense project, arguing that the effort’s goal of bolstering homeland defenses has support across ideological lines but the process for funding it has been politically charged—leaving the program’s near- and long-term future uncertain.
During a Sept. 29 hearing of the Senate Armed Services Committee’s strategic forces subcommittee, lawmakers bemoaned the Pentagon’s decision to use a controversial funding tool called reconciliation—which allows Congress to appropriate funds with a simple majority vote—to kickstart President Donald Trump’s Golden Dome initiative in 2025. That decision, they argued, took a program whose mission has broad support in Congress and enveloped it in politics.
“Should it have been necessary to go to reconciliation to get this started? I would say no. This should have been on a bipartisan basis,” Sen. Mike Rounds (R-S.D.) said during the hearing. “I won’t lay fault for why that’s happening, I’m just simply saying we need to get back to a bipartisan approach to this as soon as possible.”
Sen. Angus King (I-Maine) said the effort is one of the “most expensive and important initiatives of this government” that has strong support in Congress, making it “very bothersome” that the Pentagon and the White House opted to circumvent the traditional appropriations process to resource it.
And Sen. Deb Fischer (R-Neb.) pointed out that while Golden Dome as a program materialized under President Donald Trump’s administration, its roots are bipartisan. The Senate Armed Services Committee inserted language into the Fiscal 2024 National Defense Authorization Act codifying the need for a layered missile defense architecture.
“So, it came from us,” she said.
Yet it was Trump’s announcement in January 2025 that the Pentagon would build an expansive homeland missile defense architecture that brought major attention and funding to idea. First called “Iron Dome For America” and later changed to “Golden Dome,” the vision is for a layered architecture comprised of sensors, ground and space-based interceptors, and interconnected command-and-control systems designed to defeat a range of threats, from drones and more traditional weapons to advanced hypersonic and cruise missiles.
To date, the Pentagon’s strategy for funding the program has been to bypass the annual budget process and rely instead on reconciliation. As part of the One Big Beautiful Bill Act, which Congress passed in July 2025, Golden Dome received $25 billion—90 percent of which it had obligated as of mid-August, according to Golden Dome Director Gen. Michael Guetlein.
This year, the Pentagon requested $17 billion for the effort as part of a proposed $350 billion reconciliation package, and just $400 million in the normal “base” budget for fiscal 2027. For now, though, there appears to be little political will to pass another spending bill via reconciliation, leaving Golden Dome without a clear path for near-term funding.
That challenge is exacerbated by the fact that the federal government is now operating under a continuing resolution, a stopgap funding measure aimed at avoiding a wholesale shutdown that holds spending at prior year levels. The CR took effect Oct. 1, the first day of the new fiscal year, and because Golden Dome does not have a fiscal 2026 appropriation to serve as its baseline, the program has nothing to fall back on.
Guetlein warned in August that a CR presents a real challenge for the program, and a failure to provide any funding in fiscal ‘27 would be disastrous.
“A CR doesn’t help me under Golden Dome because I don’t have a topline to fall back to to get that percentage of the continuing resolution,” he said during the Space and Missile Defense Symposium, adding that if Congress and the Pentagon can’t find a way to pay for the effort in fiscal ‘27, “there is no Golden Dome because there is no funding.”
During this week’s hearing, Rounds urged his colleagues in Congress to find a solution.
“Let’s get back to a bipartisan [approach], and let’s include it in the underlying appropriations bill,” he said.
Meanwhile, experts testifying in front of the Senate panel agreed that it’s important for Congress to address the funding quagmire, but added that there’s a broader risk that the politicization of the program could make it a target in the future.
Tom Karako, director of the Missile Defense Project at the Center for Strategic and International Studies, noted that even Golden Dome’s name is polarizing and argued that Congress should consider potentially renaming the effort in future policy legislation. He also suggested making steps to institutionalize the project and Guetlein’s acquisition authorities within the broader missile defense enterprise.
In his written statement, Karako noted that Guetlein’s status as a direct reporting portfolio manager, or DRPM—which means he reports directly to Deputy Secretary of Defense Steven Feinberg—is meant to be temporary, and said now may be the time to start thinking about the program’s long-term management and where it should sit within the enterprise after that moniker and its associated authorities fade.
Karako offered that while the Pentagon and Congress could opt to create a permanent entity to oversee Golden Dome, that approach may lead to duplication with other organizations like the Missile Defense Agency and the military services and would take time to establish. But merging Golden Dome with MDA could be a viable solution, he said.
“Whatever the scope of mission for the future air and missile defense of the homeland, its realization and governance will benefit from unity of effort with clear authority, high level access, control of resources, and appropriate acquisition authorities,” Karako said in his statement.

articles.title: Media reveal information about Russian who may have organised sabotage at Leipzig airport
articles.body:
Media reveal information about Russian who may have organised sabotage at Leipzig airport
Russian biker Oleg Lyovushkin, who is linked to a Russian military intelligence officer, may have organised an attempted sabotage at Leipzig/Halle Airport in Germany.
Source: a joint investigation by The Telegraph and Welt am Sonntag, as reported by European Pravda
Details: According to the investigation, Lyovushkin presumably organised the attempt to plant explosives at the airport. German investigators believe that Belarusian intermediary agent Andrei Karshakov was supposed to carry out the plan.
Journalists analysed intelligence documents from Germany, Lithuania, and Poland, and also spoke with representatives of Western secret services. According to their data, Lyovushkin and Karshakov arrived in Germany to carry out the sabotage operation.
German investigators suspect that Lyovushkin conducted reconnaissance of the airport shortly before the attack, after which he instructed Karshakov to execute the plan.
Investigators also found similarities between the incident in Leipzig and other attempted Russian sabotage operations in Poland, Lithuania, and Germany.
Specifically, the explosive device seized in Leipzig was reportedly similar to devices used in other sabotage operations in Europe.
Lyovushkin, who holds a Russian passport and is an avid motorcyclist, is also linked to Denis Smolyaninov, a man Western secret services consider to be one of the coordinators of Russian sabotage operations in Europe.
According to Lithuanian intelligence, Smolyaninov headed the Ukrainian desk in Russian military intelligence and specialised in psychological operations, among other things. Documents also link him to secret sabotage campaigns in Europe.
It is noted that Lyovushkin and Smolyaninov met back in 2007. Reportedly, they have kin repeated contact over the many years.
German security agencies link the Leipzig attack to GRU Unit 29155, which, according to German intelligence assessments, plays a key role in Russian sabotage operations in Europe.
German security agencies assess that the goal of such operations could be to create a sense of insecurity among European society due to its support for Ukraine and to influence the debate on further assistance to Kyiv.
Lyovushkin himself publicly leads an inconspicuous life. He takes part in motorcycle races, travels around Europe, fishes, and skis with his family.
At the same time, journalists claim that this lifestyle may conceal his involvement in Russian sabotage operations in Central Europe.
According to German intelligence, he travelled to Germany via Türkiye this summer to prepare an attack on Leipzig/Halle Airport. Investigators stated that Lyovushkin rented a car at Berlin airport a week before the attack and over the next few days drove it to several locations where weapons were suspected of being stored.
They believe that the explosives used in the operation were transported to Germany via Bulgaria and Serbia, hidden in the cavities of trucks, and were likely temporarily stored along the route.
The journalists say that Lyovushkin's links to the GRU were known at the time he entered the country. However, he was not placed under surveillance upon his arrival.
Background:
- On 1 September, Germany directly accused Russia of a hybrid attack at Leipzig airport in early August and announced countermeasures.
- On 6 September, it was reported that German Interior Minister Nancy Faeser was planning a set of measures to cover protection against drones, sabotage of critical infrastructure, and cyberattacks, as well as the detection of spies and potential terrorists.

articles.title: Taiwan receives first new F-16s three years behind plan
articles.body:
- Taiwan's Air Force took delivery of the first two of 66 F-16V Block 70 fighters at Chihhang Air Base in Taitung on Oct. 2.
- The $8 billion order, approved in 2019, was expected to begin deliveries in 2023 but was delayed by production and software problems.
Taiwan’s Air Force has received the first two of 66 new F-16V Block 70 fighter jets bought from the United States, after the aircraft landed at Chihhang Air Base in the eastern county of Taitung around noon on Oct. 2.
The arrival comes about a month later than expected and roughly three years behind the original schedule. The two jets had been due in Taiwan by late August or early September, but stayed in Hawaii for weeks without explanation, Focus Taiwan reported, after local media said they had turned back shortly after taking off for Guam.
The United States approved the $8 billion sale of 66 F-16 Block 70 jets in 2019, during President Donald Trump’s first term. Deliveries were supposed to start in 2023 and finish by the end of 2026, but production delays, supply chain problems and software integration issues pushed the schedule back. Lockheed Martin unveiled the first newly built F-16 Block 70 for Taiwan at its plant in Greenville, South Carolina, in March 2025.
The new jets will be based at Chihhang, where they will go through ground inspections while pilots and maintainers convert to the aircraft. Taiwan’s government budgeted NT$247.2 billion, about $8 billion, for the purchase between 2020 and 2026, and says the jets will strengthen air defense along the island’s east coast, the side facing the open Pacific, where Chinese aircraft and ships have operated during large-scale drills around Taiwan.
The Block 70 is the newest production version of the F-16, built at Lockheed Martin’s South Carolina line. It carries the AN/APG-83 active electronically scanned array radar, a newer mission computer and updated electronic warfare and communications systems, along with conformal fuel tanks that hug the fuselage to add range without taking up weapons stations. It also has strengthened landing gear to handle heavier takeoff weights and weapons loads.
Taiwan already flies more than 140 older F-16A/B fighters, which have been upgraded to a similar F-16V standard in a program completed in 2023. The 66 new jets will take Taiwan’s F-16 fleet to more than 200 aircraft, giving it the backbone of a force that scrambles almost daily to shadow Chinese military aircraft.
The delivery came about a week after Trump met Chinese leader Xi Jinping in Beijing. Taiwan is still waiting for U.S. approval of a separate arms package worth about $14 billion that Trump paused after Chinese objections, AFP reported.
Taiwanese officials have said more F-16 Block 70s will arrive before the end of the year, but they have not given a number. Remaining deliveries are expected to stretch into 2027 and 2028.

articles.title: The beginning of America’s end in the region
articles.body:
The beginning of America’s end in the region
The Iran newspaper examined the reasons behind the US withdrawal from Iraq after two decades. It reported that American forces officially left Iraq, ending a twenty-year military presence.
Since the start of US and Israeli military operations against Iran on February 28, American facilities in Iraq have reportedly been targeted in more than 600 attacks. Strikes in Baghdad also damaged the US Embassy and contributed to the early closure of a diplomatic support center. Pentagon officials have long been concerned that American positions across Iraq are vulnerable to Iranian missiles and drones. Washington may further reduce its military footprint in the region after reviewing damage inflicted on US bases in the Persian Gulf. The withdrawal is therefore presented as part of a broader effort to reduce exposure to future attacks and lessen strategic risks for American personnel and facilities.
Shargh: Negotiations in a fragile state
Shargh analyzed the uncertain state of indirect negotiations between Iran and the United States. While intensive discussions continue with the involvement of regional mediators, there is still no clear indication that the two sides have overcome their core disagreements. As a result, the current atmosphere remains fragile and ambiguous rather than moving decisively toward an agreement. Hope should not be confused with optimism. So, diplomacy should neither be dismissed as a failure nor viewed as nearing success simply because talks continue. With significant differences still unresolved and military tensions growing, unrealistic optimism could be as harmful as losing faith in diplomacy altogether. Careful assessment of political realities remains essential while the diplomatic process continues. It added that the persistence of negotiations alone does not guarantee a breakthrough and that both sides still face difficult political decisions before any meaningful progress can occur.
Sobh-e-No: Iran’s new strategy toward the Strait of Hormuz
Sobh-e-No argued that security incidents in the Strait of Hormuz have become a routine feature of regional news. The waterway has evolved from a transit route into a platform through which Iran demonstrates its determination to resist pressure and confront perceived aggression. Iran is asserting not only navigation rights but also its role in shaping security arrangements and deterrence. It described a new security and energy doctrine in which passage through the strait could become increasingly difficult unless Iran’s security concerns are recognized. Quoting parliamentary speaker Mohammad Bagher Ghalibaf, it argued that if Iran’s security is threatened, no infrastructure in the region will remain fully secure and energy exports throughout the region could be affected. The strait is an increasingly important element of Iran’s strategic leverage. According to this interpretation, Hormuz is no longer viewed merely as a commercial passage but as a key instrument in broader regional security calculations.
Javan: The enemy has no path to victory
In an article on America’s position in the region, Javan argued that Iran’s military capabilities and national unity have frustrated its adversaries. Following an Iranian missile strike on September 5 that reportedly wounded several American personnel, US naval forces moved farther away from the Sea of Oman into more distant areas of the Arabian Sea. This change reflects concerns about the vulnerability of American forces to Iranian missile capabilities. After more than seven months of pressure and conflict, the United States has failed to achieve major objectives against Iran and instead faces military, energy, and political challenges. It concluded that Iran’s strategic depth, public support, and deterrence capabilities have left its opponents without a viable path to victory. The editorial described these developments as evidence of the effectiveness of Iran’s broader defense strategy and claimed that continued pressure has strengthened rather than weakened the country's ability to resist external threats.
Arman-e-Melli: Why was Netanyahu’s UAE visit made public?
Arman-e-Melli discussed the disclosure of Netanyahu’s visit to the United Arab Emirates. The paper argued that after a recent trip to New York, Netanyahu concluded that Washington’s approach toward future confrontations involving Iran may be changing. According to the analysis, the United States appears less willing to place itself directly on the front line of future conflicts and may prefer regional partners to shoulder a greater share of the responsibilities and costs. The newspaper suggested that Netanyahu is concerned by this shift and is therefore working to strengthen a regional coalition. The paper also highlighted dissatisfaction among some Arab states. It said these countries had been promised relief from Iranian pressure in exchange for cooperation, financial contributions, and logistical support, yet those expectations were not fulfilled. As a result, the article argued, distrust toward the United States has grown among some Arab leaders, complicating Washington’s efforts to build a united regional front. This growing skepticism, the paper suggested, could influence future regional alignments and security arrangements while making cooperation among regional actors increasingly difficult.

articles.title: Russia plans to intensify attacks on Kyiv, Kharkiv and Odesa to isolate them in winter, FT says
articles.body:
Russia plans to intensify attacks on Kyiv, Kharkiv and Odesa to isolate them in winter, FT says
Russia is preparing to intensify attacks on Kyiv, Kharkiv and Odesa in an attempt to isolate them from the rest of Ukraine when winter arrives. Lviv also features in Russia's plans.
Source: Financial Times, citing President Volodymyr Zelenskyy and Ukrainian and European officials familiar with intelligence data
Quote from the FT: "Specifically, the president said, Russia was gearing up to intensify attacks on Ukraine's largest cities with the aim of isolating them from the rest of the country as winter sets in. Kyiv, the eastern stronghold of Kharkiv and the southern port city of Odesa are the main targets, according to Zelenskyy and a Ukrainian intelligence assessment described to the FT by Ukrainian and European officials."
Details: The Ukrainian and European security officials said that Lviv, an important logistics hub near the Polish border, also features in Russia's plans.
The Ukrainian officials told the FT that Moscow intends to strike nuclear facilities in order to disconnect them from the power grid. They said Russia wants to increase pressure on Kyiv to force it to give in to Russian demands in early 2027.
Another element of Russia's strategy, according to the officials, is to create a new flow of refugees to the EU. They fear that a large influx of Ukrainians would place additional pressure on countries where anti-immigration sentiment is growing.
Zelenskyy told the FT that Ukrainian intelligence services received information about Russian ruler Vladimir Putin ordering the removal of restrictions that had governed previous aerial campaigns. According to Zelenskyy, the intelligence included intercepted communications between Kremlin officials.
Quote from Zelenskyy: "He said there are no rules now."
Details: The president said Putin issued the order in September, when Russia began intensifying its airstrikes on Kyiv, hitting schools, hospitals and data centres.
According to Zelenskyy, the aim of the attacks is not only to destroy infrastructure but also "to pressure people", frighten civilians, force them to leave cities and weaken Ukraine's ability to continue the war.
Background: According to an approved Russian plan reportedly intercepted by Ukraine, Russia intends to use winter strikes to cut Ukrainian nuclear power plants off from the power grid by hitting targets within a kilometre of the plants, while also launching large-scale attacks on water supply systems.

articles.title: Lithuania tests Ukraine-made SkyFortress system for detecting low-flying drones – media
articles.body:
Lithuania has begun testing the Ukraine-made SkyFortress system, designed to monitor airspace and detect low-flying drones and cruise missiles via acoustic and radio signals, the LRT news portal reports.
The system uses artificial intelligence to detect and track low-flying drones or cruise missiles and classifies objects leaving acoustic or electromagnetic signatures in real time, Lithuania's Ministry of National Defence (KAM) announced on Friday.
"Aerial threats are evolving rapidly, so we are making decisions accordingly. Instead of building everything from scratch, we are adapting systems that are already operational in Ukraine. In doing so, we are consistently strengthening the entire air defense chain—from airspace monitoring to the interception and neutralization of aerial threats... SkyFortress complements the first stage of this chain—monitoring: the system uses artificial intelligence to detect and track low-flying drones or cruise missiles," said Lithuanian Minister of National Defence Robertas Kaunas.
According to the Lithuanian Ministry of National Defence, the contract signed this summer also covers the processing of data collected by sensors, the use of libraries containing digital acoustic and radio-frequency signatures based on unclassified data, and personnel training.
During the trials in Lithuania, the system's capabilities for detecting and identifying low-flying unmanned aerial vehicles will be evaluated.

articles.title: North Korea fires ballistic missile towards the sea, South Korea says
articles.body:
North Korea fires ballistic missile towards the sea, South Korea says
A ballistic missile fired from the North Korean port city of Wonsan flies more than 700km, South Korea’s military says.
South Korea’s military says North Korea has fired at least one ballistic missile towards the sea off its east coast.
South Korea’s Joint Chiefs of Staff said on Saturday morning that its northern neighbour fired a ballistic missile from the port city of Wonsan on the eastern shore of the Korean Peninsula and that it flew more than 700 kilometres (435 miles).
Seoul’s presidential national security office convened an emergency meeting to assess the situation after the launch, the president’s office said in a statement.
The South Korean military raised an alert for further launches and said it would share intelligence with the US and Japan.
Japan issued an emergency alert on Saturday, saying: “North Korea has launched a suspected ballistic missile.”
The US Pacific Command said it was aware of the launch, adding that it was consulting closely with US allies and partners.
“Based on current assessments, this event does not pose an immediate threat to US personnel or territory, or to our allies,” it said in a social media post.
The launch came a day after Kim Yo Jong, the powerful sister of North Korean leader Kim Jong Un, ridiculed South Korean demands for the North to apologise over landmine blasts that South Korea and the US-led United Nations Command said were caused by North Korean mines planted south of the Military Demarcation Line.
The blasts seriously injured three South Korean soldiers on a reconnaissance mission inside the 4km-wide (2.5-mile) border zone that stretches across the Korean Peninsula.
South Korea has also called on the North to halt recent efforts to fortify its border, including the installation of mines and anti-tank barriers.
Kim Yo Jong dismissed Seoul’s demands as “utterly pathetic”, saying the North intends to permanently cut ties with the South.
Saturday’s launch was the latest in a series of North Korean military displays in recent weeks, including tests of a purported hypersonic missile system, live-fire exercises and the commissioning of a new warship.

articles.title: World ‘amazed’ by Iranian nation’s ‘courage, resilience
articles.body:
“The whole world is closely following what is happening and is amazed at the courage and heroism of the Iranian nation and its resilience,” Putin said on Thursday at the plenary session of the 23rd annual meeting of the Valdai Discussion Club in Moscow.
He also pointed to a deep “bench” of high-level figures in Iran’s administration, armed forces and the Islamic Revolution Guards Corps (IRGC), “people ready for self-sacrifice in the name of their people.”
The remarks come months after the United States and the Israeli regime launched an unprovoked war of aggression against the Islamic Republic, assassinating senior political and military leaders. At the same time, Tehran was engaged in indirect talks with Washington.
Putin called the killing of Ali Larijani, secretary of Iran’s Supreme National Security Council, a tremendous mistake.
“Mr. Larijani — I knew him personally well — was a very positively minded person, ready to seek mutually acceptable compromises, above all in the interests of the Iranian people,” the Russian president said, according to TASS and RIA Novosti.
“Besides any legal assessments, this is of course a mistake, because such a person would be needed today to find compromises and solutions that could bring peace to the Persian Gulf,” he stated, accoridng to Press TV.
Putin said Larijani had visited Russia for talks on Iran’s enriched uranium and was a figure with whom constructive dialogue was possible.
He recalled that Tehran had at one stage agreed to a Russian proposal to relocate the material, an arrangement Washington, and even the Israeli regime, initially accepted.
Moscow, he said, had already carried out such a transfer in 2015 and remained ready to repeat it. The Americans later hardened their position and demanded that the uranium go only to the United States, after which Iran toughened its own stance.
Larijani, Putin said, then proposed a joint Russian-Iranian enterprise on Iranian territory to dilute the material.
The Russian leader added that Moscow’s offer remains on the table.
Putin also expressed hope that the Strait of Hormuz would reopen and that illegal sanctions against Iran would be lifted, “an objective that Tehran is rightfully pursuing.”
Once that happened, he said, there would be no reason for restrictions on passage through Hormuz or Bab el-Mandeb. “We support that.”
Iran and Russia have deepened strategic ties in recent years in the face of sweeping US sanctions and Western isolation. A 20-year comprehensive strategic partnership agreement was signed last year, and Moscow continues work on new units at the Bushehr nuclear power plant.
Russian officials have repeatedly condemned the US-Israeli war of aggression and offered to help mediate a settlement that respects Iran’s sovereignty.

articles.title: Ukrainian air defense shoot down 88 out of 108 enemy targets; enemy aerial weapons recorded at 11 locations
articles.body:
Ukrainian defense forces shot down 88 enemy drones overnight into Friday, though enemy aerial weapons struck seven locations, the Air Force of the Armed Forces of Ukraine reported.
"According to preliminary data, as of 08:00, air defense assets had shot down or suppressed 88 enemy UAVs, including Shahed and Gerbera types and other drone models," the message reads.
In total, overnight into October 2 (starting from 18:00 on October 1), the enemy launched an attack using 108 strike UAVs, including Shahed (47 of which were jet-powered), Gerbera, and Parodiya-type decoy drones, from the following directions: Bryansk and Primorsko-Akhtarsk (Russia), as well as the temporarily occupied territories of Donetsk region and the Autonomous Republic of Crimea (Hvardiyiske).

Enemy aerial weapons were recorded striking 11 locations, while debris from downed drones fell in five locations.
The attack is ongoing, with several enemy UAVs still in the airspace, the command added.

articles.title: Putin to escalate attacks on Ukraine as US midterm elections approach, Zelenskyy says
articles.body:
Kanyshai Butun
03 October 2026•Update: 03 October 2026
Russia is likely to intensify attacks on Ukraine as the US midterm elections approach, Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said on Friday.
Speaking to Spanish daily El Pais, Zelenskyy said Russian President Vladimir Putin is seeking to demonstrate he is not deterred by Western sanctions or pressure from European countries.
“Putin will escalate closer to elections to show that he's so strong and he isn't afraid of Europeans, doesn't feel sanctions and of course he gives his messages all over the United States,” he said, referring to the US midterm elections weeks away on Nov. 3.
Zelenskyy said he warned US negotiators that Russia would intensify attacks around the elections, particularly against civilians. “They want Ukrainians and especially from the capital, to leave the capital,” he said, stressing Kyiv remains strong despite the attacks.
He said Russia is conducting attacks around the clock, with hundreds of drones launched daily.
Zelenskyy argued that Moscow's strategy is aimed at pushing Ukraine into “chaos,” and that Kyiv is seeking additional funding and adapting its approach to the war, which continues since February 2022.
He also accused China and India of helping Russia circumvent sanctions, and providing machinery.
He claimed Iran was helping Moscow with expertise and technology related to the war, particularly drones.

articles.title: Ukraine Successfully Uses Domestic FP-7 Ballistic Missile for the First Time, Zelenskyy Says
articles.body:

Ukraine Successfully Uses Domestic FP-7 Ballistic Missile for the First Time, Zelenskyy Says
Ukrainian forces have marked the first successful operational deployment of the domestically developed FP-7 tactical ballistic missile during Russia’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine, President Volodymyr Zelenskyy confirmed on October 1.
Footage shared on official social channels captured the launch from an undisclosed firing position.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
“Ukrainian tactical ballistics. FP-7. First combat use. Thank you for the result. Next is production. Glory to Ukraine!” Zelenskyy stated in a message accompanying the video.
The deployment marks a significant transition for Ukraine’s defense industry as it expands domestic production of long-range strike systems.
Ukrainian missile maker Fire Point updated its FP-7.x Freyja interceptor with a combined infrared and radar seeker, replacing the missile's previous infrared-only design.
The dual-mode seeker allowed the system to track targets using both heat signatures and radar reflections during its final flight phase, helping maintain lock-on even through bad weather or decoys.
Developed as part of a joint initiative with nine other European nations, the 7.25-meter-long interceptor was designed to reach speeds up to 7,200 kilometers per hour to counter short-range ballistic threats during Russia’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine.
Fire Point made significant progress on its domestic missile program during Russia’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine, aiming to complete its 850-kilometer FP-9 ballistic missile by late 2026.
Company CEO Iryna Terekh revealed in a September interview that the shorter-range FP-7 had already entered codification after roughly two years of rapid development, costing approximately $200 million for research and initial production setup.
The company worked to finish testing the long-range FP-9—designed to potentially reach distant targets, including Moscow—while overcoming tight international export controls by engineering critical components internally.

articles.title: 'He has good ideas': Putin lauds PM Modi's peace push to end Russia-Ukraine war
articles.body:
Russian President Vladimir Putin on Thursday lauded Prime Minister Narendra Modi’s efforts to seek an end to the Ukraine conflict, saying that he has “good ideas” for achieving a peaceful resolution.
"Prime Minister Narendra Modi is one of those world leaders who, despite our very good and even friendly relations, personal good relations, constantly raises the question and asks the question about putting an end to the conflict in Ukraine," Putin said.
Asked about the issue at the Valdai Club forum, Putin said Prime Minister Narendra Modi has been actively working to find mutually acceptable solutions to the Ukraine conflict.
"He has an avid interest and very good ideas aimed at finding mutually acceptable solutions. In that sense, naturally, the Prime Minister takes a neutral position but with an interest in the end of the conflict. I think it's my duty to say that directly. And we are thankful to the Prime Minister for his ideas," Putin said.
Putin thanked PM Modi for his efforts and continued support for resolving the Ukraine conflict through dialogue.
"We are thankful for his desire to put an end to this conflict through peaceful means and as soon as possible," he added.
Prime Minister Modi and Putin last met in September on the sidelines of the 18th BRICS Summit in New Delhi, where they discussed strengthening trade ties, including the implementation of the Programme for Economic Cooperation 2030, along with cooperation in infrastructure, energy, technology, defence and culture.
PM Modi has repeatedly called for peace, stressing that India has maintained a principled and humanitarian approach to the Russia-Ukraine conflict.
"India has maintained a principled and humanitarian stance on the conflict which is equally appreciated by both President Putin and President Zelenskyy. In line with this, both the leaders spoke to me to share their perspectives on the developments related to the conflict. I reiterated India's principled and consistent stand and encouraged dialogue and diplomacy to resolve the conflict," the Prime Minister said during an interview with Japanese news outlet 'The Yomiuri Shimbun' while on a visit to the country in August.
Responding to a question on India’s role in peace efforts between the two countries, Prime Minister Modi said, "I have already indicated India's willingness to support meaningful efforts aimed at achieving a peaceful resolution of the conflict. I believe, by virtue of our good relations with both sides, including key stakeholders, we can strengthen efforts dedicated to the restoration of an early and lasting peace in Ukraine."
This comes as Putin reiterated Moscow’s long-standing position that Russia has no plans to attack European countries, while warning that it would respond to any aggression with “all weapons” at its disposal.
He also accused Western countries, particularly in Europe, of escalating tensions by discussing preparations for a possible war with Moscow, conducting military drills in the Baltic Sea and seizing Russian vessels.
European leaders and intelligence agencies have warned that Russia could be capable of launching an attack on another country within the next few years, particularly if it emerges victorious from the war in Ukraine.

articles.title: Russian troops shoot down own Mi-8, killing three crew
articles.body:
- Russian forces shot down their own Mi-8 helicopter over the Voronezh region on Oct. 1, killing all three crew members.
- A ground-based air defense crew mistook the helicopter for an enemy drone, the latest in a series of Russian friendly fire helicopter losses.
Russian forces shot down one of their own Mi-8 military helicopters over the Voronezh region on Oct. 1, killing all three crew members.
The helicopter was hit by a Russian Su-35 fighter during operations to move aircraft out of the way of a Ukrainian drone strike, sources said. The Su-35 crew apparently mistook the helicopter for a Ukrainian drone.
The Mi-8 came down in a field in the Anninsky district, about 80 km (50 miles) from the city of Voronezh and roughly 200 km (125 miles) from the Ukrainian border. The crew of three, a pilot, a navigator and a gunner, were killed, Russian Telegram channel Mash reported on the evening of the crash.
The Mi-8 is the Soviet-designed twin-engine transport helicopter that forms the backbone of Russia’s military rotary-wing fleet. Armed versions carry rockets and machine guns and are used for troop transport, resupply, medical evacuation and, increasingly, for hunting Ukrainian long-range drones at low altitude.
The Su-35 is Russia’s most advanced fighter in wide service and is regularly sent up to intercept Ukrainian drones over Russian territory. A slow, low-flying helicopter can be hard to tell apart from a large drone on radar or at night, especially when Russian pilots and air defense crews are working in the same airspace during a raid.
Russian officials have not publicly acknowledged that the helicopter was downed by friendly fire. Several Russian military bloggers have hinted at the cause without stating it directly.
“The cause is a classic one, which humanity is unlikely ever to defeat, despite AI, robots, neural networks, ‘friend or foe’ and other wonders of science and technology,” wrote Ilya Tumanov, who runs the Fighterbomber Telegram channel and is known for his ties to Russian military aviation.
The shootdown is the latest in a series of friendly fire losses involving Russian helicopters, many of them during Ukrainian drone raids.
On July 2, a Ka-52 attack helicopter crashed in the same Voronezh region. Russian military blogger Vladimir Romanov said it was hit by a Verba shoulder-fired missile fired by a mobile fire group from Russia’s BARS reserve units, according to The Insider. One crew member was killed.
On March 3, Russian forces likely shot down one of their own helicopters near Millerovo in the Rostov region during a Ukrainian drone attack, The Defence Blog reported, after pro-government Russian sources said air defenses had mistaken it for a drone.
A Russian fighter jet has been linked to at least one earlier case. When a Ka-52M was shot down during a counter-drone operation in late 2025, the Telegram channel Pozivnoi Katsman suggested the strike may have come from a Russian fighter.
In June 2024, air defenses near Anapa shot down a Russian Ka-29 helicopter, killing all four people on board. By late 2025, The Insider counted at least 17 Russian aircraft lost to friendly fire since the start of the full-scale invasion of Ukraine.

articles.title: USA Imposes Sanctions on A7 Network, Which Supplied Components and Equipment to Russia’s Military-Industrial Complex
articles.body:
The U.S. Department of the Treasury has imposed sanctions against the A7 shadow banking network, which is linked to Russia and Iran.
This was reported on the department’s website.
The Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) added the A7 network to its sanctions list as a transnational criminal organization.
According to the department, the network is headed by Ilan Shor, a Moldovan-Israeli oligarch who is already under sanctions and has been convicted, and the system itself was used to circumvent sanctions and launder money.
The A7 network was used to finance the Iranian Revolutionary Guard Corps and the Hamas group, as well as to conduct transactions related to the sale of Iranian oil and the purchase of weapons.
The network used intermediaries in third countries, fictitious trade documents, and hidden VPN networks to funnel money through the international financial system.
All assets and property of the A7 network in the United States or under the control of U.S. citizens have been frozen, and any transactions involving them are prohibited under penalty of civil and criminal sanctions.
As a reminder, A7 developed a large-scale network of front companies that allows Russia to circumvent Western sanctions and purchase goods for its military-industrial complex
According to Western intelligence reports, Shor oversees these activities under the direct supervision of the Russian president’s administration.
Kyrgyzstan has long served as the main financial hub for the A7 schemes. Over $100 million in U.S. dollars and Chinese yuan passed through the bank accounts of local front companies.
To throw international oversight off track, the network created a special AI-based program that automatically forged invoices and customs documents. Instead of dual-use electronics, the documents listed civilian goods, such as car mats or light boxes.
Among the purchased goods, investigators discovered steel production equipment from the Chinese company Xi’an Heavy Equipment, which is used in the manufacture of ammunition and armor. Payments were also made for Nvidia servers for AI development and video components for Walksnail drones.
