articles.title: Ukraine secures 20mm ammunition for F-16 jets to counter jet-powered drones – Sybiha
articles.body:
Several partners, including Spain, Belgium and Poland, will soon deliver 20mm rounds for F-16 fighter jets to Ukraine, which are effective against Russian jet-powered drones, Foreign Minister Andriy Sybiha said.
"We spent the whole day (Wednesday – Interfax-Ukraine) working on the 20mm caliber issue. And we succeeded. I believe we've secured a solution on this caliber for a significant period ahead. I thank all our ambassadors. The president was calling leaders from the front line. The defense minister was calling his counterparts. I was calling foreign ministers. This is critical. Given that we haven't yet built up sufficient capacity to shoot down jet-powered drones, and with new strikes being prepared, it was critically important to help our military bring these drones down. Right now, aside from air defense systems, which are too expensive to use constantly against drones, the most effective tool is the F-16 fighter jet. That's why we're now using them extensively," Sybiha said.
He separately thanked Spain, Belgium and Poland, which has already begun the delivery process, adding that Ukraine will have the necessary ammunition very soon.
"And this is very important, because diplomacy right now is about concrete things — above all, defense capability. I think this is one of our success stories, bringing things together across many levels and sectors. And for all of us, it means fewer hits on Kyiv and other cities," the foreign minister said.
Bloomberg earlier reported, citing people familiar with the matter, that Ukraine wants to purchase tens of thousands of 20mm rounds for F-16 jets to shoot down Russian jet-powered drones. According to the news agency, intercepting one drone takes about 150 rounds on average, with daily demand potentially reaching around 10,000 rounds.

articles.title: Russian Drone Strikes 25-Story Kyiv Apartment Building as More Than 100 UAVs Target Ukraine Overnight

Russian Drone Strikes 25-Story Kyiv Apartment Building as More Than 100 UAVs Target Ukraine Overnight
A Russian drone attack on Kyiv killed at least one person and injured two others after a high-rise residential building was struck in the city’s Darnytskyi district, Ukraine’s State Emergency Service (SES) reported.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
According to the SES, the strike hit a 25-story residential building, sparking a fire on the 24th and 25th floors. Emergency crews extinguished the blaze, which spread across approximately 120 square meters, while around 40 square meters of the building sustained structural damage.
Rescuers brought two injured people out of the building and handed them over to medical personnel. The body of one person was discovered during firefighting operations, while six other residents were evacuated.
Emergency crews remain at the site, dismantling damaged structures and extinguishing remaining hotspots.
The strike was part of a wider overnight Russian aerial attack against Ukraine involving more than 100 strike drones, nearly 50 of which were jet-powered, Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said.
According to Zelenskyy, Ukrainian forces intercepted most of the incoming drones, although several strikes were recorded. In Kyiv, Russian Shahed-type drones struck the city’s Pivdennyi Bridge several times during the attack.
Zelenskyy also said Russia’s ability to increase production of drones and missiles continues to depend heavily on foreign-made components despite Moscow’s efforts to localize manufacturing.
“These supply chains run through Europe, the United States, China, Japan, and many other countries. Most of these companies are well-known manufacturers, yet their components continue to reach Russia,” Zelenskyy said. “Every Russian drone can realistically be stopped while still on the production line. What is needed is the political will of these countries. If the Kremlin has chosen more strikes, sanctions must work and be strengthened.”
The latest attack comes shortly after another Russian drone struck the grounds of Ukraine’s Institute for Nuclear Research in Kyiv, home to the VVR-M research reactor.
Ukraine’s State Nuclear Regulatory Inspectorate reported on October 1 that the strike occurred at 6:18 p.m. local time on September 30. Citing the Institute for Nuclear Research of the National Academy of Sciences of Ukraine, the regulator said the attack caused a fire that was quickly extinguished, with no casualties reported.

articles.title: Zelensky Orders Housing Support Options for Teachers Ahead of Education Workers’ Day
articles.body:
President Volodymyr Zelensky visited one of Ukraine’s schools ahead of Education Workers’ Day – celebrated annually on the first Sunday in October – just a day after Russian forces struck a school in Kyiv with a drone carrying a 50-kilogram (110-pound) warhead.
In a statement following the visit on Friday, Oct. 2, Zelensky said he had spoken with students about their studies and dreams, while also discussing salaries and housing with teachers.
JOIN US ON TELEGRAM
Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official.
He thanked educators for their daily work, saying that the country always remembers them.
“Thank you for the knowledge and support you give to children,” Zelensky said, adding that “it is very important that education in Ukraine is developing.”
Housing and pay discussed
Local authorities have been instructed to work out options for additional housing support programs, including under the eOselia – a state-backed mortgage program designed to help Ukrainian citizens purchase residential property through low-interest loans.
Meanwhile, salaries remain among teachers’ most pressing concerns particularly as their work grows increasingly dangerous.
In recent months, Russian forces have significantly intensified strikes on civilian infrastructure, increasingly targeting schools, hospitals and offices, in what Zelensky earlier described as an attempt to disrupt ordinary life.
So far, the teachers’ base salaries have already risen twice this year – by 30% earlier in 2026 and by another 20% on Sept. 1.
G7 Members Agree to Release Up to 100M Barrels of Oil Reserves to Curb Fuel Prices
Funding new shelters while strikes continue
According to Zelensky, the discussion also covered the need for proper shelters at educational institutions, an issue he said would be raised with both government and local authorities.
On Thursday, a Russian Geran-4 drone hit a school in Kyiv’s Solomianskyi district while more than 100 children and 60 teachers were sheltering inside.
The warhead broke through the floor between the second and third floors, but did not detonate. According to specialists, an explosion would have collapsed all four floors of the building.
On that same day, Zelensky condemned Russian strikes on schools and kindergartens, calling them “a deliberate tactic.” He ordered the school’s prompt restoration and energy independence.
During Friday’s school visit, Zelensky said it was good to see children able to study in person, interact with one another and stay in direct contact with their teachers.
Ukraine opened the doors of at least 25,000 educational institutions on Sept. 1 under new safety rules as the war continues in its fifth year. Currently, around 83% of school students have access to shelters.
That figure stood at just 10% in 2022.
Meanwhile, Ukraine is building another 131 state-funded shelters, including 18 underground kindergartens, and aims to raise shelter access for students and preschool children to 92% by the end of 2027.
Learning formats, however, still vary depending on local security conditions. In the Kharkiv region, where risks remain particularly high, hybrid learning is available only in underground schools and reaches about 30% of students.
In Kyiv, 91% of preschool children and students have access to shelters, though 23 kindergartens and 20 schools still lack their own and hold classes in rented safe spaces.
“We are doing everything to make the most important dream of children and all of us adults come true as soon as possible – to achieve piece,” Zelensky said.
“And it will certainly happen,” he continued.
‘No rules now’
In an interview with the Financial Times published earlier on Friday, Zelensky said Russian President Vladimir Putin had ordered his military commanders in September to abandon previous constraints on aerial attacks and intensify strikes on civilian sites.
“He said there are no rules now,” according to Zelensky, citing intelligence obtained by Ukrainian agencies.
Zelensky gave the interview inside the bomb shelter of the Kyiv school struck on Thursday.
Kremlin spokesperson Dmitry Peskov told the FT that Russian forces do not strike schools or hospitals.
So far, Ukraine’s Education Ministry has recorded more than 4,700 attacks on educational institutions since the start of Russia’s full-scale invasion in February 2022.

articles.title: Up to 1,000 missiles, drones and bombs: Russia plans the "most powerful blow" in an attempt to "freeze" Ukraine - NYT
articles.body:
Up to 1,000 missiles, drones and bombs: Russia plans the "most powerful blow" in an attempt to "freeze" Ukraine - NYT
Kyiv • UNN
Russia is planning massive strikes on Ukraine’s energy and water infrastructure.
This winter, Russia is preparing powerful strikes against Ukraine’s energy infrastructure in an effort to cause a collapse and a humanitarian crisis in Ukraine. Moscow plans to use up to 1,000 missiles, drones, and bombs. The New York Times reports, according to UNN.
Details
According to the publication, during a meeting in Paris, Energy Minister Denys Shmyhal showed European partners a plan intercepted from Russia that envisages "forcing Ukrainians into submission through the cold."
"Shmyhal described the document as an intercepted Russian plan aimed at causing the collapse of the energy system through systematic attacks. The plan outlines a campaign of strikes involving up to 1,000 missiles, drones, and bombs. They will target a wide range of facilities, including electrical substations, hydroelectric and thermal power plants, as well as boiler houses," the publication writes.
It is noted that the greatest concern is that, according to the document, Russia intends to force Ukraine’s three operating nuclear power plants—the foundation of its energy infrastructure—to shut down by striking with missiles the electrical distribution substations that connect them to the power grid. These substations are located less than a kilometer from the reactors.
The plan also states that Moscow will target Ukraine’s water supply system with dozens of ballistic missiles and glide bombs, including pumping stations and treatment facilities.
"Russia has never previously carried out large-scale strikes against such facilities. Ukrainian officials have privately expressed concern that the country has limited contingency plans in the event of serious disruptions to the water supply. The ultimate goal is to cut off Ukraine’s major cities from electricity, heating, and water, which could cause a humanitarian crisis. Kyiv, Kharkiv, and Odesa have been identified as the main targets: the plan is to reduce electricity supplies in these cities by 90%, cut heat supplies by up to 90%, and seriously disrupt the operation of the sewage system," the publication adds.
Previously
On September 30, the Russians launched massive strikes against Ukraine’s energy infrastructure.

articles.title: How a failed attack in Leipzig revealed a wider Russian campaign
articles.body:
BERLIN — If the explosive had actually detonated, investigators might not have gotten their clearest look yet at what European officials believe is a wider Russian campaign of attacks.
On Aug. 4, a drone struck the wing of a Ukrainian aircraft at Germany’s Leipzig Airport and fell onto the tarmac. Strapped beneath it was a tin can packed with explosives. The device remained intact.
That gave investigators something unusually valuable: the bomb itself. The can was sealed with a metal plate stamped with seven circular indentations, according to an investigative file from German federal police reviewed by the Axel Springer Global Reporters Network.
Advertisement
It wasn’t the first time such an improvised explosive had been discovered on European soil. Almost two years earlier, on Aug. 20, 2024, police investigators arrived at a cemetery in Kaunas, Lithuania, with a bomb disposal team. They had received a highly sensitive tip from Poland concerning explosives and a Ukrainian man alleged to have deposited them there for Russian intelligence, according to investigation files from the Lithuanian Criminal Police Bureau.
At a weathered grave, beneath artificial flowers and concrete slabs, officers recovered a plastic bag containing two tin cans. According to their labels, they contained corn. Forensic analysis, however, found they contained 968 grams of explosives, around 700 grams of TNT equivalent per can — roughly the lethal force of four hand grenades.
In January and June 2025, investigators unearthed more explosive-filled cans at various locations in Lithuania. Four were fitted with metal plates stamped with circular indentations. Investigators say they were intended to act as projectiles in an explosion. Forensic examinations found that the plates were highly likely to have been manufactured by the same machine, according to a report by the Forensic Science Service of the Police Department of Lithuania.
The device attached to the drone in Leipzig bore striking similarities to those recovered from the Lithuanian caches, including the explosive-filled tin can and the stamped metal plate.
The resemblance alone does not establish that the devices belonged to the same operation. But two Western security officials, who were granted anonymity to discuss security matters, say it fits with other evidence — including travel records, suspected logistics routes and intelligence reporting — linking the cases to a broader Russian intelligence mission.
The resemblance is one element of a pattern that German and European officials believe points to an escalating campaign of sabotage and violence across Europe, planned and coordinated by Russian intelligence officers.
Advertisement
According to three senior German and European security officials, the main driver of the campaign is Russia’s GRU military intelligence service. At its core, they say, is Unit 29155 — a military intelligence outfit linked to destabilization operations in European countries.
German authorities say they expect further “hybrid” operations as Russian President Vladimir Putin seeks to disrupt military support for Ukraine and raise the political cost of backing Kyiv.
“The population is supposed to fear a direct military confrontation and therefore question the purpose of supporting Ukraine,” said Gerhard Schindler, former president of Germany’s BND Federal Intelligence Service. “That is why he will increase both the military pressure on Ukraine and the hybrid pressure on the West.”
In response to an inquiry, the Russian Embassy in Berlin denied any Russian involvement in acts of sabotage in Europe. “We firmly reject the baseless allegations concerning Russia’s purported involvement in the alleged ‘drone incident’ at Leipzig Airport, as well as in other ‘sabotage activities,’” a spokesperson said.
Russian connection
One of the clearest trails leads to Oleg Levushkin, a dual Latvian-Russian national whom German authorities suspect of helping prepare the Leipzig attack. According to a senior German security official and investigative files reviewed by the Axel Springer Global Reporters Network, Levushkin is not a low-level recruit but a GRU-linked logistics operative with longstanding ties to senior figures in Russian military intelligence.
On social media, Levushkin offers glimpses of a seemingly ordinary life: motorcycle trips to Crimea and the Hungarian-Serbian border, a visit to Volgograd’s Motherland Calls statue, and time spent fishing, skiing and travelling across Europe with his family. The Axel Springer Global Reporters Network reviewed his profiles on the social media sites VKontakte and Odnoklassniki.
Advertisement
According to one German intelligence official and documents related to the case, investigators believe Levushkin traveled via Turkey to Berlin Brandenburg Airport in late July to prepare the Leipzig operation. He rented a car there on July 27, according to location data mentioned in German investigation files. Investigators believe the explosives entered Germany via Bulgaria and Serbia in the cavities of long-haul trucks, according to the senior official from Germany.
On July 31, the rental car was recorded near Leipzig Airport, where investigators believe he was carrying out reconnaissance ahead of the attempted attack, according to documents from the investigation. Levushkin did not reply to a request for comment.
Levushkin’s alleged links reach into the upper ranks of Russian military intelligence. According to reporting by German media as well as the London-based non-profit Dossier Center, he has maintained a close relationship for roughly two decades with GRU Colonel Denis Smolyaninov.
A December 2025 report by the State Security Department of Lithuania says Smolyaninov is “the head of the GRU’s Ukraine department, specializes in psychological operations and is linked to covert sabotage campaigns organized in Europe using the social network Telegram.”
According to the 2025 intelligence report, Smolyaninov also coordinated the activities of the Russian-linked private military company Longifolia, registered in Panama. European investigators suspect several shareholders in the company of involvement in an operation where incendiary devices were sent to Poland and Britain, according to Lithuanian investigation files. One of the parcels caught fire on July 20, 2024 while being transferred at Leipzig Airport. Another ignited two days later in Birmingham, England.
Lithuanian intelligence explicitly attributes the parcel operation to the GRU, and in particular to Unit 29155. A November 2025 dossier by Lithuania’s State Security Department reviewed by the Axel Springer Global Reporters Network describes the unit as being “tasked with carrying out killings, operations to destroy infrastructure, disrupting the activities of institutions that run counter to Russia's interests, and terrorist attacks in Western countries.”
Advertisement
Its agents, the November 2025 dossier says, are “trained in handling explosives and firearms [and] can identify human sources and build agent networks.”
Unit 29155 has previously been linked by Western governments and investigators to a series of operations across Europe, including explosions at ammunition depots in Bulgaria and the Czech Republic and the 2018 poisoning of former Russian spy Sergei Skripal in Britain, according to the dossier. The Lithuanian dossier also links the unit to more recent arson attacks, including at an Ikea store in Vilnius and a post office in Bucharest.
The Russian government’s press service did not respond to a request for comment about GRU Unit 29155 and Smolyaninov.
German officials have blamed the GRU for a failed incendiary attack on a defense company in Munich in September, while Estonia’s intelligence service said this week in a public statement that an August arson attack on defense company Milrem Robotics had been commissioned by Russian intelligence.
European security authorities interviewed by the Axel Springer Global Reporters Network expect such operations to increase in the coming months, with defense companies, critical infrastructure and people involved in supporting Ukraine among the potential targets.
The Kremlin views its relationship with Europe as a “systemic conflict,” said Omar Haijawi-Pirchner, the former head of Austria’s domestic intelligence service. Like others interviewed for this article, he said he expects an increase in drone incursions and hybrid attacks.
Advertisement
“We believe that Russia is currently under remarkably high pressure — probably higher than at any previous point during the war and at any time during Vladimir Putin’s tenure,” said a senior NATO official who was granted anonymity to discuss security matters.
“From the Kremlin’s point of view, the best option available to them seems to be to intensify the hybrid campaign they are waging against the West,” the official added.
Lennart Pfahler is an investigative reporter at WELT. Ibrahim Naber is a foreign correspondent for WELT. Alexander Dinger is head of investigations at WELT. Richard Holmes is forensic investigations editor at the Telegraph.
The Axel Springer Global Reporters Network harnesses the resources of the company’s newsrooms to publish ambitious scoops, investigations, interviews, opinion pieces and analysis. It allows journalists — including those from POLITICO, Business Insider, WELT, BILD, The Telegraph, Onet and Fakt — to collaborate on major stories for an international audience of hundreds of millions across platforms: online, print, TV and audio.

articles.title: Ukraine’s Partners Have Accelerated Repair of Ukrainian F-16s
articles.body:
Ukraine’s industrial partners have accelerated the repair of Ukrainian F-16 fighter jets following intensive use.
This was reported by a spokesperson for the Ukrainian Ministry of Foreign Affairs, Heorhiy Tykhyi.
“Our industrial partners providing technical support are not only continuing to deliver the aircraft after major overhauls, but are also doing so increasingly quickly. The turnaround times are getting shorter, not longer,” the spokesperson said.
Problems with maintaining these aircraft stem, in particular, from the fact that some components for early F-16 models are no longer manufactured, and they are becoming increasingly difficult to procure.
“However, recent reports about an allegedly catastrophically low level of aircraft readiness and excessively long maintenance times simply do not correspond to reality,” Tykhyi noted.
Recently, Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy told the Financial Times that about half of the F-16 fighter jets have been in Europe for repairs and maintenance for a long time.
According to him, the return of some aircraft is being delayed to such an extent that Ukraine is losing precious time when the fighter jets are most needed to defend its airspace.
Zelensky noted that Kyiv is seeking assistance from Western partners to shift most of the maintenance work to Ukrainian territory. He said that keeping the aircraft closer to the theater of operations will allow them to be returned to service more quickly.
As of the end of September, Ukrainian pilots flying F-16 fighter jets had already shot down more than 3,150 enemy aerial targets.
Due to a shortage of AIM-120 and AIM-9 air-to-air missiles, Ukrainian F-16 pilots are increasingly firing at drones with 20-mm cannons. To address this, Ukraine is working on a large-scale procurement of 20-mm ammunition for the F-16s.
Last year, to support pre-flight training for F-16 fighter jets, the Come Back Alive Foundation provided the military with mobile maintenance systems.

articles.title: Digested week: My heart sank at seeing Labour’s ‘Hope Again’ conference slogan. But then came Andy Burnham | John Crace
articles.body:
Monday
Words I thought I’d never write. We owe a huge debt of gratitude to the Tory party. Look, I know we ended up with Theresa May and Boris Johnson in the Conservative party leadership contests of 2016 and 2019 – and they were shockers, both of them – but at least the Tory MPs twice ensured we dodged the bullet of Michael Gove. Last week, Sky broadcast The War Game, a reality show for superannuated politicians and former senior civil servants and military officers. The setup was that the Russians had engineered an attack on a British warship in the North Sea and over the course of four episodes set in the Cobra emergency situation room, the assembled cast had to figure how to respond. We were left hanging at the final credits, but a nuclear apocalypse felt like the most likely outcome. And for that we have The Govester to thank. He was playing the prime minister and – to be blunt – he had an absolute shocker. For the first two episodes he seemed to be in a coma. All he could manage was to repeat back what the last person had said to him and then shout “asap”. But that was far more preferable to the Gove that turned up for the last two episodes. Despite frequently being warned about the dangers of escalation and the inadequacy of the UK war machine, Mikey kept on taking the option that would get the most people killed. Why bomb one Russian city when you can bomb two? The game ended with what were almost certainly nuclear warheads minutes away from destroying a major city in the UK. Still, Gove wasn’t the only deadbeat. Nicola Sturgeon, acting the deputy prime minister, was as hopeless as you would expect of someone who failed to notice her kitchen filling up with new appliances. It was terrifying TV. Not so much in the premise. What was really scary was the knowledge that our politicians were even more clueless than the rest of us.
Tuesday
Pep Guardiola timed his departure well. Perhaps he had an inkling of what was coming down the road. The top bods at Manchester City have predictably responded to being found guilty of 114 charges of financial misconduct by insisting they will appeal and drag out proceedings. No doubt hoping that either the charges will go away or they can reduce the potential penalties. I wouldn’t bet against it. My main reaction when the news broke that City had been found guilty was surprise. Not that I thought they were innocent – there wasn’t a football fan who didn’t think they were bang to rights – but that the Premier League finally got round to doing something about it. The earliest charges date back 17 years and it just felt as if nothing was ever going to happen. What happens next is anyone’s guess. Obviously any fine would be more or less meaningless as the City owners have bottomless pockets. Removing titles is equally pointless. Who would turn up for an open-topped bus ride for a cup won years ago? The issue of compensation is more nuanced. Because where does it all end? Can I file a claim for mental distress, not to mention the travel and ticket costs, for having paid to see countless matches which had been financially rigged against Spurs that are now null and void? There again, I have had two of my best nights ever at the Etihad. When Spurs secured a Champions League place for the first time and when we won a Champions League quarter-final thanks to City having an injury time goal disallowed by VAR. There has also been talk of a 50-point deduction. Probably not enough to ensure they finish behind Spurs. We’re only five games into the season and already 13 points adrift.
Wednesday
By a very rough calculation, I reckon I’ve spent the best part of six months of my life at party conferences. And yes, I am a lucky man to be doing a job I love, but it is sometimes hard not to feel a wee bit jaded during the conference season. Living out of a suitcase and listening to a series of speeches from politicians who can often barely hold their own attention let alone an audience’s, can make the days feel very long. And I was prepared for more of the same when I arrived in Liverpool for this week’s Labour conference. My heart sank when I saw banners, mugs and T-shirts with the slogan “Hope Again” everywhere. There’s nothing more guaranteed to see me sliding into despair then people loudly instructing me to look on the bright side. To make it worse, I had to endure the chancellor, John Healey, lie through his teeth and say “I am an optimist”. You’re fooling no one, John. He had clearly been told to be upbeat and dropped the H-word about 20 times. But on every occasion he gasped “Hope” it looked like a dagger had been plunged into his heart. Come the end, the whole audience was signing up to Dignitas. But then, Andy Burnham. By far and away the most powerful, emotional and gamechanging leader’s speech of the century. I can’t tell you how rare it is for a politician to hold an audience in his hands for an hour and say exactly what he thinks, feels and believes. Only Nigel Farage comes close, though what he offers is only anger, grievance and division. Burnham was offering something else. I may not have agreed with the details of all of it and most of it may never happen, but this was a world of social care, closer ties to the EU and electoral reform to which most in the socially progressive world could sign up. It was as though the sun had come out.
Thursday
When I turned 50, friends used to assure me that 50 was the new 40. That felt almost true. I can remember my Dad’s 50th birthday and he looked ancient to me. For my 60th birthday, those same friends were confident that 60 was the new 50. There was the slight drawback that I had already had a knee replacement, but I still went to the gym four times a week and my career was in good shape. Next week I will be 70. No one has even tentatively suggested that 70 might be the new 60. Seventy is unequivocally old. Some might even say that 70 is the new 80. I am now undeniably at the business end of life. My children are both in their 30s and have gone on to live their best lives. Much of my work as a parent is done. I had a heart attack two and a half years ago and am doing my best to avoid another one. My wife is being treated for cancer. Yes, I still enjoy my work and go to the gym four times a week but, as the great Leonard Cohen so exquisitely put it, “I ache in the places where I used to play”. It’s been weird watching the series 70 Up. I’ve always felt a kinship with the men and women in the documentary because I’ve followed them since I was 14 when they were the same age and felt grateful that my own life had not been part of the social experiment. But now we hear that 70 is to be the end point of the series. As though the lives have come to a meaningful end. I’m not quite so ready to go quietly into the night. I plan to keep going for a while yet. And for those of you who would like to join me trying to make sense of the world, there are still tickets available for my shows at the Komedia in Brighton on 18 October and at the MAC in Birmingham on 31 October.
Friday
My happy place. The Celebrity Traitors is back and all is more or less well with the world. The first episode may not have quite lived up to the hype but as a scene setter it was more than good enough. The side missions increasingly feel pointless – we all know everyone is in it for their ego and career rather than the charity cash – and in any case the celebs always need time to bed in and show their true colours. Though not Ross Kemp, who was showing worrying levels of paranoia from the off. Who will be the Alan Carr, a true star of the series? Who will be the Stephen Fry, all affected diffidence? And who will be the David Olusoga, the one who tried to work things through with careful intelligence yet always comes to the wrong conclusion? The first to show his face was actor Michael Sheen who declared that he didn’t know what he was letting himself in for and then said “I’m a huge fan of the game”. Hmm. Maybe he’s been watching with his eyes closed. The rest of the celebs trooped in one by one and we were up and running. Things soon hotted up when Claudia nominated Maya – never heard of her – and Richard E Grant as traitors. Richard was so thrilled – he had been desperate to be a traitor – that he promptly blew the show wide open by telling all the other celebs that he was a traitor. A move that may prove to be utterly inspired or catastrophically dim. Given a night to sleep on it, Richard was inclined to believe it might have been the latter and spent the rest of the day trying to persuade everyone it was a bluff. Sit back and enjoy the next five weeks.

articles.title: Putin Ordered Russian Military to Abandon Any Restraints on Airstrikes, Zelenskyy Tells FT

Putin Ordered Russian Military to Abandon Any Restraints on Airstrikes, Zelenskyy Tells FT
Russian leader Vladimir Putin ordered his military leadership in September to abandon previous restraints on air attacks against Ukraine, President Volodymyr Zelenskyy told the Financial Times, citing intelligence obtained from intercepted Kremlin communications on October 1.
According to Zelenskyy, Ukrainian intelligence learned that Putin issued the directive as Russia began sharply intensifying strikes against civilian infrastructure, including schools, hospitals and data centers.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
“He said there are no rules now,” Zelenskyy said.
The Ukrainian President said the order came as Moscow stepped up attacks on Kyiv and other major cities, marking a broader effort to increase pressure on Ukraine through strikes far beyond the battlefield.
Zelenskyy pointed to the October 1 Russian drone strike on a school in Kyiv as an example of how widespread such attacks have become.
Children were inside the school’s shelter when the drone struck the building and sparked a fire. No casualties were initially reported at the site.
The latest Russian air campaign has also hit energy, communications and commercial infrastructure across Ukraine.
According to the Financial Times, the escalation has unfolded alongside Ukraine’s expanding long-range campaign against Russian oil refineries, ports, storage facilities and other infrastructure deep inside Russia.
Those Ukrainian strikes have disrupted parts of Russia’s fuel industry and brought the consequences of the war increasingly into Russian cities and regions previously considered far removed from the front.
Zelenskyy said Ukrainian intelligence believes Moscow’s response has been to remove earlier limitations on how Russian forces conduct their air campaign.
Russia has repeatedly denied deliberately targeting civilians, even as strikes have damaged or destroyed residential buildings, schools, hospitals and other civilian facilities across Ukraine throughout the full-scale war.

articles.title: Russian Drones Hit Kyiv’s South Bridge Again as Traffic Collapses
articles.body:
Russian forces struck Kyiv’s South Bridge again on Friday afternoon, according to Kyiv Mayor Vitali Klitschko.
The bridge, on which the capital’s green metro line runs, is one of three major crossings across the Dnipro River that separates the city and has come under repeated attack since Thursday.

Klitschko wrote at 5:50 p.m. that the bridge was hit again, and emergency services were heading to the site. Videos circulating on social media also show a dark plume of smoke rising from the bridge against the sunset.
“Another hit on the Southern Bridge. Let me remind you that after several enemy attacks, the bridge is currently closed to traffic and the metro,” Klitschko wrote.

articles.title: Iran weighing options against US, Israel as nuclear talks stall, Israeli defense official says
articles.body:
Iran is weighing how to respond to growing US pressure as nuclear negotiations with Washington remain stalled, creating an increasingly complex regional situation, a senior Israeli defense official said on Friday.
"The Iranians are looking for tools within this campaign. They are asking themselves how they can get out of this situation. It is reasonable to assume that they are also discussing the possibility of influencing the elections in order to understand the other side," the official said.
The senior defense official said there had recently been a large number of unresolved incidents, some of which could potentially develop into attacks on the Israeli home front from a variety of directions, and not necessarily from Iran.
"There were many warnings and many nights when the system was occupied with clarifying the situation and raising and lowering the alert level. There were many nights of heightened readiness. Hezbollah? It definitely factors into Iran's calculations if Iran enters into a confrontation with Israel," the official said.
According to the defense official, the Iranians are constantly assessing the situation in the US and the extent of Washington's readiness to enter into a confrontation with them, and this affects Tehran's own assessment of the situation.
Economic pressure mounts on Iran
The official also stressed that conditions in Iran are deteriorating and that the effect of US sanctions can be clearly seen.
The number of tankers leaving the Persian Gulf through the Strait of Hormuz has been rising, and according to IDF data, an average of 30 to 40 tankers are now passing through each day. That figure reflects levels seen before the war. In other words, Iranian influence in the strait is declining.
The official also noted that the Iranian rial had reached a new low in recent days, with nearly 2.5 million rials now equivalent to one US dollar. At the same time, he clarified that Iran had not yet reached hyperinflation.
The official illustrated the economic situation by citing a critical article in an Iranian newspaper identified with the regime that compared the price of eggs in Iran with the average salary, adding that the cost of living in Iran was now "unbearable."
Compounding the economic pressure is what the official described as a US naval blockade of Iran that began this week. In addition to the sanctions, he said, the measure contains elements that are humiliating for Tehran because it prevents even family visits to neighboring countries.
As a result, the Iranians quickly approached neighboring countries and asked them to restore civilian flights. So far, according to the official, only Iraq has agreed, while there are currently no flights with Azerbaijan.
Israel prepares for risk of escalation
Israeli defense officials assess that Tehran is considering how to respond to the situation, what tools remain available to it, and what form its response should take. As evidence, they point to Iranian efforts to target vessels in the Strait of Hormuz that have so far failed.
The defense establishment believes Iran's range of options has narrowed significantly because of the naval blockade. This comes alongside Iranian attempts to carry out attacks abroad that have also failed, according to the assessment.
Israeli defense officials further assess that unless Iran attempts to break the blockade through a deliberate military move or reaches understandings with the US, it will be forced to contend with worsening domestic problems caused by the sanctions.
The IDF is therefore preparing for the possibility that an Iranian initiative could spiral out of control, such as a cruise missile striking a US vessel and causing fatalities, creating a situation in which it would be unclear how Washington would respond.
Israeli defense officials also assess that if the Iranians conclude that they are about to come under attack, or that the regime is losing ground in its confrontation with the US, they could potentially launch attacks against US assets in Jordan or Israel.
A senior official said the Iranians understand very well what the price of such a move would be, and that this is why they have not attacked Israel.

articles.title: Russian Attack Kills 1 in Kyiv High-Rise, Shuts Down Bridges Across the Capital
articles.body:
A Russian attack on Kyiv early Friday damaged the upper floors of a 25-story residential building in the Darnytskyi district, killing one person and injuring two others, authorities said.
Kyiv Mayor Vitali Klitschko said the strike caused a fire on the upper floors of the high-rise, prompting emergency crews to respond to the scene.

Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official.
At 7:45 a.m., the Kyiv City Military Administration (KMVA) confirmed that one person had been killed and two others injured in the attack.

“Rescuers evacuated two injured people from the building and handed them over to medical personnel. The body of a deceased person was discovered while extinguishing the fire. Another six people were evacuated,” the report states.

Russian forces also struck the Pivdennyi (South) Bridge again overnight, while drone debris fell in an open area in the Holosiivskyi district, damaging windows of a non-residential building and several cars. No fires or casualties were reported there.

articles.title: Ukrainian Mirage 2000-5F Shoots Down Banderol Missile With Cannon for First Time
articles.body:
A French Mirage 2000-5F fighter jet has, for the first time in history, shot down a Russian S8000 Banderol small-sized cruise missile using its aircraft cannon.
France transferred aircraft of this type to Ukraine from the stocks of its Air and Space Force in 2025, according to French Aid to Europe.
The aircraft’s primary cannon armament consists of two 30 mm DEFA 554 automatic aircraft cannons, which are integrated into the fuselage.
The fighter carries 125 rounds of ammunition for each cannon, with a rate of fire of up to 1,800 rounds per minute. The guns use 30×113 mm high-explosive fragmentation and armor-piercing incendiary ammunition, with a muzzle velocity of approximately 815 m/s.
The S8000 Banderol was developed by the Russian company Kronstadt. Its maximum speed is 620–650 km/h, while its cruising speed is 520–560 km/h.
The missile is powered by a Chinese-made Swiwin turbojet engine weighing 8.5 kg. At a maximum rotational speed of 65,000 rpm, the engine produces up to 81.6 kgf of thrust. With these engine characteristics, the missile’s stated range is up to 500 km.
The missile is equipped with an OFBC-150 high-explosive warhead with a total mass of 114.3 kg, of which 49.5 kg is explosive filler.

articles.title: The U.S. Navy has awarded a $24.4 billion contract to accelerate the production of air defense and missile defense interceptors
articles.body:
The U.S. Navy has awarded a $24.4 billion contract to accelerate the production of air defense and missile defense interceptors
Kyiv • UNN
The U.S. Navy and Raytheon have signed a five-year agreement worth up to $24.4 billion for the production of SM-6 missiles. The contract may be extended for another two years.
The U.S. Navy and Raytheon, a company within RTX Corporation, have signed a $24.4 billion contract to accelerate production of Standard Missile-6 (SM-6) missiles. UNN reports this, citing Raytheon and the U.S. Navy.
Raytheon, an RTX business, has signed a five-year contract, with options for an additional two years, worth up to $24.4 billion to supply Standard Missile-6 (SM-6) interceptors, which will significantly increase stocks of critical munitions capable of carrying out both offensive strikes and missile defense missions
The SM-6 supply contract is the latest in a series of major munitions contracts that the Pentagon has awarded this year in an effort to push contractors to ramp up production more quickly. It follows a previous multiyear agreement worth $20.7 billion for the supply of Raytheon’s AMRAAM air-to-air missiles, signed in late September, and a $58.6 billion contract for the supply of Patriot interceptors, which was awarded to Lockheed Martin.
The company said that the SM-6 is the only combat-proven weapon capable of conducting air defense and anti-ship warfare while also providing missile defense.
It has been successfully tested from various U.S. Navy ship platforms and ground-based launchers, providing the fleet with a versatile and highly reliable weapon to counter the full spectrum of kinetic threats faced by modern naval forces.
Acting U.S. Secretary of the Navy Hung Cao said: "Maritime power requires weapons that are produced quickly and in large quantities."
This investment expands production and provides the firepower our military needs to fight, win, and return home safely

The U.S. Department of Defense signed a seven-year, $22.9 billion contract with RTX’s Raytheon business to significantly increase production of Tomahawk cruise missiles.

articles.title: Speed up EU health security prep, says NATO chief medic
articles.body:
Want to receive this newsletter straight to your inbox? Sign up here to receive the reporting and intel from the Gastein Health Forum.
SNEAK PEEK
— Health security dominated the penultimate day at the European Health Forum Gastein, with calls for Europe to be better prepared to protect health infrastructure.
— Parliament’s environment committee backs an opinion on the Biotech Act supporting a one-year patent extension.
Advertisement
— Europe’s response to the U.S. most-favored-nation policy was a hot topic at Gastein,with France’s new pharma deal stealing the spotlight.
Welcome to Friday’s Morning Health Care! It’s been a big week at Gastein and it only cost attendees a bout of food poisoning, burnout and one unlucky Italian getting lost in the woods, spending the night by a waterfall before being rescued by helicopter. This year also bids farewell to Clemens Martin Auer, who hands over the Gastein presidency to Nick Fahy, director of the health and care research group at RAND Europe.
GEAR UP: Europe needs to better prepare to protect health infrastructure, delegates heard, as health security dominated the penultimate day at the European Health Forum Gastein.
Spread out: Petter Iversen, chair of NATO’s Committee of the Chiefs of Military Medical Services, said there were different ways Europe could protect health infrastructure, which continues to be under attack in Ukraine. “You can spread things out, use a larger geographical area and hide things,” he told Morning Health Care on the sidelines of the conference.
Advertisement
Hiding hospitals: One option is to move hospitals into underground facilities to protect them from attacks, he said. “When we are building infrastructures in the future … we might have to think about dual use. If you’re building a parking cellar, maybe you should have enough power or electricity, and also water supplies, so you can actually build a kind of hospital in there.”
Eastern Europe is already experiencing increasing threats from Russia, with drones and cyberattacks now frequent events, Iversen said. Countries closer to Russia had good plans in place, he said. “Situational awareness is sharper closer to the eastern flank,” he said. “You feel the pressure on a daily basis.”
Where we’re vulnerable: European pharmaceuticals and production are also at risk since supply chains are dependent on countries like China, he said. “We need to prepare to reduce our dependencies from whom we will not want to be dependent upon if it comes to a major crisis.”
Prepare for everything: The health care system needed to be resilient enough to withstand shocks, including those that went beyond war, like earthquakes, summer heatwaves or cyberattacks putting stress on the sector, said Jarno Habicht, the World Health Organization’s outgoing representative in Ukraine. “You might have more patients, but you might be also without electricity, so we need to be ready for the shocks,” he told Morning Health Care.
Read more about what Iversen and Habicht said on health security and Ukraine here.
POLITICAL ADVERTISEMENT
Sponsor: European Federation of Pharmaceutical Industries and Associations (EFPIA)
The political advertisement is linked to the EU Biotech Act
INFORMAL MEETING: Health ministers met in Dublin on Thursday where they discussed tobacco and nicotine pouches, the Biotech Act, medical devices reform and cardiovascular health.
Advertisement
On tobacco: Health Commissioner Olivér Várhelyi said the Commission remained committed to publishing a comprehensive review of tobacco legislation, including on advertising rules, this year and that there will be a focus on nicotine addiction. “We are very well advanced in the preparation of the proposals,” he said in a press conference following Thursday’s meeting.
We’re close: Forthcoming legislation would address vapes and heated tobacco products; their use being twice as high among young people than the broader population, Várhelyi said. It is important the tobacco products directive is revised to address nicotine addiction “so that we can deal with the cross-border element of this and create a genuinely harmonized system,” added Irish Health Minister Jennifer Carroll MacNeill who joined Várhelyi at the press conference. “Colleagues are concerned about the capacity of nicotine addictive companies to create new and novel ways of getting children addicted to nicotine,” she said.
Presidential priorities: The Irish presidency of the Council of the EU is pushing for the Biotech Act and Medical Devices Regulation to be finalized as the Council works on its position (more on where this is up to in the Parliament later). “This is the moment to deliver this because this is the moment when long-term decisions are made in this sector,” Várhelyi said. “But for this to succeed, we can only achieve it if we have speed, if we have simplicity and if we have predictability.”
POLITICAL ADVERTISEMENT
**A message from EFPIA: Fierce competition means the global life science landscape is shifting, demanding a bold response. The Biotech Act is an important signal of the kind of ecosystem Europe wants to create, but it cannot deliver change alone. Europe cannot expect to attract greater investment in medicine innovation while access remains slow and unpredictable. Read more.**
Sponsor: European Federation of Pharmaceutical Industries and Associations (EFPIA)
The political advertisement is linked to the EU Biotech Act
FRENCH DEAL DOMINATES MFN TALKS: France’s new pharma agreement this week has shaken up the Gastein forum, seeping into nearly all conversations (whether on panels or by the coffee machine lines) on competitiveness, drug pricing and geopolitical relationships. Some are reeling from what they say was a very unexpected announcement, which throws into doubt what the rest of the bloc can do, while others see it as an inevitable evolution of U.S. pressure.
Recap: France announced this week a new deal with the pharmaceutical sector on drug pricing, to provide “more clarity and predictability to pharmaceutical companies.”
Stay united: Morning Health Care reported yesterday that patients, payers, EU lawmakers and capitals urged European countries not to seek individual agreements to counter the effects of the U.S. most-favored-nation policies, urging instead for a united Europe. During a panel on Europe’s upgraded pharmaceutical legislation, speakers reiterated the message Thursday. Morning Health Care contacted the French government for comment but did not get a response.
Advertisement
Austria is on board: “As Europe… if we do not now see the need to act more [uniformly] and more together, I don't know when we should see it,” said Stefan Eichwalder, director of the health systems division at the Austrian health and social affairs ministry.
It doesn’t mean not doing anything: “It would be dangerous not to act now, but then I think we need to find ways of working together,” he said. Eichwalder added that it was important that national deals — with industry or the U.S. — do “not weaken the position of the EU, and in the end, the position of any member state within the EU.”
The bottom line: Countries should work together “no matter how difficult it is,” he said. “I don't see a solution for Europe to go 27 different different routes.”
Think this through: Yannis Natsis, director of the European Social Insurance Platform, said countries should be asking themselves this question: If we were to accept paying higher prices, what can we get in return? “From a first reading of this agreement, France is committing to pay higher prices in return for what exactly? And what are companies committing to delivering in exchange for these higher prices?”
The bigger picture: “Many narratives are going around. Narratives that are used by different sectors to serve specific interests,” Natsis said. “And in this case, this narrative is used to ask and demand higher prices. But again, the question is: if we were to pay these higher prices in Europe… what happens to the other countries? Because if France signs an agreement, if Germany signs an agreement, what about the rest of us?”
Pushing back: Richard Bergström, vice president of European affairs at health data firm IQVIA and former chief of pharma lobby EFPIA, pushed back. “If you read the French deal… there’s a lot of wins for the governments as well,” he told panelists from the audience. “There are requirements on clinical trials, requirements on manufacturing in Europe, and most importantly, there is a gain at the end of life cycle.” It’s a “quite balanced deal,” he added.
Advertisement
OVER IN BRITAIN: The U.K.-U.S. drug pricing deal — which is hailed by the Trump administration and industry as a blueprint for other European countries — is running up against some challenges, our colleague Caroline Hug writes in. Four pilots rolled out to try to meet U.S. demands to double medicines spending as a percentage of GDP by 2028 are currently falling short. Britain’s new Science Minister Chris McDonald has signaled the government is willing to try new ideas.
Pilots ongoing: The government — with industry and the U.S. administration — launched the pilots running through September 2027, and the results will inform the next drug-pricing scheme.
The line: “What’s really important here is that we start with what is the objective we want to achieve, rather than the means by which we want to achieve it,” McDonald told Morning Trade U.K. during a fringe event Tuesday at the Labour Party Conference. “I don’t mind trying things, and then if they don’t work, then learning from that and moving on and trying some other things.”
New blood: McDonald replaces former Science Minister Patrick Vallance, who played a key role in the U.K.-U.S. pharma negotiations. One pharma industry figure told MTUK that McDonald “brings rare commercial instinct to the policy debate.”
Deal mode: “It was quite hard to reach an agreement across the entirety of the industry [on pilots],” said Shaun Grady, AstraZeneca U.K. chairman, pointing to varying demands of some pharma companies versus big pharmas like GSK and AstraZeneca which “invest very significantly in the U.K.” He added that conversations are “now moving much more into a bilateral phase where each company will engage with the government.”
BIOTECH ACT
APPROVED: Parliament’s environment committee has confirmed its position on the Biotech Act, with 53 in favor of adopting the opinion led by Nicolás Gonzalez Casares and 11 against. It supported keeping a 12-month extension of patents under certain conditions. Parliament’s legal committee also voted to keep the one-year extension in its opinion.
Advertisement
Coming to the table: The co-leads on the Biotech Act — Vytenis Andriukaitis (S&D) in the health committee and Wouter Beke (EPP) in the industry committee — will meet in Strasbourg next week to try and find a compromise on the patent extensions they can bring back to shadow rapporteurs.
Making progress: Andriukaitis told Morning Health Care on the sidelines of Gastein that political groups will likely have “more compromised solutions” on supplementary protection certificates, cross-border clinical trials and financing for the law by the end of October.” Read more about what he said here.
Feedback: Shadow rapporteurs on the Biotech Act on Thursday submitted their feedback to the co-rapporteurs following a roundtable between MEPs, Commission officials and industry on Tuesday.
Remember: Some MEPs weren’t happy at being offered a roundtable in lieu of an independent assessment on the supplementary protection certificate extension (SPCs) while some NGOs were also upset they didn’t get a seat at the table. Catch up on the controversy here.
UCPM
COMMITTEES BOOST PREPAREDNESS, CIVIL PROTECTION FUND: Lawmakers in the health and environment committee adopted their position on the EU’s next civil protection mechanism (UCPM), which now includes health emergency preparedness and response.
Details: The compromise text boosts the budget of the mechanism from €10 billion to €12.42 billion, earmarking 40% of the funding for civil protection, 40% for health emergencies, and 20% for flexibility. The position was approved with 61 votes in favor, nine against and nine abstentions. It will now need to be put to a vote in Parliament.
Advertisement
Sneaky global health reference: The adopted text includes several references to strengthening global health infrastructure. For example, it says that “strengthening cooperation … as well as the global health infrastructure and the World Health Organisation is essential to enhance the global ability to act.”
WHAT WE’RE READING
There have been four more deaths from the West Nile virus in the Netherlands, the NL Times reports.
**A message from EFPIA: The Biotech Act can be an important step towards Europe’s life sciences future. Done well, it can make clinical research faster, attract more investment to Europe, help biotech companies scale, and ensure Europe is the place where the next generation of medicines is developed. However, it cannot deliver the change that Europe urgently requires in isolation. Access shapes where capital flows right from the start. When market access is slow or fragmented, investors notice and capital follows opportunity elsewhere. Reversing Europe’s decline in research and development investment would require sustained structural reform, stronger action at the Member-State level, and a rethink of how healthcare systems invest in innovation. Europe has both scientific excellence and talent. Now it must create the right conditions for companies to choose Europe as a place to research, develop and deliver new medicines to patients. If we get it right, the reward is higher growth, greater resilience, and better health. The choice is ours. Read more.**

articles.title: Ukraine lost another MiG-29 and its pilot on Thursday. It needs the jets to guard its cities, and almost none are left to replace them
articles.body:
- Ukraine has lost another Mikoyan MiG-29 fighter as well as its pilot
- The Ukrainian MiG fleet is slowly dwindling owing to combat losses and wear and tear
- The Ukrainian air force is acquiring new Western types to replace the MiGs and other ex-Soviet jets
Ukraine has lost another Mikoyan MiG-29 fighter and its pilot. The Thursday shoot-down extends the steady attrition of the Ukrainian air force MiG fleet, potentially drawing down the fleet to its pre-war strength.
That means Ukraine may have lost as many of the twin-engine, supersonic MiG-29s as it has received from its allies or restored from surplus stocks since February 2022.
It's an ominous milestone. The Soviet-vintage MiG-29 is no longer the Ukrainian air force's most important fighter. That honorific belongs to the air force's ex-European Lockheed Martin F-16s.
But the MiG-29 is still the air force's second most important fighter—and will remain so through 2027 as Ukraine awaits its first ex-Swedish Saab Gripens, due early next year, and French-made Dassault Rafales, due from 2028. Ukraine sorties MiG-29s for ground attack missions targeting Russian troop concentrations, strikes on Russian air defense systems, and air defense sorties over Ukrainian cities and ports.
The air force announced the loss of the MiG-29 and its pilot, Capt. Marat Mambetov, shortly after it occurred on Thursday. Mambetov, 25, was a flight commander in the 40th Tactical Aviation Brigade, known as the "Ghost of Kyiv" brigade. "Flying a MiG-29 fighter jet, [Mambetov] carried out missile and bomb strikes against Russian occupiers along one of the front-line directions," the air force stated. "During the mission, his aircraft was hit by an enemy missile. The pilot ejected, but tragically did not survive."
It's the 37th confirmed combat loss of a Ukrainian MiG-29 since Russia widened its war on Ukraine in February 2022, according to a tally by the Oryx open-source intelligence collective. Oryx has also registered damage to an additional three Ukrainian MiG-29s.
Thirty-seven write-offs, plus the likely grounding of several previously flyable MiG-29s owing to intensive wear and tear since 2022, may have reduced the Ukrainian air force's MiG-29 fleet to around three dozen active jets.
Fighter subtraction
The math is simple. The air force probably had between 30 and 35 MiG-29s in service when Russia attacked in February 2022. As losses cut into the fleet, Poland donated 14 surplus MiGs, Slovakia donated 10, and Azerbaijan reportedly donated three. Meanwhile, Ukrainian engineers tapped a global pipeline of spare parts to reactivate an estimated 20 grounded MiG-29s moldering in hangars at various Ukrainian airfields.
That's as many as 82 MiGs in and, as of Thursday, 37 out owing to Russian action—plus additional jets grounded due to airframe fatigue. The resulting active fleet should number around three dozen planes, around as many as Ukraine had on the eve of the wider war.
There aren't many more old MiGs that Ukraine could obtain to bolster the fleet. Poland still has as many as nine very tired airframes, but Kyiv and Warsaw have consistently failed to negotiate a transfer. There may yet be a few ex-Soviet MiG-29s, grounded for years or even decades, that Ukrainian engineers can restore to flightworthy status. Other than that, options are scarce.
Ukraine’s Swedish radar planes have flown inside Russian missile range for six months. None has been shot down.
The three dozen MiGs still in the inventory may have to last a little while alongside the few survivors of Ukraine's other Soviet-vintage warplanes, including Sukhoi Su-27s, Sukhoi Su-24s, and Sukhoi Su-25s.
Older Western types—the 80 or so F-16s European allies have pledged, about half delivered, as well as potentially a dozen or so ex-French Dassault Mirage 2000s—are steadily replacing the ex-Soviet jets. (So far, Ukraine has lost five F-16s and one Mirage.) Next year, the transformation of the Ukrainian air force from a largely Soviet-equipped force to a largely Western-equipped force will accelerate when the first of 32 Gripens arrive. Sixteen Rafales are to follow from 2028.
Barring catastrophic combat losses among Western types and assuming Ukraine can maintain and arm these new warplanes, by the end of 2027, the air force may not need its remaining MiGs and Sukhois, which by then could be very tired.
Russian missiles are steadily reducing the MiG and Sukhoi fleets, effectively forcing Ukraine to switch to new types.

articles.title: Ukraine has limited contingency plans for Russian attacks on water supply – NYT

Ukraine has limited contingency plans for Russian attacks on water supply – NYT
Ukrainian officials have said they are concerned that Ukraine does not have a sufficiently developed contingency plan in the event of large-scale Russian strikes on its water supply system.
Source: The New York Times, citing its sources
Details: Russia has never previously carried out large-scale strikes on water infrastructure facilities.
A Russian plan for attacks on Ukrainian infrastructure, which Ukraine reportedly intercepted, states that Moscow intends to target Ukraine's water supply system with dozens of ballistic missiles and glide bombs, including pumping stations and water treatment facilities.
The New York Times notes that Ukrainian officials have privately expressed concern that the country has limited contingency plans for major disruptions to its water supply.
Background: According to an approved Russian plan reportedly intercepted by Ukraine, Russia plans to cut Ukrainian nuclear power plants off from the power grid during its winter attacks by striking targets within a kilometre of the plants, as well as carrying out large-scale attacks on water supply systems.

articles.title: Zelenskyy on importance of sanctions: every Russian drone can be stopped on the production line
articles.body:
Zelenskyy on importance of sanctions: every Russian drone can be stopped on the production line
President Volodymyr Zelenskyy has stressed that Russia's escalation of aerial attacks depends on foreign companies whose components continue to reach the aggressor state.
Source: Zelenskyy on X (Twitter)
Quote: "No matter how hard Moscow tries to fully localise the production of its drones and missiles, its ability to escalate remains critically dependent on foreign components. These are supply chains running from Europe, the United States, China, Japan and many other countries.
Most of these companies are well-known manufacturers, but their components still make their way to Russia. Every Russian drone can actually be stopped right at the production line. What is needed is the political will of these countries. If the Kremlin has chosen more strikes, sanctions must work and must be strengthened. Thank you to everyone who is helping."
Background:
- A bipartisan group of members of the US House of Representatives, responding to reports of a new strategy towards Russia, called on US President Donald Trump not to ease sanctions on Russia and instead to use the Graham Act.

The Tel Aviv-based asset manager holds hundreds of millions of dollars in frontline military contractors actively outfitting the Israeli military. Kushner has described Phoenix as his firm’s best investment.
Capitalizing on the Israeli military supply chain
Phoenix Financial holds at least $456 million across nine publicly traded companies supplying Israeli armed forces.

Phoenix also maintains substantial positions in Next Vision, which manufactures specialized cameras for military reconnaissance drones, Bet Shemesh Engines, which produces jet engines for combat warplanes, and Reshef Technologies, maker of electronic artillery shell fuzes. Escalating regional hostilities drive unprecedented war ministry orders, inflating stock valuations and yielding massive commercial returns for Phoenix investors.

articles.title: Zelenskyy reported that Putin lifted restrictions on strikes, and Russia intensified attacks on civilian targets - FT
articles.body:
Zelenskyy reported that Putin lifted restrictions on strikes, and Russia intensified attacks on civilian targets - FT
Kyiv • UNN
According to Ukrainian intelligence, Putin ordered the removal of restrictions on air campaigns in September. After that, Russia intensified strikes on Kyiv.
Kremlin leader Vladimir Putin instructed his military commanders to abandon the rules of warfare, leading to a sharp increase in Russia’s strikes on civilian targets amid significant attempts to alter the balance in the war, according to intelligence intercepted by Kyiv. This was reported by the Financial Times, writes UNN.
Details
Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy told the Financial Times that Ukrainian intelligence services had received information that the Kremlin leader had "lifted the restrictions that governed previous air campaigns."
"He said that there are no rules now," Zelenskyy said, referring to intelligence that included intercepted communications from Kremlin officials.
Zelenskyy said that "Putin issued the order in September, when Russia began intensifying its airstrikes on Kyiv, hitting schools, hospitals and data centers." The Ukrainian president said that a bombed school showed how widespread such strikes had become.
