articles.body:
Trump threatens to double tariffs on South Korea if they do not pay for Alaska natural gas pipeline – US politics live
President has claimed pipeline project was part of a deal made last year to lower tariffs on imports from South Korea in return for billions of dollars of investments in the US
Trump threatens to double tariffs on South Korea if they do not pay for Alaska natural gas pipeline
As he left the White House for a campaign rally in Alabama on Friday, Donald Trump was asked by a reporter if he had “jumped the gun” by announcing on Wednesday that South Korea had agreed to pay for a $54bn natural gas pipeline in Alaska, only for a Korean official to contradict him on Thursday, saying that Korea had only agreed to “initiate a review” of the possible investment.
“No, I didn’t jump the gun,” Trump replied. “Let’s see if they don’t want to do it. That’s okay with me. I’ll just charge them more.”
When he announced the pipeline project in an Oval Office ceremony on Wednesday, the president claimed that the Korean investment was part of a deal he struck in 2025, to lower tariffs on imports from South Korea in return for billions of dollars of investments in the US.
“They said they didn’t sign it?” Trump asked the reporter on Friday. “Tell them if they don’t sign shortly, I’m going to double it up, okay?”
As he apparently threatened to double tariffs on imports from South Korea, Trump repeated his incorrect claim that tariffs on imports are fees paid by the country that exports goods to the US. In fact, tariffs are, as the US supreme court clarified when it ruled many of Trump’s tariffs an illegal form of taxation on Americans, paid by US importers.
Democratic lawmakers push to keep Trump administration from closing archives in California and Illinois
Senator Adam Schiff reaffirmed his support on Friday for legislation introduced this week by Democrats that would stop the Trump administration from closing archives of government records in California and Illinois.
“The administration is threatening access to historical and irreplaceable records, including closing down one facility in California that is home to countless photos and family heirlooms,” Schiff said in a statement. “Congress must exercise its oversight power to save decades of regional and national history.”
Schiff and his California colleague Alex Padilla joined two Illinois Democrats, Tammy Duckworth and Dick Durbin, to introduce the National Archives Protection Act, which would ensure archival records remain accessible to the public.
One of the facilities the administration reportedly plans to close, in the San Francisco Bay area, hosts original records from the US supreme court case United States v. Wong Kim Ark, which affirmed that the constitution grants birthright citizenship to anyone born in the US.
Trump concludes remarks to supporters in Alabama claiming 'the most successful presidency in history'
The blessed sound of YMCA has just been heard in Mobile, Alabama, signaling that Donald Trump’s rally speech is over.
In his remarks, which included a plea to supporters to “just close your eyes and pretend I’m on the ballot,” Trump mentioned various Republican candidates in passing, but mainly made the case for himself, casting his second term in office as an unalloyed triumph, marred only by “bad press”.
“If you want to keep America the strongest, most successful nation the world has ever seen – we are right now more respected than at any time in the history of our country, and that’s where the bad press,” Trump said, “you have to vote Republican.”
“Just think of what the Trump administration and our Republican majorities have accomplished in less than two years’ time,” he went on. “Nobody’s ever seen this before. Nobody’s ever done it. We have the most successful- it’s not two years; it’s substantially less - the most successful presidency in history.”
Late in the speech, Trump named Republican candidates and elected officials who were on hand, including senator Katie Britt, who achieved viral fame this week for the look of horror on her face as her colleague Eric Schmitt badly botched an attempt to make former special counsel Jack Smith look bad.
Trump then singled out the far-right, anti-Muslim influencer Laura Loomer for praise.
“A great Republican strategist, a great person, a killer,” Trump said. “When she’s angry at you, it’s a very terrible situation. Laura Loomer. Thank you. Laura. She’s great.”
Loomer, an influential outside Trump adviser whose extreme views and statements led to criticism of Trump during the 2024 campaign, when she traveled with him to events, posted a photograph of herself with Trump on Air Force One earlier in the day.
Trump regales supporters in Alabama with familiar tales, some imaginary
Donald Trump is regaling supporters in Alabama with a version of his rally speech that includes many of his familiar boasts and grievances, a number of which are based on entirely imaginary claims.
To take one example, Trump once again claimed that he was instantly blamed for high prices by the media after just one day in office.
“I took over and in my first news conference on January 21st … a day after that beautiful day we had in quite cold weather, the inauguration. A day later, I had a news conference and they said, ‘affordability’. I said, ‘I just got here. What do they mean?’” Trump insisted, despite the fact that he was, in fact, asked no questions about affordability at all during that news conference.
In the first weeks of his administration, Trump repeatedly claimed that prices were dropping and then, at a cabinet meeting two months into his second term, claimed for the first time that he had been unfairly blamed for high egg prices. “When I came in, after one week, they were screaming at me about eggs. Eggs had nothing to do with me,” the president said on 24 March 2025. He has repeated the false claim that reporters blamed him for high food prices dozens of times since.
Later in the address, Trump said, as he has dozens of times since he visited Saudi Arabia in May 2025, that the Saudi king had praised him for almost instantly turning around the US economy.
“Less than two years ago, our country was dead,” Trump told supporters in Alabama on Friday night. “Remember that? I told you, the king of Saudi Arabia was talking to me. He said, you know, ‘Sir, just a short time ago, your country was dead. The whole Middle East, the whole world was laughing at you. And now you have the hottest country anywhere in the world.’”
As the Guardian has reported previously, Trump did not meet the Saudi king, who is elderly and not often seen in public, during his visit last year. Instead, he was hosted by the Saudi crown prince, Mohammed bin Salman. There is also no evidence that the Saudi prince made this statement to Trump, but there is video of Trump making a version of that claim to bin Salman during an address to a US-Saudi investment event in Riyadh on 13 May 2025.
“The days of economic misery under the last administration are rapidly giving way to the greatest economy in the history of the world,” Trump said before directly addressing the crown prince in the audience. “We are rocking. The United States is the hottest country, with the exception of your country, I have to say, right? … No Mohammed… You’re hotter. At least as long as I’m up here, you’re hotter. But groceries, gasoline, energy and all other prices are down with no inflation. We have no inflation.”
Two weeks after his return to the US, Trump began saying that this observation had been made not by him, but to him. “I went to Saudi Arabia,” Trump told reporters in the Oval Office on 28 May 2025. “The king told me, he said, ‘you got the hottest com-’ we have the hottest country in the world right now.,” Trump said. “Six months ago this country was stone cold dead. We had a dead country.”
As he repeated the story, again and again, Trump began to also attribute his own claim, that the US was “dead” under Joe Biden, to the Saudi king as well. In remarks at the Nato summit in the Hague in June 2025, Trump insisted that the Saudi king had told him: “A year ago, your country was dead. You had a deadhead running it. You had a country that was dead”.
Since then, Trump has repeated the tale dozens of times.
Donald Trump is basking in cheers from his supporters in Alabama where he started by fondly recalling his first visit to Alabama in 2015, when he spoke to 30,000 wildly enthusiastic fans at a football stadium in Mobile, including a school teacher smiling broadly while holding her infant up to Trump. An image of that moment went viral on social media, in an early indication of how deep Trump’s support might be.
As Donald Trump’s war against non-partisan reporting on his presidency continues, the White House released a supercut of him insulting CNN a dozen times since he returned to office last year, and posted it on a government YouTube channel on Friday.
The video, which shows Trump railing against the people running the news network, soon to be controlled by his supporters, also includes a clip from June of the president deriding one CNN correspondent, the former Daily Caller journalist Kaitlan Collins, because she “never smiles” while asking him questions.
Senator Tommy Tuberville, an Alabama Republican, just concluded remarks at the campaign rally in Mobile Donald Trump is headlining.
Tuberville, who is running for Alabama governor against Democrat Doug Jones, urged Trump supporters to “go out and vote” in the midterms to send a message “to all the states across the country that we’re here as Alabamians, and we’re here to stay.”
“And if you want to move here, move, but don’t bring you down politics with you when you come,” Tuberville added.
Alabama added 30,000 new residents in 2025, AL.com reported, “thanks to a continued influx of new arrivals from other states.”
“You’re here for a treat tonight from a guy that again I call my friend,” the former football coach said. “Everybody’d give up on him after the first election,” Tuberville added, apparently in reference to Trump’s loss to Joe Biden in the 2020 presidential election.
Tuberville was one of the Republican senators Trump called during the Capitol riot on January 6 2021 to urge him to help delay the certification of Biden’s electoral college victory, according to the House select committee that investigated Trump’s effort to overturn the results of that election.
A federal judge has blocked the Trump administration from constructing a border wall at Big Bend national park in Texas on Friday. US District Judge Kathleen Cardone’s ruling means that the construction will have to cease until a lawsuit opposing it is resolved.
In August, crews contracted by US Customs and border protection (CBP) began bulldozing at the mouth of Big Bend National Park’s famed Santa Elena Canyon. The plan was to construct new border security infrastructure, which was dubbed the “smart wall”.
The plan was met with swift backlash from local leaders and landowners for its fast-moving plans. Construction was briefly paused in mid-August but resumed at the beginning of September.
In a statement following Judge Cardone’s ruling, Tiernan Sittenfeld, the CEO of the National Parks conservation association, said:
Today’s court ruling halting the destruction is a victory for Big Bend and for all of America’s national parks. While national park advocates are grateful for this halt to border construction in Big Bend, the devastating toll it has already taken on this national park must be studied and remediated. The administration must repair the damage it has done to the beautiful, fragile desert ecosystems that make Big Bend National Park one of America’s most iconic places.”
Trump personally directed spending of taxpayer funds on ads celebrating himself – report
Donald Trump personally directed the use of $20m in taxpayer funds to purchase advertising time on national television to air a series of political ads that celebrate his presidency in the run-up to the midterm elections, the New York Times reported on Friday.
The campaign, which has featured four pro-Trump ads so far, has been called illegal government propaganda by critics.
“The money for the ads was freed up on Sept. 19, when the Office of Management and Budget shifted $20 million in Customs and Border Protection funds to a budget category called One Big Beautiful Bill Commemorative Events,” the Times reported, citing anonymous sources familiar with the spending.
The first pro-Trump ad, broadcast on Fox News last week, uses audio of Trump telling supporters in Las Vegas last month: “Together we will defeat communism, socialism and Marxism in America,” and a rapid-fire montage of images of Trump beneath the onscreen text: “America will never be a communist country,” as a chorus sings the words “love me”, taken from a song of that name by JMSN. In the original speech, Trump explicitly identified the enemy as “Dumocrat communists in Congress”.
The last 10 seconds of the ad included text at the bottom the screen saying: “Paid for by the US government.”
The second ad was a White House produced highlight reel of Trump’s address at Mount Rushmore on the weekend of 4 July.
The third ad was a recycled 2024 Trump campaign ad showing a moody, black-and-white shot of Trump staring into the camera as the soundtrack plays the closing riff of a campaign speech he gave dozens of times in 2023 and 2024. The ad was played on giant screens during the 2024 Republican national convention before Trump’s speech accepting his party’s nomination.
The most recent ad, first broadcast this week, is a celebration of Trump’s decision to start a war with Iran, and features audio taken from the president’s 28 February declaration that the United States military had begun major combat operations there. That ad concludes with images of Iranians in New York celebrating the initial strikes the next day. It makes no mention of the fact that the war is ongoing, seven months later.
As fears grow over US economy, Trump calls his ballroom project 'pretty cool' and claims his new helipad 'is getting all sorts of awards'
Donald Trump is now flying to Alabama for a campaign rally but, before he left the White House, he took a moment, as fears grow over a US economy that added just 29,000 jobs last month, to boast about his new helipad and point to a massive crane towering over the White House ballroom he is constructing.
“I hope you like what you’re seeing here,” Trump told reporters, pointing to the new helipad. “That’s getting all sorts of awards,” he said, without explaining who, exactly, was handing out awards for White House home improvement projects.
“And the best of all,” the president continued, turning to point at the ballroom construction site. “Look at that. You see the new crane? The red boom, that’s one of the biggest cranes in the world; that lifts up the steel for the roof. Pretty cool, right?”
Trump expresses sympathy for Cornell students accused of rape, 'because they won’t get a fair shake' from New York attorney general Letitia James
Speaking to reporters as he left the White House for Alabama on Friday, Donald Trump expressed sympathy for the Cornell University students accused of gang-rape, saying “they won’t get a fair shake” from Letitia James, the state’s attorney general, who has been charged with investigating the alleged gang-rape as a special prosecutor.
Trump was asked by the Fox News correspondent Peter Doocy to comment on the appointment James by Kathy Hochul, the New York governor.
“Letitia James is a corrupt person,” Trump replied. “I feel badly for whoever she’s looking at, because they won’t get a fair shake.”
The president has harbored an intense hatred of James since she won a civil fraud lawsuit against him and his family real estate business in 2024, when a New York state judge ruled that he was liable for conspiring to commit fraud by inflating his net worth to obtain favorable loan terms.
Trump ended the brief exchange with reporters after taking that question from Doocy. Earlier this week, Trump suggested that Doocy would be a good fit for the job of defending him as his White House press secretary.
Trump threatens to double tariffs on South Korea if they do not pay for Alaska natural gas pipeline
As he left the White House for a campaign rally in Alabama on Friday, Donald Trump was asked by a reporter if he had “jumped the gun” by announcing on Wednesday that South Korea had agreed to pay for a $54bn natural gas pipeline in Alaska, only for a Korean official to contradict him on Thursday, saying that Korea had only agreed to “initiate a review” of the possible investment.
“No, I didn’t jump the gun,” Trump replied. “Let’s see if they don’t want to do it. That’s okay with me. I’ll just charge them more.”
When he announced the pipeline project in an Oval Office ceremony on Wednesday, the president claimed that the Korean investment was part of a deal he struck in 2025, to lower tariffs on imports from South Korea in return for billions of dollars of investments in the US.
“They said they didn’t sign it?” Trump asked the reporter on Friday. “Tell them if they don’t sign shortly, I’m going to double it up, okay?”
As he apparently threatened to double tariffs on imports from South Korea, Trump repeated his incorrect claim that tariffs on imports are fees paid by the country that exports goods to the US. In fact, tariffs are, as the US supreme court clarified when it ruled many of Trump’s tariffs an illegal form of taxation on Americans, paid by US importers.
FBI director Kash Patel has reportedly commissioned a classified report to examine where the agency “fell short” and to ensure “those failures are not repeated”, according to MS Now, citing unnamed current and former officials and a copy of an internal memo.
The officials told MS Now that while they don’t know the contents of the report, they expect it includes the FBI work into the Russia investigation and the more recent special counsel investigations involving the alleged mishandling of classified documents, and attempts to overturn the 2020 election.
The sources also said that by formalizing the so-called “Patel Report”, it will be more difficult to challenge long-running political arguments within the FBI.
Hakeem Jeffries has joined the chorus of Democrats using today’s job report to slam the Trump administration’s economic agenda.
“Inflation is up, job creation is down and the reckless war of choice in Iran has been a disaster,” said the House minority leader, who is hoping for his party to reclaim the majority in the lower chamber this November. “Republicans have crashed the economy.”
New figures, released by the Bureau of Labor Statistics, show that the number of new jobs added in the US was weaker than expected, while unemployment saw an uptick. The US added 29,000 new jobs in September, significantly fewer than the roughly 90,000 economists forecasted. Unemployment increased slightly to 4.2% – up by 0.1 point compared with last month’s data.
Democrats quickly slammed the figures as emblematic of Donald Trump’s “failing economic agenda”. Elizabeth Warren, the top Democrat on the Senate banking committee, added that the president’s leadership “keeps pushing prices up”. Meanwhile, Chuck Schumer, the Senate minority leader, noted that “American families are being squeezed on all sides by Trump’s disastrous economy”, in response to Friday’s figures.
The White House, however, projected confidence about the latest figures. Taylor Rogers, a spokesperson, highlighted the addition of “9,000 manufacturing jobs and 12,300 factory construction jobs over the month” as proof that Donald Trump’s “reindustrialization agenda is working”. She noted that “wages are up over last year” – despite the fact they have not kept up with inflation.
Also today, G7 leaders agreed to release up to 100m barrels of diesel reserves within four months, to mitigate the ongoing energy crisis as a result of the US-Israel war on Iran. On Truth Social, Trump welcomed the news after urging European allies to release their diesel reserves as fuel prices continue to rise, and he weighed an export ban. The president added that “the process will begin immediately”.
The top Republican aligned Super Pac, the Senate Leadership Fund (SLF), will pause it’s multimillion-dollar ad spend in North Carolina in support of Michael Whatley, the GOP nominee for the open US Senate seat, according to multiple reports. The SLF initially announced a $71m investment in the North Carolina race back in April – noting that Whatley – the former chair of the Republican National Committee with backing from Donald Trump – was a “battle-tested leader”. Semafor first reported the news that SLF shifting its spending priority, and is now reserving a seven-figure sum for the Senate race in Kansas – which has become increasingly competitive as Trump’s approval rating hits a record low nationwide.
Ahead of Donald Trump heading to Mobile, Alabama today, it’s worth pointing out a new poll from AP-Norcwhich shows that a majority of Americans blame the president for their struggle with the cost of living. Environmental groups sue Trump administration for slashing fuel economy rules
A group of environmental organizations have sued the Trump administration over its recent move to slash clean-car rules that had been aimed at reducing planet-heating emissions and boosting electric vehicles.
On Monday, the administration relaxed the Corporate Average Fuel Economy (Cafe) standards that regulate how far new vehicles need to travel on a gallon of gasoline.
Donald Trump said last week that the less stringent mileage requirements would “take the waste out of building cars in America” and save families “thousands on a new, beautiful and safe car”, while boosting auto production in the US.
Trump has repeatedly pledged to end what he falsely calls an EV “mandate”, referring incorrectly to Joe Biden’s target that half of all new vehicle sales be electric by 2030. No federal policy has mandated auto companies to sell EVs.
Sean Duffy, the US transportation secretary, hailed the new initiative – called Freedom Means Affordable Cars – which the agency said would reduce the average cost of new vehicles by $1,300, and save consumers $138bn over the next five years.
The lawsuit is currently a petition to review the Department of Transportation’s move.

Their list now includes, Virginia’s sixth, Washington state’s fifth, North Carolina’s 13th, Kansas’s second, Texas’s ninth, Oklahoma’s fifth, New Jersey’s second and Michigan’s first. This means the DCCC has identified 66 critical districts as competitive, in order for Democrats to reclaim control of the lower chamber.
While some forecasters expect the party to win the House, many of the competitions are neck-and-neck. The last time Democrats saw a so-called “blue wave” was in 2018 – when they flipped 41 seats.
Top Republican Super Pac pauses ad spend in North Carolina, focuses on Kansas – reports
The top Republican aligned Super Pac, the Senate Leadership Fund (SLF), will pause it’s multimillion dollar ad spend in North Carolina in support of Michael Whatley, the GOP nominee for the open US Senate seat, according to multiple reports.
Democrats are hoping to flip the Tar Heel state in the upcoming midterm elections, where they need to net four seats in order to reclaim control of the Senate. Roy Cooper, North Carolina’s former governor, is the Democratic nominee and is leading Whatley in every poll, in some cases by double digits.
The SLF initially announced a $71m investment in the North Carolina race back in April – noting that Whatley – the former chair of the Republican National Committee with backing from Donald Trump – was a “battle-tested leader”. Semafor first reported the news that SLF shifting its spending priority, and is now reserving a seven-figure sum for the Senate race in Kansas – which has become increasingly competitive as Trump’s approval rating hits a record low nationwide.
While a Democrat hasn’t won a Senate seat in the Sunflower state in almost a century, the race between Republican incumbent Roger Marshall and his Democratic challenger, pastor Adam Hamilton, has become more of a concern for the GOP. The Cook Political Report, a prominent election forecaster, downgraded the competition from “leans Republican” to “likely Republican” at the end of September.

articles.title: Ukrainian forces reportedly strike oil facilities in Russia's Volgograd, Samara regions
articles.body:
Ukrainian forces strike oil facilities in Russia's Volgograd, Samara regions, General Staff says
Ukrainian forces struck oil infrastructure in Russia's Volgograd and Samara oblasts overnight, Ukraine's General Staff said on Oct. 2.
The General Staff reported fires and explosions at the targeted facilities, including 'Lukoil-Volgogradneftepererabotka' in Volgograd Oblast and the 'Samara' line-production control station near the settlement of Prosvet in Samara Oblast.
President Volodymyr Zelensky said on Oct. 2 that "successful operations" were carried out in the Black Sea and in Russia's Voronezh, Nizhny Novgorod, Volgograd, Samara, and Krasnodar regions. Airfields, industrial facilities, oil refineries, a missile and space center, and an ammunition depot belonging to the Russian forces were targeted over the last day.
"We are giving justified responses to Russia's escalation with our own long-range sanctions. Important results are achieved practically every day," Zelensky wrote on X.
Ukrainian activist Serhii Sternenko and the Exilenova Plus monitoring channel had previously identified the targets as the Volgograd Oil Refinery and the Samara oil distribution station, a major oil-transport facility previously targeted by Ukrainian forces.
The Volgograd refinery, owned by Russian energy giant Lukoil, is one of the country's largest oil-processing facilities, with an annual capacity of roughly 15 million metric tons of crude oil.
Ukrainian forces have repeatedly targeted the refinery during the full-scale war, including strikes earlier this year that damaged primary and secondary refining units and temporarily halted production.
The Samara oil distribution station near the settlement of Prosvet plays an important role in Russia's oil transportation network. The facility blends different grades of crude to produce Urals, Russia's main oil export blend.
Ukrainian drones previously struck the Samara station in April, causing a large fire and damaging five crude oil tanks, each with a capacity of 20,000 cubic meters, a source in the Security Service of Ukraine told the Kyiv Independent at the time.
President Volodymyr Zelensky said on Oct. 1 that Ukrainian forces had successfully struck an oil facility in Samara Oblast as part of a series of long-range attacks on Russian military and energy targets.
Ukraine has intensified strikes against Russian oil refineries, depots, and transportation infrastructure in recent months in an effort to disrupt fuel supplies to the Russian military and reduce Moscow's energy revenues.

articles.title: Zelenskyy expects 400 jet-powered drone interceptors to be produced in October, but their effectiveness varies
articles.body:
Zelenskyy expects 400 jet-powered drone interceptors to be produced in October, but their effectiveness varies
President Volodymyr Zelenskyy says Ukraine could produce around 400 units of one model of high-speed interceptor drone for countering Russian jet-powered drones as early as October, but there are questions over their effectiveness.
Source: Zelenskyy in an interview with the Financial Times, as cited by the president's press service
Details: Zelenskyy said F-16 fighter jets currently destroy 50-60% of jet-powered drones. This is one method, and Ukraine is working extensively to obtain weapons for the F-16s. The second method is high-speed interceptors. Ukraine is currently testing five interceptor models.
However, their effectiveness is problematic: it is 70% one day and 30% the next. Therefore, the answer to the question "When can we scale up the production?" is that Ukraine does not have billions to produce a million ineffective interceptors.
The main issue is the engines. Zelenskyy said Ukraine imports a lot and produces some itself, but these volumes are insufficient.

articles.title: U.S. in mega deal to build more long-range anti-air missiles
articles.body:
The U.S. Navy has awarded Raytheon a five-year contract worth up to $24.4 billion to accelerate production of the Standard Missile-6, its principal long-range anti-air and anti-surface weapon.
Announced on 1 October by Acting Secretary of the Navy Hung Cao, the multi-year procurement agreement includes two additional option years. The U.S. Navy says the long-term commitment is intended to give the RTX business the stability and predictability needed to expand production capacity, while delivering cost savings through a negotiated deal rather than year-by-year buys.
“Maritime strength demands weapons at speed and scale,” Cao said in the release. “This investment expands production and delivers the firepower our warfighters need to fight, win, and come home safe.”
The SM-6 has become one of the most versatile weapons in the surface fleet’s inventory. Fired from the Mk 41 Vertical Launch System aboard Arleigh Burke-class destroyers and Ticonderoga-class cruisers, it can engage aircraft, cruise missiles and ballistic missiles in their terminal phase, and can also be used against surface ships. Its active radar seeker allows it to engage targets beyond the horizon of the launching ship when cued by other sensors, a key element of the U.S. Navy’s Cooperative Engagement Capability. U.S. warships have fired SM-6s in combat during operations in the Red Sea and Middle East since late 2023, including against Houthi anti-ship missiles, drawing down stocks of a weapon that costs several million dollars per round.
Adm. Daryl Caudle, Chief of Naval Operations, linked the contract directly to the size of the fleet’s magazines. “Combat credibility depends on having enough weapons, produced at the speed and scale the Fleet requires,” he said. “This SM-6 award gives industry the demand signal and stability to expand production, strengthen the munitions industrial base, and build the magazine depth our Fleet needs. That is the Foundry delivering for the Fleet – and ensuring our Sailors have the combat power to fight and win.”
The award is being managed by the U.S. Navy’s Portfolio Acquisition Executive (PAE) Munitions, an organisation responsible for the development, procurement and delivery of naval munitions and strike capabilities. It follows a recent Tomahawk contract, which the service describes as part of the same effort to speed up weapons production across the portfolio.
“This award demonstrates what is possible when the Department leverages innovative acquisition approaches to deliver capability at the speed of relevance,” said Van Hendrey, Portfolio Acquisition Executive for Munitions. “Through PAE Munitions, we are bringing together the authorities, resources, and partnerships needed to accelerate production, reduce costs, and strengthen the industrial base that supports our warfighters.”
Raytheon produces the SM-6 at its facilities in Tucson, Arizona, with final assembly at Redstone Arsenal in Huntsville, Alabama. The missile has also been cleared for export to a number of U.S. allies, with Japan and Australia among the nations to have pursued it for their own air defence destroyers.
According to the U.S. Navy, the agreement will support a larger workforce, higher manufacturing throughput and stronger supply chains for the missile, as part of a wider push to rebuild the defence industrial base and keep Navy and Marine Corps forces supplied with advanced weapons.

articles.title: US looks to expand use of canoe-sized drones to deter migrant crossings
articles.body:
US looks to expand use of canoe-sized drones to deter migrant crossings
WASHINGTON, Oct 2 - The Pentagon may expand its use of autonomous surveillance boats on the Rio Grande and in the Gulf of Mexico after the canoe-sized vessels helped authorities detect and deter illegal border crossings and narcotics trafficking during a pilot program that began in January, a US official said.
The unmanned surface vessels, built by San Diego-based startup Seasats, patrol the river for long periods without crews and are part of a growing push by the military and law enforcement agencies to use relatively inexpensive, autonomous systems for surveillance and security missions.
The border mission also highlights how a new generation of venture-backed defense startups is positioned to win business once dominated by traditional contractors, as the Pentagon looks for faster, cheaper ways to deploy emerging technologies that can operate around-the-clock.
Defense officials are studying whether the boats, which draw power from solar panels, could be deployed more widely as part of broader efforts to monitor remote stretches of the Rio Grande. Aside from Seasats, companies named Saronic, Saildrone and Splash provide similar marine drones.
Defense officials want to increase the robotic fleet from its current test group of 10 vessels by as many as 50 to relieve the strain on Coast Guard cutters and crewed aircraft patrolling the border with Mexico as part of President Donald Trump's crackdown on illegal immigration.
Maritime drones are "cost-effective solutions to interdict and put people in these areas that narco traffickers are now moving towards," said M. Roosevelt Ditlevson, assistant secretary of defense for Homeland Defense and Americas Security Affairs.
Small drones and other unmanned platforms have proliferated across the US military in recent years after their repeated successes in the war in Ukraine.
DRONES CAN OPERATE FOR MONTHS
Seasats' 11-foot, 340-pound Lightfish is a low-profile autonomous vessel that costs roughly $240,000 and can be launched from a boat ramp or the back of a pickup truck. The drone can operate for months at a time in rough seas.
The vessels carry sensors — including electro-optical, infrared and sonar sensors — that feed real-time tracking data directly into military software networks, including Palantir Technologies' Maven Smart System and Anduril Industries' Fortress platform, alerting Customs and Border Protection and Coast Guard units.
The Pentagon said that in an average month, the Lightfish drones have assisted in 452 detections, 350 apprehensions and 100 turnbacks, which refer to when a group of people abort a border crossing attempt after realizing they have been discovered.
They "see that the vessel is waiting there for them, and they know that they've basically been found out," Ditlevson said.
The drone maker gained international attention in July when Reuters reported that a commercial Lightfish vessel operating inside the Philippines' exclusive economic zone navigated close enough to a Chinese People's Liberation Army Navy guided-missile destroyer to capture detailed close-up video, demonstrating how low-cost autonomous craft can monitor multibillion-dollar military assets.
With continued success, Ditlevson said Lightfish orders could rise by 50 boats and potentially also operate in the Gulf of Mexico, forming a radar fence between Texas and Key West. But Ditlevson said use will expand in increments, exploring different technologies.
"We're agnostic to the vendor. We want the best technology," he told Reuters in an interview.
Seasats Chief Executive Mike Flanigan said uncrewed systems provide persistent coverage that traditional, fuel-heavy assets cannot match.
"A plane or a ship might go really far really fast, but if you say, 'I want to keep that Boeing 737 over a patch of ocean for a day,' it just can't do it," Flanigan said. "The boat doesn't cover nearly as much territory as fast, but it can stay there for months at a time, which is the key differentiator for these security and monitoring applications."
As tighter border security and targeted military operations have reduced drug smuggling routes, cartels have increasingly pushed into coastal waterways and near-coastal regions. The expanded drone use in the Gulf of Mexico is a precursor to testing the vessels in the harsher seas of the Pacific Ocean near San Diego. REUTERS

articles.title: South Korea unveils new laser combat vehicle
articles.body:
- South Korea publicly showed its Cheongwang Block 2 8x8 laser vehicle and a 100-kW towed laser prototype during Armed Forces Day events on Oct. 1.
- In a live demonstration, the Cheongwang Block 1 shot down two target drones, while two others crashed or were brought down before engagement.
South Korea put its Cheongwang laser weapons on public display for its 78th Armed Forces Day on Oct. 1, showing two new prototypes for the first time, but a live demonstration of the system already in service ran into trouble before the laser burned two target drones out of the sky.
The new hardware included the Cheongwang Block 2, a prototype laser combat vehicle built on an 8×8 wheeled armored chassis, and a prototype 100-kW towed high-energy laser designed to shoot down incoming rockets, artillery shells and mortar rounds. South Korea has not said how far along either program is or when they could enter service.
The demonstration at Gyeryongdae, the military headquarters complex in South Chungcheong province, used the 20-kW Cheongwang Block 1, a fixed-site laser that has been in service since late 2024. Four target drones were prepared. The first crashed on takeoff after a gust of wind damaged the fiber-optic cable used to control it. The second could not complete its flight in poor weather and flew outside the designated safety zone, so the military cut its power and brought it down.
The remaining two drones flew into the laser’s engagement area, and Cheongwang shot both down, setting them on fire as they fell trailing black smoke. Because the other two never reached the laser, the demonstration does not show how well the system would perform against a larger group of drones or in tougher conditions.
Cheongwang works by holding a high-powered fiber laser on a small drone until the heat damages its airframe or key parts and it can no longer fly. The main attraction for militaries is cost. Hanwha Systems, which helped build the system, has put the cost of a single laser shot at about 2,000 won, roughly $1.40, compared with interceptor missiles that can cost hundreds of thousands of dollars or more. That figure covers only the electricity for a shot, not the cost of buying and maintaining the system, and a laser still needs enough power and cooling to keep firing.
The Block 1 was developed under South Korea’s Agency for Defense Development, making South Korea one of a small number of countries able to build its own laser weapon. South Korean officials say replacing an imported part, the laser oscillator that generates the beam, with a domestic one raised the system’s local content from 76% to 90% and increased its output from 20 kW to 30 kW. They also said the upgrade cut the time needed to bring down a small rotary-wing drone from two to four seconds to one to two, and for a fixed-wing drone from over 10 seconds to a few seconds. It is not clear whether the laser used in the Oct. 1 demonstration had the new oscillator.
The setbacks were not the first for South Korea’s unmanned systems at public events this year. On Sept. 16, several civilian drones, including a jet-powered one, crashed during an unmanned technology demonstration hosted by the Ministry of National Defense. In August, two medium-sized loitering munitions crashed into the sea during live-fire tests by the Republic of Korea Navy and the Agency for Defense Development aboard the amphibious assault ship ROKS Marado.
President Lee Jae-myung said at the Armed Forces Day ceremony that the government would speed up development of high-energy laser interceptors and artificial intelligence-based command and control systems.

articles.title: DARPA wants AI built into running its biotech research
articles.body:
- DARPA awarded Systems Planning and Analysis a $10.9 million task order to support management of its new and ongoing biotechnology programs through October 2031.
- The order calls for AI-enabled support, drew three offers, and obligated $3.9 million in fiscal 2026 research funds at award.
The Defense Advanced Research Projects Agency, the Pentagon’s research arm that funds high-risk military technology, has hired Systems Planning and Analysis to help manage its biotechnology programs, and it wants artificial intelligence built into how that work is done.
The Alexandria, Virginia-based company received a $10.9 million task order for operational and program support services, the U.S. Department of War said. The order covers technical, administrative, programmatic and financial management of new and ongoing biotechnology programs, carried out in what the notice calls an “AI-augmented, -integrated, and -enabled manner.”
The notice does not explain what that means in practice. It does not say which tasks AI tools would handle, which tools would be used, or whether DARPA requires specific software.
Work will take place in Arlington, Virginia, where DARPA has its headquarters, and is expected to run through October 2031. DARPA obligated $3.9 million in fiscal 2026 research, development, test and evaluation funds at award. The order was competed, and three companies submitted offers.
The deal is a cost-plus-fixed-fee and award-fee order. SPA will be reimbursed for its costs and paid a fixed fee, plus an additional fee that depends on how DARPA rates its performance.
DARPA has no labs of its own. Its program managers fund outside teams at universities, laboratories and companies, and lean on support contractors for engineering, science, financial management, administrative and acquisition work. That support role is what SPA will fill for the biotechnology portfolio.
The notice does not name the DARPA office involved. The agency’s biotechnology research is run by its Biological Technologies Office, whose most recent office-wide solicitation, issued in October 2025, sought proposals in AI and machine learning for biology, combat casualty care, human performance under extreme stress, and bio-inspired materials and sensors. That solicitation stopped accepting proposals on Sept. 30.
SPA has done this kind of work for DARPA before. In 2023, it was one of six companies, along with Booz Allen Hamilton, ManTech, Amentum, ECS and Strategic Analysis, selected for DARPA’s Technical and Analytical Support Services II contract, a five-year vehicle with a combined $1.25 billion ceiling covering advisory work for all of the agency’s technical and support offices. DARPA received 12 offers for that contract.
Earlier this year, SPA won a five-year, $151.4 million contract to provide scientific, engineering and technical assistance to DARPA’s Information Innovation Office, which runs the agency’s AI and cyber programs. The company said at the time that it had supported DARPA for more than 17 years.
Founded in 1972, SPA employs nearly 3,000 people and is owned by private equity firm Arlington Capital Partners. Much of its work is analysis and engineering for the U.S. Navy, including the Strategic Systems Programs office that manages the service’s submarine-launched ballistic missiles.

articles.title: Poland is preparing a law on the state’s full readiness in the event of war - media
articles.body:
Poland is preparing a law on the state’s full readiness in the event of war - media
Kyiv • UNN
Poland’s Ministry of National Defence has drafted a bill to coordinate defence management and speed up the deployment of troops to a state of war. The document is undergoing consultations.
Poland is preparing a bill on the state’s full readiness in the event of war. The bill aims to streamline the national defense management system and accelerate the process of redeploying troops to critical locations. Rzeczpospolita reports on October 2, UNN writes.
Details
The Polish Ministry of Defense has reportedly drafted a bill on national defense readiness. According to the publication, until recently the title itself included the phrase "on the state’s defensive readiness for war." The bill is currently at the stage of interministerial consultations.
The country’s Ministry of Defense confirmed to Rzeczpospolita that work on such a bill is ongoing. According to the information, the aim is "to strengthen the defense capabilities of the Republic of Poland, improve cooperation between the armed forces and services responsible for internal security, and adapt existing legislation to modern threats, including hybrid, cyber, and disinformation threats."
"This is the preparation of the state for the pre-war period, which Prime Minister Tusk spoke about some time ago," said a source connected with the presidential center. It is reportedly intended to fill the gap between the functioning of the state in peacetime and the formal introduction of martial law.
Its aim is also to "organize organizational and legal arrangements and increase the readiness of public administration bodies to perform tasks during a state of permanent and full defensive readiness of the state, in particular by clarifying the duties and competencies of the authorities." The Polish Ministry of Defense notes that currently, decisions concerning the preparation of the state for defense and the functioning of the defense management system are scattered across several resolutions of the country’s Council of Ministers issued after the adoption of the Homeland Defense Act in the spring of 2022.
"This regulatory model makes it difficult to ensure regulatory consistency and a unified approach to the performance of defense tasks by public administration bodies and other entities participating in the state’s defense system. Another significant problem is the scope of issues currently regulated at the level of subordinate legislation. Some existing provisions directly concern the tasks, competencies, and responsibilities of public administration bodies and other entities performing defense tasks, which justifies regulating them by law," the Polish Ministry of Defense stated.
The purpose of the law is to increase the readiness of state institutions for the threat of war
The bill aims to streamline the state defense management system and improve the readiness of public administration to perform tasks in a state of permanent and full defensive readiness, that is, even before the official declaration of martial law. Among other things, this will allow the earlier deployment of troops, including allied forces, link Poland’s Defense Response Plan with the NATO Response System, and prepare infrastructure.
The law will also expand the number of organizations participating in the permanent service system and the national defense management system, regulate the rules governing the work of civilian officials in command positions with limited leave to return home, amend the planning of non-war operational activities, and amend documentation concerning defense programs. Amendments will also be made to the rules for training, defense courses, and defense exercises.
According to the Polish Ministry of Defense, "due to the complex legislative process, it is currently unknown when the bill will be submitted to the Sejm." The publication’s conclusions indicate that the National Security Bureau (BBN) is also awaiting the submission of such a bill.

The list includes Artur Orlov, chairman of the board of the Movement of the First, a Russian state-backed social movement for children and young people. Orlov is a Russian officer, tank battalion commander and combatant in the war against Ukraine. Russian ruler Vladimir Putin appointed him to head the movement in 2024.
Five heads of the movement's regional branches in the temporarily occupied territories of Donetsk, Luhansk, Kherson and Zaporizhzhia oblasts and Crimea have also been sanctioned:
- Denis Chernobai
- Riyal Aliyev
- Aleksei Lavrentyev
- Viktoria Kostromina
- Yekaterina Kozyr.
Russia established the Movement of the First in 2022 on Putin's initiative as one of the tools for militarising children. According to a report by the OSCE Moscow Mechanism expert mission, it has more than 344,000 members in the occupied territories alone.
The list also includes Yelena Milskaya, chair of the board of trustees of Russia's National Centre for Assistance to Missing and Affected Children.
Defence Intelligence of Ukraine has information that in October 2022 she used the centre's volunteers as cover for the mass abduction and illegal deportation of Ukrainian children, including orphans, from the occupied territories of Ukraine to Krasnodar Krai via Crimea.
At least three of the seven people – Orlov, Chernobai and Milskaya – have been sanctioned by Canada, while Milskaya has also been sanctioned by the EU.
"The Movement of the First in the occupied territories is not about children's clubs. It is a conveyor belt through which Russia turns Ukrainian children into Russian soldiers for a war against their own homeland. Britain has named those who run this conveyor belt from Crimea to Luhansk. We thank the United Kingdom: everyone who commits crimes against Ukrainian children must know that they will be held personally accountable," said Maksym Maksymov, head of Bring Kids Back UA.
The UK government said millions of Ukrainian children in the occupied territories are subjected to Kremlin propaganda programmes, including weapons training and drone operation. Their aim is to strip children of their Ukrainian identity and prepare them to serve the state attacking their homeland.
Those on the sanctions list have had their assets frozen, been banned from entering the UK, faced restrictions on trust services and been prohibited from serving as directors of companies.
Background:
- Defence Intelligence of Ukraine previously named 10 people involved in the militarisation of Ukrainian children in the occupied territories. They included Artur Orlov, Aleksei Lavrentyev, Riyal Aliyev, Yekaterina Kozyr and Viktoria Kostromina.
- The Russian curriculum is being imposed on almost 2,000 schools in Ukraine's temporarily occupied territories, shaping the education of over 582,000 children. Schools are introducing new subjects that emphasise "patriotic" indoctrination and cultivate loyalty to the Russian state ideology.
- Russian forces are actively militarising children in the temporarily occupied territories of Ukraine, including through Yunarmiya and cadet classes. Another tool is the Movement of the First, which regularly holds military-style games and public ceremonies for handing out Russian IDs. More than 340,000 children and young people from the occupied territories are among its participants.

articles.title: UN urges more US action on Marshall Islands nuclear legacy
articles.body:
Breadcrumb
UN urges more US action on Marshall Islands nuclear fallout legacy
The United States needs to take additional steps to remedy the nuclear legacy in the Marshall Islands by providing healthcare and releasing secret archives, according to a UN report presented to its human rights body on Thursday.
The US, which administered the Pacific islands after World War Two, conducted 67 nuclear weapons tests in the Marshall Islands from 1946 to 1958, including "Castle Bravo" at Bikini Atoll in 1954
The human cost of these tests has been "severe and lasting", the UN human rights office report said, adding that there has not yet been a just settlement of the claims
"The damage needs to be repaired," Awa Dabo, Deputy High Commissioner for Human Rights, told the UN Human Rights Council in Geneva
The UN cited examples of the ongoing impact, such as elevated levels of cancer, displacement from contaminated areas and lasting social stigmas affecting exposed persons who are referred to as "poison people"
The report called for the US to provide remedy in the form of healthcare and to declassify all information pertaining to the nuclear legacy
The US State Department said it had already reached a full and final settlement of all claims with the Marshall Islands in 1986 and said it continues to provide medical and cancer assistance and environmental monitoring programmes for those affected
"The United States has recognised the effects of its nuclear testing program and has accepted and acted on its responsibility to the citizens of the Republic of the Marshall Islands," the State Department said.
Marshallese residents, including Alson Kelen who was displaced from Bikini and lost both parents to cancer, addressed the council and called for a meaningful resolution to the legacy
The Marshall Islands' representative, Senator David Anitok, told the UN body: "The continued denial of an effective remedy has forced us to come before this Council to ask for help"
Washington disengaged from the UN Human Rights Council last year, alleging an anti-Israel bias, and its seat was left empty on Thursday

articles.title: Kiev trying to spark war on Korean peninsula – Seoul
articles.body:
Kiev trying to spark war on Korean peninsula – Seoul
South Korea has accused Ukraine of trying to spark war on the Korean Peninsula, with President Lee Jae-myung threatening a response unless Kiev apologizes for breaching a confidentiality agreement.
Vladimir Zelensky announced publicly last week that Ukraine had transferred two North Korean prisoners to South Korea. Seoul says the arrangement was supposed to remain secret, but Kiev has denied that claim.
Writing on X on Friday, Lee said Ukraine had initially requested secrecy, then disclosed the transfer unilaterally and made him look like “a liar” by denying the agreement.
He further accused Kiev of responding to demands for an apology by trying to shift the conversation to an imminent military clash between North and South Korea, describing its conduct as “attempting to provoke a war on the Korean Peninsula.”
“If the refusal to acknowledge the facts and issue a public apology continues, we will take additional measures,” Lee warned, stressing that South Korea’s national dignity is at stake.
The dispute began with Zelensky’s September 23 address to the UN General Assembly, when he announced the transfer of the North Korean soldiers and said it was “not easy to capture them alive.” The servicemen were reportedly taken prisoner in January 2025 in Russia’s Kursk Region, where North Korean troops helped repel a Ukrainian incursion.
According to Seoul, Kiev initially sought secrecy to avoid domestic criticism for giving up prisoners who could have been exchanged for captured Ukrainians. South Korea also cited the safety of the soldiers and their families, alongside sensitive diplomatic and security concerns.
Zelensky adviser Dmitry Litvin responded to Seoul’s apology demands by denying any secrecy agreement existed, prompting South Korea to summon Ukraine’s acting ambassador on September 28.
Ukrainian Foreign Minister Andrey Sibiga subsequently tried to downplay the falling out, calling it a “diplomatic misunderstanding” and said he was working to resolve it.
South Korea has provided the country with humanitarian and financial assistance since 2022 and pledged another $100 million in July, but has drawn the line at weapons deliveries. Lee did not specified what measures he would take, but analyst Cho Han-bum told Reuters they would most likely involve assistance programs.
The Zelensky government has repeatedly clashed with countries providing substantial support throughout the conflict. In Poland, Ukraine’s continued glorification of nationalist forces responsible for massacring Poles has provoked outrage and demands from politicians to halt free weapons deliveries despite Warsaw’s extensive assistance.
Public enthusiasm for aid has also shown signs of weakening in recent years, including in Germany, where polling this year found declining support for increased military assistance. Earlier surveys in France and Italy also revealed divisions over continued support for Kiev.

articles.title: NYT reveals Russian plan to attack Ukraine's energy system
articles.body:
NYT reveals Russian plan to attack Ukraine's energy system
Russia plans to disable Ukraine's energy system in three stages. This is according to a plan published by journalists based on information intercepted by Ukraine.
Source: The New York Times
Details: The plan lays out three stages of attacks.
The first is to disable substations near Ukraine's western borders that import electricity from Europe. The second is to disable hydroelectric power plants. The third is to disconnect Ukraine's three operating nuclear power plants: Khmelnytskyi, Rivne and Pivdennoukrainsk.
Russia plans to use up to 1,000 missiles, drones and aerial bombs. The targets include substations, thermal power plants, hydroelectric power plants, boiler houses and other energy infrastructure.
The ultimate goal is to cut major Ukrainian cities off from electricity, heating and water supplies, potentially causing a humanitarian crisis.
Kyiv, Kharkiv and Odesa have been identified as the main targets. Russian forces plan to cut electricity supplies to these cities by 90%, reduce heating supplies by up to 90%, and seriously disrupt their sewage systems.
However, The New York Times notes that it is unclear whether Russia will follow the strategy outlined in the plan and whether it would succeed if it did.
Background: Ukrainian officials have said they are concerned that Ukraine does not have a sufficiently developed plan in case of large-scale Russian strikes on water supply systems.

articles.title: Half of Ukraine's F-16s undergoing repairs in Europe, with returns delayed – Zelenskyy
articles.body:
Half of Ukraine's F-16s undergoing repairs in Europe, with returns delayed – Zelenskyy
President Volodymyr Zelenskyy has said that around half of Ukraine's F-16 fighter jets spend extended periods in Europe undergoing repairs and maintenance. He said the return of some aircraft is delayed for so long that Ukraine loses valuable time when the fighter jets are most needed to protect its airspace.
Source: Zelenskyy in an interview with the Financial Times, as reported by European Pravda
Details: The president spoke about the difficulties Ukraine faces in countering Russian drone attacks. He said F-16 fighter jets had proved effective against new Russian jet-powered drones, but too many of the aircraft – around half – spend extended periods in Europe undergoing repairs and maintenance.
Zelenskyy also said Kyiv was seeking help from its Western partners to move more maintenance work to Ukraine, arguing that keeping the aircraft closer to the theatre of operations would allow them to be returned to service more quickly.
He stressed that efforts to keep pace with Russian drone capabilities were facing obstacles, including a shortage of engines for interceptor drones.
"Engines [are] the key, we really import a lot of engines. There are some engines of our production, but not enough," Zelenskyy said.
Background:
- In late September, Zelenskyy announced an agreement with Belgium under which Ukraine is to receive three F-16 fighter jets by the end of the year.
- He also recently told the Norwegian prime minister about Ukraine's need for air defence systems and support for its F-16 fleet.

articles.title: North Korea launches ballistic missile as tensions grow over border mine blasts
articles.body:
North Korea has fired at least one ballistic missile, Seoul's military said, a day after Pyongyang called the South "despicable" for demanding an apology over a blast in the demilitarised zone that wounded three of its soldiers.
"Our military detected a ballistic missile launched from the Wonsan area of North Korea toward the East Sea," Seoul's Joint Chiefs of Staff said on Saturday, referring to the body of water also known as the Sea of Japan.
Pyongyang has denied being behind the landmine blast last month inside the Demilitarised Zone (DMZ), the heavily mined buffer dividing the two Koreas since their 1953 armistice.
Seoul as well as the US-led United Nations Command said the blast was caused by North Korean mines laid on the South Korean side of the border.
South Korea's military demanded an official apology from the North earlier this week.
A day later, South Korea's dovish President Lee Jae Myung urged Pyongyang to return to dialogue.
Kim Yo Jong, the powerful sister of North Korea's leader, called Seoul "despicable" Friday, once again denying Pyongyang was behind the blasts.
The test came amid heightened tensions between the countries following land mine blasts that injured three South Korean soldiers last month. South Korea and the US-led UN Command have said the blasts were caused by North Korean mines.

articles.title: US delivers F-16V fighter jets to Taiwan as island eyes threat from China
articles.body:
US delivers F-16V fighter jets to Taiwan as island eyes threat from China
Amid threats from China, Taipai is growing concerned about the Trump administration’s commitment to arming the island.
The United States has delivered two F-16V Block 70 fighter jets to Taiwan as the island seeks to build its defence capabilities to deter a feared attack by China.
The aircraft, built by US defence contractor Lockheed Martin, are part of an $8bn deal for 66 F-16Vs approved during President Donald Trump’s first term. They landed on Friday following months of delay due to repeated requests from Beijing to the US to stop arming Taiwan.
The jets, which flew via Hawaii and Guam, touched down at noon (04:00 GMT) local time. They arrived a week after Trump met Chinese President Xi Jinping in Washington.
Taiwan is eyeing a rising military threat from Beijing, which claims the democratically governed island as its own territory.
“Of course we won’t only have delivered these two [F-16Vs] by the end of the year,” Minister of National Defence Wellington Koo said.
The arrival of the planes comes amid growing concern in Taiwan about the Trump administration’s commitment to arming Taipei.
The US is bound by law to provide Taiwan with the means to defend itself, but the two have no formal diplomatic relations.
Trump said in May, after meeting Xi in Beijing, that he was holding out on a new $14bn package for Taiwan, though he did approve one worth $11bn in December 2025.
Washington has said there has been no change in policy.
“We continue standing with friends and allies across the Indo-Pacific to advance our shared prosperity, security, and values — that includes Taiwan,” a US State Department spokesperson said when asked about the delivery.
The F-16Vs, which received an upgrade in 2023, have advanced avionics, weapons and radar systems to better counter the Chinese air force, including its J-20 stealth fighters.
However, Washington has been unwilling to provide Taiwan with its most advanced fighters, such as the F-22 or F-35.

articles.title: US withdrawal from Iraq marks new Phase for Resistance Front: Qaani
articles.body:
US withdrawal from Iraq marks new Phase for Resistance Front: Qaani
TEHRAN– Brigadier General Esmaeil Qaani, commander of Iran’s Islamic Revolution Guard Corps (IRGC) Quds Force, has described the United States’ withdrawal from Iraq and its failure to achieve its objectives in the war against Iran as significant setbacks for Washington, saying the developments signal a new phase for the Resistance Front across West Asia.
Speaking in a ceremony in Tehran on Thursday night, marking the second anniversary of the martyrdom of Hezbollah leaders Sayyed Hassan Nasrallah and Sayyed Hashem Safieddine, Qaani said Washington had underestimated Iran’s capacity to withstand military pressure and had failed to achieve its intended objectives.
He said US officials had expected to force Iran to surrender within four days, or two weeks at most, but encountered a reality far removed from their calculations.
Qaani attributed Iran’s ability to withstand the assault to the resilience of its people, their continued presence on the scene and the country’s military preparedness. He said these factors, alongside developments across the region, were contributing to a new phase in the meaning and practice of resistance.
The Quds Force commander also emphasized that Iran had continued to support regional movements and peoples under pressure despite the war, adding that Tehran’s commitment to its allies and to the cause of oppressed nations remained unchanged.
Iraq's sovereignty and the US military withdrawal
Addressing the withdrawal of US forces from Iraq, Qaani said the development reflected the determination of the Iraqi people and the role played by resistance groups in opposing the American military presence.
He said the Iraqi people were celebrating a victory achieved through national resistance and the efforts of the Resistance Front.
Qaani called for closer coordination among Iraq’s government, state institutions and resistance groups, arguing that such cooperation could strengthen the country’s sovereignty, stability and capacity to determine its own future.
He also said the remaining elements of the US presence in the region should be removed, adding that Washington was seeking to downplay the significance of its withdrawal from Iraq by focusing public attention on other issues, including aircraft movements.
The withdrawal marks a significant development in the long history of the US military presence in Iraq. American forces invaded the country in March 2003, overthrowing Saddam Hussein’s government.
Although US-led coalition forces withdrew in December 2011, American troops returned in 2014 as part of the campaign against Daesh, the Takfiri terrorist group that had seized large areas of Iraq and Syria.
According to the reports, the latest withdrawal was completed under an agreement between Baghdad and Washington to end the US-led military mission in Iraq. Iraqi Prime Minister Ali al-Zaidi described the handover as the beginning of a new phase centered on national sovereignty, stronger state institutions and balanced partnerships with other countries.
Qaani presented the development as part of a broader regional shift, arguing that the consequences of the US military presence and its eventual withdrawal extended beyond Iraq.
 
Iran stood firm despite US-Israeli attack
Turning to the war against Iran, Qaani said the United States and Israel had launched their joint attack after concluding that earlier methods of exerting pressure, including diplomatic approaches and the use of intermediaries, had failed to achieve their objectives.
He said their expectation of securing Iran’s surrender within days had been overturned by the Iranian nation’s resistance and the country’s ability to withstand the assault.
According to Qaani, Iran remained steadfast under the guidance of the late Leader of the Islamic Revolution, Ayatollah Seyyed Ali Khamenei, and successive enemy plans failed to achieve their intended results.
He also recalled Ayatollah Khamenei’s emphasis on Muslim unity during Friday prayers held a week after Nasrallah’s martyrdom, saying the late Leader had stressed the importance of solidarity among Muslim nations and support for peoples facing aggression.
Qaani argued that threats against one nation should concern others across the Islamic world, warning that allowing aggression against one country to go unchallenged could expose other nations to similar pressure.
He called for strengthening a common front for defense, independence and dignity stretching from Afghanistan to Yemen and from Iran to Gaza and Lebanon.
The Iranian commander further said that, despite the pressures of war, Iran had not abandoned its regional partners or the peoples it considers to be victims of US and Israeli actions.
Emphasize on Hezbollah's continued military operations
Qaani also praised Hezbollah’s performance in Lebanon, describing the conflict as one of the most difficult wars the movement had faced since its establishment.
He rejected claims that the Lebanese resistance movement had been rendered incapable of fighting following the martyrdom of Nasrallah, Safieddine and other senior commanders, saying a new generation of fighters had continued operations against Israeli forces.
According to Qaani, Hezbollah fighters entered the battlefield shortly after the war began and continued fighting despite the loss of senior leaders. He cited an incident in which Hezbollah fighters reportedly targeted 20 Israeli tanks in a single night in a Lebanese village.
The Quds Force commander further stated that 373 Israeli tanks and armored personnel carriers had come under attack during the period in question, adding that at least one-third had been destroyed and another third damaged and forced out of the battlefield.
Qaani said the continuation of Hezbollah’s operations demonstrated that the movement retained its capacity to fight despite the extensive losses it had suffered in its leadership.
According to him, Israel had suffered unprecedented fatalities during the conflict compared with other periods in its history, adding that Israeli authorities were concealing the true scale of their casualties.
Referring to Hezbollah Secretary-General Sheikh Naim Qassem’s description of the movement’s fighting spirit as being inspired by Ashura and Karbala, Qaani said the resistance movement had continued along the path established by its martyred leaders.
Regional resistance and Muslim unity
 
Beyond Iraq and Lebanon, Qaani referred to developments involving Yemen’s resistance forces, stating that they had seized 5,400 square kilometers during the first phase of an operation and were close to capturing more than 1,000 additional square kilometers.
He said the various components of the Resistance Front had become more closely coordinated, with each contributing through calculated planning and actions that had taken their adversaries by surprise.
For Qaani, the significance of these developments lay not only in individual military operations but also in the wider political and strategic implications of cooperation among regional resistance movements.
He concluded that the Resistance Front would continue its activities with honor and determination, drawing inspiration from the sacrifices of Nasrallah, Safieddine and other figures killed in the conflict.
The ceremony in Tehran brought together the themes that dominated Qaani’s remarks: Iran’s resistance to the US-Israeli military campaign, the implications of the US withdrawal from Iraq, Hezbollah’s continued operations in Lebanon and the importance of solidarity among Muslim nations.
His statements reflect Tehran’s broader regional outlook, which views foreign military deployments, the sovereignty of regional states, and the role of resistance movements as interconnected issues in the future security architecture of West Asia.

articles.title: Zelensky: Russia launched over 100 attack drones at Ukraine overnight, nearly 50 of them jet-powered
articles.body:
Zelensky: Russia launched over 100 attack drones at Ukraine overnight, nearly 50 of them jet-powered
According to Ukrinform, President Volodymyr Zelensky said this in a Facebook post.
"Last night, the Russians launched more than 100 attack drones at Ukraine, nearly 50 of them jet-powered. Our warriors neutralized most of them, but unfortunately, there were also hits. In Kyiv, 'Shaheds' struck the Pivdennyi Bridge several times. In the morning, a residential high-rise was hit. Tragically, one person was killed. My condolences to their family and loved ones. In Kherson, the Russians 'defeated' a kindergarten; in Kharkiv, they attacked a grocery store, and an institute and critical infrastructure were damaged," Zelensky said.
According to him, enemy strikes also hit apartment buildings in Kramatorsk and Sumy. The Dnipro, Odesa, Kharkiv, Kyiv, Poltava, and Rivne regions also came under attack. As of now, four people have been reported injured in the overnight Russian attack. Emergency services are working wherever they are needed.
"No matter how hard Moscow tries to fully localize the production of its drones and missiles, its ability to escalate remains critically dependent on foreign components. These are supply chains running from Europe, the United States, China, Japan, and many other countries. Most of these companies are well-known manufacturers, but their components still make their way to Russia," Zelensky said.
He stressed that every Russian drone can in fact be stopped while it is still on the production line.
"What is needed is the political will of these countries. If the Kremlin has chosen more strikes, sanctions must work and must be strengthened. Thank you to everyone who is helping.," Zelensky added.
As reported, public transport traffic on some bridges in Kyiv has been temporarily restricted due to overnight enemy attacks.
